emotion_lines.ANX: The anxiety you’re feeling right now, {name}, is a sign that your wish to protect what matters to you has gotten a little ahead of you.
emotion_lines.TIR: The exhaustion you’re feeling right now, {name}, isn’t laziness; it’s an honest signal from a body and mind that have been working hard for a long time.
emotion_lines.LON: The loneliness you’re feeling right now, {name}, means your wish to connect with someone is just that big.
emotion_lines.HUR: The hurt you’re feeling right now, {name}, shows how much that relationship matters to you.
emotion_lines.CON: The overwhelm you’re feeling right now, {name}, doesn’t mean you’re lost; it means you’re still drawing the map.
emotion_lines.SHA: The self-blame you’re feeling right now, {name}, also means your wish to do well is just that big.
emotion_lines.GRI: The sadness you’re feeling right now, {name}, is proof that you cared deeply about what you lost.
emotion_lines.HOP: The excitement and nerves you’re feeling right now, {name}, are a sign that your heart is moving toward a new beginning.

CAR_REST.title: Close one last file to mark the end of work
CAR_REST.how: When you finish work, tidy up your work files and leave only the first thing you’ll do tomorrow.
CAR_REST.why: When the end of work is marked where you can see it, it’s easier for your mind to switch from work mode to rest mode.

CAR_START.title: Write the smallest possible starting sentence
CAR_START.how: If there’s a task you’ve been putting off, rewrite the first step as a sentence you could start within one minute.
CAR_START.why: When the start shrinks to one minute, the pressure that kept you putting it off drops, and once you’ve touched it, the next step comes more easily.

CAR_CHOOSE.title: Pick one place to give your best and one place where “good enough” will do
CAR_CHOOSE.how: Think of the tasks and choices on your plate lately, and write down one place where you really want to give your best and one where “this is good enough” will do. It’s not about cutting corners; it’s about deciding where your energy goes.
CAR_CHOOSE.why: Giving your best everywhere wears you out fast. Instead of cutting corners, split things up so your best goes where it really matters.

CAR_CONNECT.title: Share it, even lightly, instead of carrying it alone
CAR_CONNECT.how: Pick one thing at work that’s been too much lately and share it in a sentence or two with a coworker you trust or someone close to you.
CAR_CONNECT.why: A worry you carry alone feels heavier than it is, so just saying it out loud splits the weight a little.

CAR_BOUNDARY.title: Before work, decide one line you’ll keep today
CAR_BOUNDARY.how: Within what you can manage, pick one after-work activity you want to protect, just for today.
CAR_BOUNDARY.why: When you set the line in the morning, you give away less of your own time even at the end of a busy day.

CAR_LETGO.title: Rewrite “I’m a ___ person” as “This time, I ___”
CAR_LETGO.how: Think of one thing that didn’t go the way you hoped, and if you have a sentence that judges all of you, like “I’m just not good enough,” write it down. Rewrite it as a judgment about an action, like “I didn’t have enough time to prepare for this presentation,” and add one thing you’d try differently next time. It’s fine to be honest when you judge the action.
CAR_LETGO.why: “This presentation fell short” and “I fall short as a person” are different things, so write the judgment about the work separately from you.

DIR_REST.title: Store a question that doesn’t have an answer yet
DIR_REST.how: Write down one worry you don’t have to settle right now, and pick a date to think about it again.
DIR_REST.why: Not every question needs an answer today, so storing one for a while gives your mind room to rest.

DIR_START.title: Shrink the plan until you’re 90% sure you can do it
DIR_START.how: Write down one thing you want to do this week and rate, as a percentage, how sure you are that you can pull it off. If it’s under 90%, cut the time or the amount and rewrite it, and on days you still don’t get to it, treat that as information for resizing, not as laziness.
DIR_START.why: When a plan is too big, the days you miss leave nothing but self-blame, so shrink it to what you can do and resize it on the days you miss.

DIR_CHOOSE.title: Ask “Whose standard is this?” about a goal you’re holding onto, and rewrite it in your own words
DIR_CHOOSE.how: Write down one goal you’ve been pouring energy into, and next to it, mark where that standard came from (parents, work, social media, or you). Then rewrite the goal once in your own words, like “In the life I want, ___ is enough.” You don’t have to change the goal; just checking whose it is is enough.
DIR_CHOOSE.why: You get to decide what a good life looks like, so start by checking whose standard your current goal is.

DIR_CONNECT.title: Hear, lightly, from someone who’s been there
DIR_CONNECT.how: Look up articles or videos from people who’ve already walked the path you’re interested in, or, if you can, ask one of them a quick question.
DIR_CONNECT.why: Real stories ease vague fears and make it less lonely to be figuring things out on your own.

DIR_BOUNDARY.title: Write down what someone you envy does, separately from your own worth
DIR_BOUNDARY.how: Write down one specific thing a person you envy does, and ask yourself, “Does that make them a better person than me?” Then write one thing you could learn from it, and one line on why it has nothing to do with your worth. You don’t have to make the envy go away.
DIR_BOUNDARY.why: What someone does is separate from their worth, so turn the envy into one thing you can learn and take with you.

DIR_LETGO.title: Put down one goal you don’t need to chase right now
DIR_LETGO.how: Instead of adding another goal, put down one goal you don’t need to aim at directly right now, and write down why.
DIR_LETGO.why: Taking one goal off your list frees up more of you for what’s left, and the more you get absorbed in meaningful work, the more naturally results tend to follow.

LOV_REST.title: Keep doing what fills you up, apart from the relationship
LOV_REST.how: Pick one activity that makes you happy regardless of the relationship, and do it once this week.
LOV_REST.why: When all your attention is on one person, you tire out quickly, so time that fills you up makes the relationship feel lighter too.

LOV_START.title: Prepare two questions for someone new
LOV_START.how: Write down two easy questions you could ask someone the first time you meet.
LOV_START.why: Having a few words ready eases first-meeting nerves and gives you a bit more courage to start the conversation.

LOV_CHOOSE.title: Know what you put first in a relationship, and use it to choose
LOV_CHOOSE.how: Write down the three things that matter most to you in a relationship, and use one of them as your guide for choices this week.
LOV_CHOOSE.why: When you know what you put first, the other person’s reactions shake you less, and choices within the relationship get easier.

LOV_CONNECT.title: Share one memory you made together
LOV_CONNECT.how: Send someone you like a short message about a good memory that just came to mind.
LOV_CONNECT.why: Remembering a good moment together connects you without pressure and warms things up a little.

LOV_BOUNDARY.title: Write down how often you like to be in touch
LOV_BOUNDARY.how: Write down how often you’re comfortable texting or talking and which situations feel like too much, then put together a sentence to explain it when you need to.
LOV_BOUNDARY.why: When you know the distance that feels right to you, you can be in a relationship without losing yourself.

LOV_LETGO.title: Rewrite what you said to yourself the way you’d say it to a close friend
LOV_LETGO.how: Write down one harsh thing you’ve been saying to yourself lately, and rewrite it gently, the way you’d say it to a close friend.
LOV_LETGO.why: When a relationship gets shaky, the voice that blames you tends to get louder, so just switching to kind words loosens things a little.

FAM_REST.title: Three breaths before you reply
FAM_REST.how: When a message from family feels like a lot, don’t answer right away: take three breaths, then decide for yourself when you’ll reply.
FAM_REST.why: Leaving a gap before you react lets you talk without getting swept up in emotion and while still protecting yourself.

FAM_START.title: A different opening line
FAM_START.how: If there’s a conversation that always slides into the same fight, try starting it with a different line this time, like “How have you been lately?”
FAM_START.why: When the start of a conversation changes, the familiar pattern of conflict can shift a little at a time too.

FAM_CHOOSE.title: My part and the part to share
FAM_CHOOSE.how: Make two columns for the family tasks on your plate right now: what you really have to do yourself, and what someone else could share.
FAM_CHOOSE.why: Once you can see where your responsibility ends, the weight of carrying everything alone gets lighter.

FAM_CONNECT.title: An easy 15 minutes
FAM_CONNECT.how: Spend an easy 15 minutes with one family member, like a walk or a cup of tea.
FAM_CONNECT.why: As time spent together adds up, more than words do, the warmth between you slowly rises.

FAM_BOUNDARY.title: One sentence that protects you
FAM_BOUNDARY.how: Have one sentence ready for when the comparisons or meddling start, like “I’d rather not talk about that right now.”
FAM_BOUNDARY.why: A sentence you’ve prepared helps you hold your line gently, even when emotions are running high.

FAM_LETGO.title: What you hoped for and what is
FAM_LETGO.how: Write down, side by side, what you hoped your family would be and what it is now, and give the feeling in that gap a one-word name.
FAM_LETGO.why: When you accept the gap between hope and reality, you can turn the energy you spent on what won’t change back toward yourself.

SOC_REST.title: Plan an evening with no one on purpose
SOC_REST.how: Keep one evening this week free of plans and save it just for yourself.
SOC_REST.why: The energy you spend around people sometimes refills when you’re alone, so a quiet evening makes the next get-together feel lighter.

SOC_START.title: Read one post in a community about a hobby you’re into
SOC_START.how: Read one announcement or recap in an online group for an activity you’re interested in, and get a feel for the atmosphere.
SOC_START.why: Getting a feel for the place before you step in lowers the bar for starting new connections.

SOC_CHOOSE.title: Write three lines about how you want to feel once a conflict is settled
SOC_CHOOSE.how: Pick one conflict that’s been putting you on edge lately, and write two or three lines about how you’d like to feel once it’s settled (for example, “leaving work feeling less tense”). From those, pick one line you can act on even if the other person doesn’t change, and try it this week.
SOC_CHOOSE.why: If you wait for the other person to change, you stay stuck, so start by writing down how you want to feel day to day.

SOC_CONNECT.title: Check in without asking for a reply
SOC_CONNECT.how: Send a light check-in to someone who’s been on your mind, and tell them they don’t need to reply.
SOC_CONNECT.why: A check-in without the pressure to reply keeps things easy on both sides and can reconnect a tie you thought had faded.

SOC_BOUNDARY.title: Decide in advance when you’ll head home
SOC_BOUNDARY.how: On days you’re seeing people you haven’t seen in a while, think ahead about a time to head home that you can keep comfortably.
SOC_BOUNDARY.why: Deciding on an end time in advance lets you enjoy the get-together more and keeps you from pushing on when you’re worn out.

SOC_LETGO.title: Put down the pressure to respond right away
SOC_LETGO.how: When it feels like you have to answer a message or request immediately, ask yourself whether it would be okay to wait about an hour.
SOC_LETGO.why: Trying to respond right away every time leaves your mind no room to rest, so allowing yourself to be a little late eases the tension in your relationships.

LIF_REST.title: A 30-minute bedtime routine
LIF_REST.how: Thirty minutes before bed, turn off your screens and do the same things in the same order: wash up, stretch, dim the lights.
LIF_REST.why: A routine in the same order tells your body “it’s time to rest now,” which makes it easier to fall asleep.

LIF_START.title: One daily anchor
LIF_START.how: Choose one habit to anchor your day, like a set wake-up time or breakfast, and keep it for just five days this week.
LIF_START.why: Once one small habit settles in, a daily rhythm that fell apart can come back together around it.

LIF_CHOOSE.title: Three columns for your money
LIF_CHOOSE.how: Split this month’s spending into three columns: “fixed costs / must-haves / could cut back.”
LIF_CHOOSE.why: When vague money worries are laid out as numbers, you start to see the parts you can actually choose.

LIF_CONNECT.title: Share one everyday worry
LIF_CONNECT.how: Tell someone you trust, briefly, about the one thing in your daily life that feels like the most right now.
LIF_CONNECT.why: Even a day-to-day worry you’ve carried alone can show a way forward once you say it out loud, or at least feel lighter.

LIF_BOUNDARY.title: The 24-hour cart rule
LIF_BOUNDARY.how: Make a rule: anything you want to buy goes in your cart, and you look at it again after 24 hours.
LIF_BOUNDARY.why: Giving it time makes it easier to tell a passing urge from a real need.

LIF_LETGO.title: Just one thing you can do
LIF_LETGO.how: Split your current worries about daily life into “things I can do this week / things I can’t do right now,” and do just one thing from the first list.
LIF_LETGO.why: When you put down the worries you can’t act on, you can gather your strength for what you can.

REST.title: Write down “why I can’t rest,” then rest for 10 minutes
REST.how: Think of a moment this week when work or chores kept you from resting, and write down your reasons why you “can’t rest”; then pick one time when 10 minutes of rest would be fine, and actually rest. If thoughts come up while you rest, just name them: “That’s a to-do thought.”
REST.why: Even the strength that keeps your days running wears out if you squeeze it too hard, so give 10 minutes to learning how to rest.

START.title: Pick a small thing you’d like to do again
START.how: Pick one activity you used to enjoy but have forgotten about, and just set a date to do it again.
START.why: An activity you’ve enjoyed before is easier to start, so setting a single date is enough to get you moving again.

CHOOSE.title: Get every worry out of your head, then pick only the two biggest
CHOOSE.how: Write down everything weighing on you as it comes to mind, group similar things together, and pick only the two that matter most. Move the rest to a “look at later” list. You don’t have to solve it all at once.
CHOOSE.why: When worries pile up all at once, they all feel heavy, so keep only the two biggest and set the rest down for now.

CONNECT.title: Keep a relationship going with a light check-in
CONNECT.how: Send a short one-line check-in to someone who’s been on your mind lately.
CONNECT.why: One light message keeps the tie between you going and eases the feeling of being alone a little.

BOUNDARY.title: Remember a recent time you were glad you said no
BOUNDARY.how: Think of one choice that protected your time, and write down what it protected.
BOUNDARY.why: Remembering a time it felt good to hold your line makes it easier to choose to protect yourself next time.

LETGO.title: On a shaky day, write one line: “How did I bounce back before?”
LETGO.how: On a day when you were getting better and then got shaky again, instead of “I’m back to square one,” write one line on “What helped last time things were like this?” Taking one step back after two or three forward is a natural part of the process, and trying one of the things you wrote down again today is enough.
LETGO.why: A shaky day doesn’t mean you’re back at the start, so remember how you bounced back before and try it again.

deadline_words: by the end of the week

near.title: The answer is close at hand
near.body: All three cards lean the same way, so the thread that untangles this worry is closer than you might think. You have the power to change what’s happening now, and The Key Ahead is already sitting where you can see it.

step.title: This untangles one step at a time
step.body: Because your old way of handling things has built up over a long time, this worry is more likely to loosen bit by bit than all at once. Habits that have set in take time to change, and as small changes add up along the way, things start to shift.

slow.title: This may not resolve right away
slow.body: This worry is tangled up with a lot of circumstances, so a clear answer may not show up right away. With this much tangled together, untangling it takes time too. Still, the power to notice where your energy is leaking out is on your side even now.

watch.title: There’s no need to rush this
watch.body: Right now, looking after the tired you comes before solving the worry. The weight you feel is this heavy because you’ve been trying hard for this long. Things keep moving even if you don’t rush to find an answer, and some things only become clear once a little of your strength comes back.

near_q.title: The answer on your side is close at hand
near_q.body: How this turns out depends on the other person’s feelings and the situation, so the cards don’t decide that answer for you. But looking only at your side, the thread is close at hand, and you still have plenty of strength to sort out your own feelings.

step_q.title: On your side, this untangles one step at a time
step_q.body: The outcome depends on the other person and the situation, so the cards don’t tell you in advance. On your side, things are more likely to sort themselves out bit by bit than all at once, and your heart needs time to settle accordingly.

slow_q.title: Your side may take time to sort out, too
slow_q.body: The outcome depends on the other person and the situation, and your own feelings may be hard to sort out right away too. The longer you wait, the easier it is for your mind to fixate on the outcome. Still, how you spend your days in the meantime is up to you, even now.

tone.deadline: This worry has a deadline, so what shapes how it goes is less a perfect answer and more the size of what you can actually get done by that day.
tone.other_locus: The outcome of this worry depends on another person or the situation, so what makes the difference is less the outcome and more where your heart rests in the meantime.

story_head.START: Your three cards show the path from the things you’ve been putting off to a small first step.
story_head.CHOOSE: Your three cards show the path from a crowd of options to the one you choose.
story_head.CONNECT: Your three cards show the path from a shaky relationship to the relationship you want.
story_head.REST: Your three cards show the path from days of just getting through to rest that refills you.
story_head.BOUNDARY: Your three cards show the path from weight you’ve held alone to a line that protects you.
story_head.LETGO: Your three cards show the path from what you’ve been holding onto to your next step.

apply_head.START: This worry starts to ease when you take even a small step yourself.
apply_head.CHOOSE: This worry starts to ease when you decide what you’ll choose.
apply_head.CONNECT: This worry starts to ease when you know what kind of relationship you want.
apply_head.REST: This worry starts to ease when you fill yourself back up first.
apply_head.BOUNDARY: This worry starts to ease when you sort out what to keep and what to put down.
apply_head.LETGO: This worry starts to ease when you accept what’s already happened.

story_p1.START_START: When there was a thing you wanted to do, you may often have put it off until you were “a little more ready,” or else jumped in before you’d thought it through. That pattern has only set in harder: the more things pile up unstarted, the more your frustration and impatience grow.
story_p1.START_CHOOSE: When there was a thing you wanted to do, you may often have put it off until you were “a little more ready,” or else jumped in before you’d thought it through. love_qsub.name: Is this a crush, a situationship, or real interest?
love_qsub.need_rule: CONNECT if the wish to get closer is central; CHOOSE if deciding whether to confess or make a move is central
love_qsub.reframe: The cards can't speak for that person's heart, but they can show the kind of closeness you, {name}, want right now, while every little signal sends your feelings back and forth.
love_qsub.caution: Don't state for sure whether the other person is interested

love_qsub.name: Left on read, slow replies, one-word texts
love_qsub.need_rule: CONNECT if they want to keep talking; REST if being tired of waiting is central
love_qsub.reframe: Rather than measuring that person's feelings by how fast they reply, you can first look after your own feelings, {name}, which shake while you wait.
love_qsub.caution: Don't advise texting more or cutting contact

love_qsub.name: Why they went quiet or ghosted
love_qsub.need_rule: LETGO if contact has already stopped and they're holding on to the reason; CONNECT if the wish to keep it going is still strong
love_qsub.reframe: Only that person knows why they drifted away without a word, but together we can look at what you, {name}, need after being left without an explanation.
love_qsub.caution: Don't feed “what did I do wrong” self-blame. Don't advise them to keep trying to make contact

love_qsub.name: Hot and cold, mixed signals, pulling away
love_qsub.need_rule: CONNECT if they want to protect the relationship; BOUNDARY if they're tired of adjusting and want to keep their own place
love_qsub.reframe: Rather than asking why that person pulls away and comes close again, you can look at what kind of distance feels comfortable to you, {name}, amid the hot and cold.
love_qsub.caution: Don't judge the other person with labels like “emotionally unavailable”

love_qsub.name: Avoiding labels, being kept on the hook, being tested
love_qsub.need_rule: CHOOSE if they're weighing whether to continue or end it; BOUNDARY if they hate being jerked around and want to draw a line
love_qsub.reframe: What to call this relationship is for the two of you to decide, but you, {name}, can decide now what you want from it.
love_qsub.caution: Don't label the other person as “a player keeping people on the hook”

love_qsub.name: Are they serious, or is it casual?
love_qsub.need_rule: CHOOSE if they're judging whether to trust and continue; CONNECT if the wish to go deeper is central
love_qsub.reframe: The cards can't confirm that person's sincerity, but they can help you name what you, {name}, need in order to feel trust in this relationship.
love_qsub.caution: If controlling signs like love bombing appear, run the violence check first

love_qsub.name: What a partner who doesn't show feelings really feels
love_qsub.need_rule: Mostly CONNECT
love_qsub.reframe: You can't measure love only by how much it's shown, but the cards can show when you, {name}, feel loved.

love_qsub.name: Interest after a blind date or first meeting
love_qsub.need_rule: CONNECT if they hope for another meeting; START if suggesting it first is central
love_qsub.reframe: Rather than how that person felt that day, you can start with what you, {name}, liked about the meeting.

love_qsub.name: Suspecting cheating or someone else
love_qsub.need_rule: CHOOSE if weighing whether to trust, check, or continue; BOUNDARY if setting the line they can live with is central
love_qsub.reframe: The cards can't reveal what that person is hiding, but they can show what you, {name}, want to protect while you're worn down by doubt.
love_qsub.caution: Don't state for sure whether they're cheating. Don't advise secretly checking the other person's phone

deck.shuffle: Every time ‘Shuffle again’ is pressed, the server shuffles the 22 cards into a new random order (crypto RNG). Only card backs are sent to the screen; only the server knows which card is in which spot.
deck.pick: The user picks 3 of the 22 cards themselves. Each card flips face-up as soon as it's picked and moves to the slots above. Pick order = The Road So Far → The Current Now → The Key Ahead (v3.0 past–present–future). A flipped card can't be undone.
deck.log: Each shuffle saves a shuffle_id with the card order and orientation (for replay and audit). The number of reshuffles is also logged.
deck.reversed_rule: v1.8 reversed: on shuffle, each card has a 50% chance of being reversed (same as traditional tarot; server-side, crypto). Reversed doesn't mean a ‘negative card’; it's read as the card's energy still held inward (blocked) or overused in one direction (too much). On flip, the card art appears rotated 180 degrees, with the card name upright just below the art plus a ‘reversed’ tag. The back design is vertically symmetric, so the orientation can't be known before drawing.

scoring.display_order: Only the on-screen order is shuffled, seeded by session ID (no effect on results).
scoring.status: On hold (unused since v1.1) — worry-matched 7-card mode. Kept for possible later use in A/B tests or a ‘see recommended cards’ feature.

pages.6:
**This worry starts to ease when you refill yourself first.**

Your tendencies, as seen in the cards
**You often keep running even when you're exhausted, afraid that resting means falling behind.** Your effort gets a lot done, but when a worry hits, you forget how to really stop, and that drains you even more.

For example, there were probably times you stayed up all night before a deadline and still showed up to work the next day as if nothing had happened. There may also have been weekends that didn't feel like rest because you were sorting through your to-do list in your head. Right now, it tends to show up as not wanting to do anything even after you get home and sit on the couch, and as simple work decisions taking longer than usual. When you keep pushing through at work without rest, the same tasks can start to feel bigger and harder. The key to this worry isn't finding ways to work better, but the real rest that refills your energy to work again.
pages.7:
**This eases one step at a time.**

Because the way you've done things has built up for so long, this worry eases bit by bit rather than all at once. Habits that have set in take time to change, and in the meantime small changes pile up one by one and shift the direction.

What The Key Ahead changes
The Key Ahead points somewhere different from The Current Now. The difference is that it moves the energy spent on holding on to everything toward refilling yourself first and really resting. Compared with The Road So Far, there's a lot of overlap, since you've been dealing with the same thing for a long time. But instead of the old way of pushing through without rest, it points toward refilling first and really resting, so this key makes room for rest in the way you've been getting by.

Why we read it this way
◦ ‘Rest on the Rock’ in The Road So Far came out with its energy curled inward. The way you've done things so far still weighs on you, so getting started may take a little longer.
◦ ‘The Guardian's Post’ in The Current Now came out with its energy tied up. Right now this worry has a strong grip on you, so things tend to move slowly.
◦ ‘The Embrace’ in The Key Ahead came out with its energy moving forward. This is the position that shapes the outcome most, so we read it as speeding things up.

If you notice changes like these, things are starting to ease
◦ On a day off, what you want to eat comes to mind before what you have to do.
◦ After listening to a friend's problems, you think you should take a break too.
◦ On a night after a mistake, the things you blame yourself with get shorter than usual.
pages.8:
Here are two suggestions that follow straight from what you just read. One brings The Key Ahead into your daily life, and the other loosens what's holding you back in The Current Now.

▸ Bringing ‘kindness you give yourself too’ from The Key Ahead into daily life
• Kind words for yourself
Say to yourself the things you'd say to others. Write one line in a notebook to your tired self, like ‘You did good today.’ When you focus on sharing the kindness you give others with yourself too, you get refilled first, and your care for others lasts longer.

▸ To loosen ‘the urge to control even small changes’, seen in The Current Now
• Leave one slot in your schedule open
Deliberately leave one slot in today's schedule unplanned and watch how it goes. The urge to control even small changes builds tension, so try letting that open slot go however it goes.
pages.9:
These are small practices that bring the page 8 suggestions into this week. Today and This week try the first suggestion in a small way, and Within 3 days tries the second.

• Today: Write yourself a thank-you for your effort (1 min)
Pick one thing you did today and write yourself one line like ‘You worked hard.’ As a first step toward sharing kindness with yourself too, give a word to what you did today.

• Within 3 days: Watch your open time (15 min)
During 15 minutes you've left unplanned, do whatever you feel like at that moment, then write one line about how it went. The urge to control loosens when you see open time go fine, so less tension builds up.

• This week: One kind line every evening (this week)
Every evening this week, write yourself one kind line you might say to someone else. Gather them and read them over at the weekend. When you give yourself kind words every day, you get refilled first, and your care for others lasts longer.

These practices aren't the right answer; they're small experiments to find what works for you, Minjun. If a moment sticks with you as you try them, you can keep talking about it with Sowella.

cards.name: The First Splash
cards.core: You can make your first splash even if you're not perfectly ready.

positions.now: Until now, every time an idea for what you wanted to do came up, you've likely turned it over quietly in your head and waited for the right time. That excitement never went out, and it led to today's worry. You may have looked at new things from the sidelines and then quietly set them aside more than once.
positions.hold: Right now, your usual routine is starting to feel stifling. If this keeps up, the plans in your head will grow while you stay in the same place. The moment you picture what you want to do, your heart races, but practical reasons quickly follow.
positions.step: From here, focus on what feels fun rather than on doing it well. Then the pressure drops, even with unfamiliar things, and your hands move first. A thing you tried lightly at first can quietly grow into a hobby or work you keep up.

reversed.core: Your wish to start is still hesitating at the water's edge.

positions.now: Until now, you've likely paced at the starting line for a long time, telling yourself to research more and prepare more before moving. Meanwhile, regrets piled up one by one. There may have been days it stung to hear that someone with a similar idea had already started.
positions.hold: Right now, you really want to do it, but the worry of looking clumsy is holding you back. If this keeps up, even when a good moment comes, it's easy to let it pass by saying "not yet." As unstarted things pile up in your head, the pressure that you have to do them keeps quietly growing.
positions.step: From here, focus on starting while you're still clumsy rather than on getting it perfect. Once you don't have to be good from the start, your shut-down motivation slowly loosens. When you hold your first result in your hands, you'll see what to fix, and the direction of your next step becomes clear.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that the time spent hesitating is part of getting ready, and a small try, dipping in just one toe, is enough.
asks: When you think about what you want to do, is "What if I fail?" the first thing that comes to mind?
How many times have you put off starting because you felt you had to be good from the beginning?

frag.now: time spent only preparing
frag.hold: hesitation before the first step
frag.step: a start that's allowed to be clumsy

basic.desc: The First Splash reversed means your wish to start is still hesitating at the water's edge. The pressure to do well may be making the first step feel heavy. It often comes up when you keep looking up information about what you want to do but push the actual start to "next week."
basic.overview: You want to try, but the pressure to do it well keeps delaying your first step. Right now, just dipping a toe in is enough, rather than a grand start.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you kept putting off things you wanted to try because you felt you had to be good from the start?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you hesitating in front of a thing you want to try because you're afraid you won't be good at it?
asks_pos.step: From here, which do you want to choose: preparing perfectly, or trying little by little while still clumsy?

key_rx.title: Pick a small way to start
key_rx.how: Break the task you've been putting off into its smallest pieces in a notebook, and put just one first step, one that's allowed to be clumsy, on this week's schedule.
key_rx.why: When you focus on starting small instead of doing it well, the bar drops and starting feels less scary.

today.title: Do a two-minute first step
today.how: Shrink the first step of the task you've put off until it fits in two minutes, and do it now. It's okay to be clumsy.
today.why: When you focus on just starting, even a two-minute start is enough to get your stalled heart moving.

week.title: One clumsy start a day
week.how: Every day this week, do one small step of the task you've put off, and instead of judging what was clumsy, just check off that you tried.
week.why: Repeating small starts keeps the bar low, so starting feels less scary.

direct.slow_short: the urge to prepare more

slow_rx.title: Cut your prep list to three
slow_rx.how: Write down every bit of preparation you think you need before starting, keep only the three you truly need, and cross out the rest.
slow_rx.why: The urge to prepare more keeps piling up reasons, so cutting the prep you need keeps you from letting chances pass.

three.title: Finish prep and start
three.how: Finish your three remaining prep items within 15 minutes, then go straight into the first step of the task you've put off.
three.why: Putting a time limit on preparation, before "I'm not ready yet" piles up, keeps you from letting chances slip by.

signs: You open the first screen of the task you've put off and work on it, even for a few minutes.
Even when you don't feel fully ready, there are days you start and say "that's enough for today."
Watching others no longer shrinks you; instead you think, "I was like that at first, too."
reversed.tendency: When you want to do a new thing, you often wait until you're fully prepared before moving. That care means fewer mistakes, but when you face a worry, it's easy to keep pushing the start back.

basic.desc: The First Splash is a card of new beginnings and curiosity. It stands for the courage to take a light first step even when you're not perfectly ready. Like signing up for a new workout or opening up studies you've put off, it suits the moment you just try, even in a small way.
basic.overview: Like an otter jumping into the water for the first time, this card shows the heart that starts a new thing lightly. It says a small try, taken before you're fully ready, becomes the starting point of a new direction.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you pictured things you wanted to try many times, only in your head?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, do you really want to try but stay in place because you don't know where to begin?
asks_pos.step: From here, which do you want to choose: starting once you're fully prepared, or trying now even if you're clumsy?

frag.hold: the excitement of being about to start
frag.step: a light first step

practices.title: Start for just 5 minutes
practices.how: Do the task you've put off for just five minutes, and give yourself permission to stop when the five minutes are up.
practices.why: Lowering the threshold to five minutes eases the pressure that made you put it off, and the feeling of having moved brings the next step.

practices.title: Curiosity notes
practices.how: Write a few things you were curious about today in your notes app, and look one of them up for just 10 minutes.
practices.why: Curiosity moves you more lightly than worry about results, so new tries feel less scary.

practices.title: Pick a thing you can be clumsy at
practices.how: Choose one thing this week you don't have to be good at, and label it "practicing."
practices.why: Calling it "practicing" eases the pressure to do well, so it's easier to treat mistakes as learning.

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that a small first splash opens the way more than perfect preparation does.
cards.about: This card speaks to times when you want to start a new thing or stand before an unfamiliar path. It sits in the place of The Fool in traditional tarot, which traditionally means a pure beginning and adventure. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the courage to take a first step even when you're not perfectly ready.
cards.about_when: This card speaks to times when you want to start a new thing or stand before an unfamiliar path.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of The Fool in traditional tarot, which traditionally means a pure beginning and adventure. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the courage to take a first step even when you're not perfectly ready.
asks: Is there a thing you want to do that you're putting off with "once I'm a bit more ready"?
Have you recently paced before a start for a long time, afraid you'd be clumsy because it's your first time?

now: The wish to try a new thing usually comes when where you are starts to feel a little small. For example, if you catch yourself picturing a different scene in the middle of your usual work, your heart may already be scouting new water. Even if that feeling is still faint, the sense that you want to change things is itself a sign that your energy is alive.

Is there a thing your eyes keep drifting to lately without you meaning to? It doesn't have to be a big goal. Tonight before bed, take about three minutes and write one line in your phone's notes: "What I'm curious about lately." Just giving that small pull a name brings your start one step closer.
hold: Under the wish to prepare more, there's often a wish not to look clumsy. If you've been saying "let me look into it a bit more" for weeks, at work or at home, there may be a wish to avoid an awkward first attempt behind those words. It's natural for the awkwardness of a first try to feel big when you want to do well.

Try writing down what "fully ready" actually means to you. Write about five lines on a sheet of paper, circle what you truly need before starting, and draw a triangle by what you can fill in along the way. Once it's written down, you may find that some of those items can only be filled in after you start.
step: The smaller the first step, the lighter the weight of failure. For example, if you want to start exercising, walking around the block before signing up anywhere counts, and for studying, reading one page of the table of contents instead of a whole book is a real first step. If your goal is the experience of having tried, not a set result, what to do next starts to show up as you go.

What's the smallest version you can do today? One search or 10 minutes of practice, just enough to test the water, is plenty. For example, set a timer for 10 minutes this evening and stop without regret when it goes off; that takes a lot of the pressure off. If you jot down how it felt afterward, your next splash gets much easier.

now: Hesitating to start also means you want to do this well. For example, if you've looked up a thing you want to try many times and closed the window, that may not be laziness but a sign that you're still carefully checking things out. Even now, with just your toes in, you may not be stuck; you may be testing the water's temperature and getting ready.
hold: The rule that you must be good from the start is often a shield to make mistakes hurt less. For example, trying to get your first practice flawless makes it hard to even begin, but deciding "today is a day I'm allowed to be clumsy" can make your hands move much more easily. Lowering that bar a little isn't about being sloppy; it's about making room to start.
step: A very small try leaves you with a feeling more than a result. For example, it's enough to follow along with just the first part of a thing you've wanted to do for five minutes, then write one word about how it went. Even one sense that "that was better than I thought" can make your next splash much lighter.

image.scene_prompt: The character splashing happily into shallow water at dawn for the first time, small ripples, hopeful beginning.

key_rx.title: A note that only records trying
key_rx.how: Pick one new thing, do it, and write one line in your notebook about how it felt, not about whether you did it well.
key_rx.why: Focusing on the experience of trying lowers the bar of doing it well, so starting gets much lighter.

today.title: Try it for 5 minutes
today.how: Set a timer for five minutes and start the task you've put off. When it ends, write just one line about how it felt.
today.why: When you focus on the experience itself, five minutes feels like enough, and starting gets lighter.

week.title: Three things you tried this week
week.how: Choose three new things to try this week, do them one by one, and each time write one line about how it felt.
week.why: Repeating the experience of trying gradually lowers the bar of doing well, and starting becomes fun.

direct.slow_short: the habit of thinking ahead of doing

slow_rx.title: Pick a first move instead of more thinking
slow_rx.how: Write every thought in your head in a notebook, then circle just one first move you can do right now.
slow_rx.why: When thinking runs ahead, the first step keeps getting pushed back, so deciding on one first move makes starting easier.

three.title: Do the first move right away
three.how: Do the first move you circled within 10 minutes. Even if you don't finish, taking the first step is enough.
three.why: The habit of thinking ahead grows when the first step keeps slipping, so actually moving within 10 minutes stops the slide.

signs: On a weekend morning, "Why not just try it?" comes before "Can I pull this off?"
Even when you're clumsy at a new thing, you laugh it off with "I'll get better next time."
The time you spend researching before starting a thing you've wanted to do gets shorter.
cards.tendency: You're often drawn to new things first. You have the energy to move lightly when you're curious, but when you face a worry, you can get stuck thinking and take the first step late.

cards.name: Eight Arms
cards.core: You already have quite a lot of what you need in your hands.

positions.now: Until now, whenever you hit a wall, you've likely pulled out every skill you have and worked it out yourself head-on. You've built up a fair amount of know-how that way, yet you've been stingy about giving yourself credit. Even on days when work piled up, you still got it done, so the people around you may have trusted you with things.
positions.hold: Right now, a list of your shortcomings is filling your head. If this keeps up, it's easy to miss what you already hold and keep chewing on what's missing. Even when you're praised, you brush it off modestly and go straight to thinking about what's left to do.
positions.step: From here, focus on naming, one by one, the people who can help you and the skills you've built. You'll see that you already have plenty to work with, without getting anything new. When you can picture the faces you can ask for help, you'll panic less and find a way, even with unfamiliar problems.

reversed.core: The strength you have is scattered here and there and can't find its place.

positions.now: Until now, you've likely been unable to say no to requests and kept taking on one task after another. People called you hardworking, but it was hard to come away with results you could call your own. While looking after everything else, there may have been many days you only got to your own work late at night.
positions.hold: Right now, there are so many things to keep track of that you can't go deep into any of them. If this keeps up, it's easy to fall into days that are busy but unrewarding. When you hold on to one thing, another comes to mind, and you end up jumping between many open windows.
positions.step: From here, focus on separating what you have to do from what you can put down. As the load gets lighter, you can fully commit to what's left, and the joy of finishing comes back. As finished tasks add up, you also get better at choosing what to take on and what to turn down.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that you don't need to put strength into every arm; the way shows up when you gather your strength into the one arm you need most.
asks: Have you been having day after day with lots to do, yet feeling you didn't really finish anything?
Have you ever tried to take care of everything and had no strength left for what mattered most?

frag.now: tasks you've grabbed all at once
frag.hold: strength scattered in many directions
frag.step: strength gathered in one place

basic.desc: Eight Arms reversed means the strength you have is scattered in many places and can't find its place. The wish to get it all done may be breaking your energy into pieces. It's worth thinking of when you're grabbing so many things at once that, at the end of the day, you don't feel you finished anything.
basic.overview: You're holding on to everything at once, so your strength is split up all over. Just choosing one of the eight and seeing it through can make you feel lighter.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you stayed busy, grabbing the next task before finishing the last one?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, in trying to do everything, are you running out of strength for what matters most?
asks_pos.step: From here, which do you want to choose: holding many tasks at once, or seeing one thing through to the end?

key_rx.title: Pick the one thing you really need
key_rx.how: Write all your tasks in a notebook and circle only the one thing you truly need right now. Move the rest to next week's column.
key_rx.why: When you focus on choosing the one thing you truly need, your strength comes together and you get the satisfaction of seeing it through.

today.title: Pick just one task for today
today.how: Pick only the most necessary task for today and write it at the top of your notes. Move the other tasks down.
today.why: Focusing on choosing the one thing you need settles where to put your strength today.

week.title: Finish one thing a day
week.how: Every morning this week, decide on today's one thing, and start the next task only after finishing it. In the evening, check off what you finished.
week.why: As days of gathering your strength into one needed thing add up, the same effort gives you a stronger sense of seeing things through.

direct.slow_short: grabbing all your tasks at once

slow_rx.title: Put down what you're holding
slow_rx.how: Get every task in your head out onto a notebook page, and draw a line through the ones you won't touch today to set them down for now.
slow_rx.why: Grabbing all your tasks at once scatters your strength and only makes you anxious, so writing them out where you can see them eases the load.

three.title: Trim your to-do list
three.how: Look at each task you wrote down, ask "Can this wait past this week?", and cross off the ones where the answer is yes.
three.why: Grabbing everything at once eases when you trim the list, and your strength gathers on what's left so you actually have results to show.

signs: Even with a long to-do list, the one thing you really need today stands out first.
On an evening when you've finished one thing, the satisfaction lasts longer than on a day you dabbled in everything.
Even when a new offer comes in, you can say you'll think about it after finishing what you're doing now.
reversed.tendency: You often take on whatever comes your way, all at once. So you get a lot done, but when you face a worry, your strength easily splits in many directions and you feel rushed.

basic.desc: Eight Arms is a card of the resources you already have and the drive to put them to use. It means the tools you need are closer than you think. It says that the more you have to do, the more the way opens when you use your existing experience and the help around you instead of looking for new tools.
basic.overview: Like an octopus's eight arms, this card tells you that much of the strength and tools you need are already beside you. It says strength comes from recognizing what you already have rather than getting more.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you tried many ways to solve every problem with your own hands?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you so focused on what's missing that you've forgotten the strengths you already have?
asks_pos.step: From here, which do you want to choose: filling in what's missing, or making good use of what you have?

frag.now: experience built by facing things head-on
frag.hold: hands ready to try
frag.step: the resources in your hands

practices.title: Draw a resource map
practices.how: Write your worry in the middle of a sheet of paper, and around it list eight resources you can use. People, time, experience, and things all count.
practices.why: Seeing what you have instead of what you lack turns that stuck feeling into a sense that "there are things I can use."

practices.title: Use one strength in a new way
practices.how: Choose one thing you're good at and use it today somewhere different from usual.
practices.why: Using a familiar strength in a new place grows the sense that "I can do this," and your satisfaction with the day rises too.

practices.title: Just one arm today
practices.how: Pick only one task to finish today from your to-do list, and move the rest to tomorrow's column.
practices.why: Narrowing to one task keeps your strength from scattering, and the feeling of finishing gives you the energy to start the next one.

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that what you need isn't a new thing but the eye to recognize what's already in your hands.
cards.about: This card speaks to times when there's a lot you have to do and a lot you can do, all at once. It sits in the place of The Magician in traditional tarot, which means the power to make things happen with the talents and tools you have. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the strength to recognize the resources already in your hands.
cards.about_when: This card speaks to times when there's a lot you have to do and a lot you can do, all at once.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of The Magician in traditional tarot, which means the power to make things happen with the talents and tools you have. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the strength to recognize the resources already in your hands.
asks: Do your days often slip by because there's so much to do that you don't know where to start?
Do you notice what's missing before what you're already doing well?

now: When you really want to get things done, your arms reach out in many directions on their own. For example, if you spend your day thinking about chores, other plans, and postponed goals even while doing one task, feeling busy is a natural result. This busyness may come from a conscientious wish to take responsibility for a lot.

Of all the places you're reaching right now, which do you really want to hold on to? You don't need to put the same strength into every arm. Write down everything you're doing on a sheet of paper, then put a star next to just the two you find yourself looking at longest. Choosing the one or two that pull you most gives you a center, even in the middle of the busyness.
hold: Noticing your shortcomings first also comes from a strong wish to do better. For example, if one regret stays in your head late into the night more than ten things that went well, at work or in a relationship, your attention may be leaning toward "what's missing." But if that attention stays there too long, the work you've done and the help beside you can easily fade into the background.

Think of one recent moment when you felt, "I did pretty well there." The strength you used then is strength you can use on this worry, too. Next to the list of what you lack, write a list of what you have. For example, if you write just three things on the left, "still missing," and three on the right, "already have," you may find the right side fills up faster than you'd expect.
step: When you lay out your resources where you can see them, a vague worry turns into the question, "What can I try with this?" For example, if you write things like "two hours on weekend mornings," "a habit of organizing carefully," and "having gotten through a similar task before," the arms you can use come into view one by one. Just as an octopus uses each of its eight arms differently, each thing you have can take on a different role.

Divide a page into four boxes and fill them in: time, people, experience, and small skills. For example, if the time box says "20 minutes in the morning" and the experience box says "having broken a complicated task into a list," you could use those morning 20 minutes this week to break your worry into small written pieces. If you pick one thing you can use right away this week and connect it to your worry, you may get a sense that the answer is closer than you thought.

now: The more arms you have, the harder it is to spread your strength evenly. For example, if day after day you're busy from morning to night but feel in the evening that you finished nothing, it may be a sign your strength is split in too many directions. Feeling that your strength isn't landing anywhere may not mean you lack ability, but that there are too many places to use it.
hold: Under the feeling that you have to do it all, there may be a fear that you can't let anything slip. For example, even with ten things on today's to-do list, often only two or three really need to be finished today. Give yourself permission not to put the same strength into every arm.
step: Keeping just one arm doesn't mean throwing the rest away; it means letting them rest for a while. For example, this week you make just one task the main one and write the rest on the side of your notes as "look at again next week." When you gather your strength on the one thing that pulls you most right now, your scattered energy starts to come back together.

image.scene_prompt: The character on a rock, each arm holding something useful: a shell, a pearl, sea glass, a small lantern, a starfish. Confident and playful.

key_rx.title: List what you have
key_rx.how: In a notebook, write in separate columns the time you can use, the people you know, and the experience you have. Even if it's not much, write what you can see.
key_rx.why: Focusing on recognizing the resources you already have shows you the time, people, and experience in your hands, so starting gets easier.

today.title: Write three things you have
today.how: Pick one each of the time, people, and experience you have right now, and write each on its own line in your notes.
today.why: As a first step toward recognizing your resources, this makes what you have today visible.

week.title: Add one thing you have each day
week.how: Every day this week, add one more thing you have to the list, and on the weekend pick one and actually use it.
week.why: Recognizing your resources every day makes what's in your hands look bigger, so starting gets easier.

direct.slow_short: the habit of seeing what's missing first

slow_rx.title: Write what you have next to what's missing
slow_rx.how: Write "what's missing" on the left side of a notebook page, and on the right, pair each with a thing you have that could stand in for it.
slow_rx.why: When you see what's missing first, your own strength goes unused, so pair each missing thing with one you can use.

three.title: Pair what's missing with what you have
three.how: Write five things you felt were missing for the matter you're worried about, and pair each with one of your own that could stand in.
three.why: The habit of seeing what's missing first eases when you pair things up in writing, and you can see where your strength can actually be used.

signs: When you think about a task, you start by naming what you already have rather than what's missing.
You suddenly notice that a thing you did before can be used in what you're doing now.
You remember, "Oh, I know someone who's good at this."
cards.tendency: You often make your own way by trying things yourself. You have solid follow-through, but when you face a worry, your eyes can go to what's missing before what you already have.

cards.name: Quiet Watching
cards.core: Sometimes the answer only becomes audible once things get quiet.

positions.now: Until now, even if you didn't say much, you've likely noticed a lot by watching the mood and how people were doing. That sharp eye served you well, but you rarely said out loud what you felt. You may have picked up on small changes others missed and quietly looked after someone.
positions.hold: Right now, an uneasy feeling you can't quite put your finger on won't settle. If you just follow other people's opinions, it's easy to end up on a path that looks right but feels wrong inside. The harder you try to ignore a feeling you can't explain, the more the same thought comes back night after night.
positions.step: From here, focus on noticing your first gut feeling before you come up with reasons. When you respect your own senses, you'll have fewer regrets after you choose. The option your body reacts to first, in a quiet moment, is closer to your own standard.

reversed.core: Your inner voice is buried in the noise and hard to hear.

positions.now: Until now, at every important crossroads, you've likely asked many people and compared options, looking for a way not to get it wrong. Along the way, you lost track of which direction first drew you in. A choice that looked good may have quickly cooled the moment someone shook their head.
positions.hold: Right now, so many opinions are talking at once in your head that there's no room to hear your own thoughts. If this keeps up, it's easy to get worn out before choosing and end up deciding nothing. Even choosing one item off a menu takes a long time because you look up other people's reviews first.
positions.step: From here, focus on cutting down the number of voices you listen to and on time alone in quiet. Once the noise settles, what you originally wanted comes to mind naturally. Once you've walked a path you chose all the way through, your next decision comes much faster.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that when you turn down the outside noise for a while, your inner voice starts to come through again.
asks: While searching and asking around before a decision, have you ever lost track of where your own heart was?
Is there a matter you sense you already know but are trying hard to ignore?

frag.now: a decision put off while gathering information
frag.hold: intuition hidden behind thinking

basic.overview: There's so much outside talk and information that your own voice is hard to hear. It speaks to a time when, the more you feel the answer is out there, the more easily your first feeling gets blurry.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you looked up other people's opinions and reviews first rather than trusting your own judgment?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, have you been having days with so many thoughts that you can't even tell how you feel?

key_rx.title: Time to turn down the outside noise
key_rx.how: For 20 minutes a day, turn off notifications and skip searching and the news. Leave your phone in another room and sit quietly.
key_rx.why: When you focus on turning down outside noise instead of gathering more information, your buried feelings become clear again.

today.title: Sit for 5 minutes with notifications off
today.how: Turn off your phone notifications and sit quietly for five minutes without looking at anything.
today.why: When you focus on turning down outside noise, your feelings start to surface even in a quiet five-minute gap.

week.title: A quiet 20 minutes every day
week.how: Every day this week, at the same time, spend 20 minutes with notifications off and no information-hunting. When it's over, write one line about the feeling that came up.
week.why: Repeating these breaks from outside noise lets your buried feelings come through more and more clearly.

direct.slow_short: thinking of worries first with every choice

slow_rx.title: Write down all your worries at once
slow_rx.how: Write in a notebook every worry that comes with the choice, and check each one: "Can I do anything about this now?" If not, cross it out.
slow_rx.why: When worries come first, you just gather more information and your mind never rests, so moving your worries onto paper keeps the choice from being put off.

three.title: Get the worries out and cross them off
three.how: Look at your worry list, keep only one thing you can do today, and cross out the rest. Do the one you kept right away.
three.why: Thinking of worries first with every choice eases when you sort them, and one doable thing moves your choice forward.

signs: The time you spend digging through reviews on your phone before bed gets a little shorter.
On a quiet walk, it suddenly comes to you what you were really worried about.
You don't feel uneasy even if you don't read every opinion pouring into the group chat.
reversed.tendency: You often gather information and double-check many times until you feel sure. You end up knowing more, but when you face a worry, your first feeling can blur and deciding gets even harder.

basic.desc: Quiet Watching is a card of intuition and quiet observation. It means you can hear the answer within you when you watch without rushing. It's also a sign to let a decision rest for a day instead of rushing it, and to watch which way your heart leans.
basic.overview: This card stands for the answer within you that you hear when you watch quietly: your intuition. It says that when you step back instead of rushing to an answer, you can see where your heart is heading.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you guessed the answer inside while saying nothing and only watching?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are other people's opinions covering up what your heart really wants?
asks_pos.step: From here, which do you want to choose: following the "right answer" others give, or trusting the feeling inside you?

practices.title: A 3-minute breathing space
practices.how: Spend one minute noticing the thoughts and feelings coming up now, one minute on your breath, and one minute on your whole body, in that order.
practices.why: Pausing briefly to notice the present moment takes you a step back from thoughts on autopilot and gives you room to hear yourself.

practices.title: Write down your body's signals
practices.how: Picture each option you're weighing, one at a time, and write one line on whether your body tightens or relaxes.
practices.why: Your body reacts before your thoughts do, so tightening and relaxing can tell you which option you really want.

practices.title: A one-line evening journal
practices.how: Before bed, write one line about "the moment my heart moved most today."
practices.why: A record built one line a day becomes a map of feelings you used to let slip by.

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that the answer is heard first inside you, once you're quiet, rather than outside.
cards.about: This card speaks to times when you have a lot of thoughts but can't tell which way your heart leans. It sits in the place of The High Priestess in traditional tarot, which means intuition, inner wisdom, and knowing that hasn't surfaced yet. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the inner voice you hear when you watch quietly.
cards.about_when: This card speaks to times when you have a lot of thoughts but can't tell which way your heart leans.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of The High Priestess in traditional tarot, which means intuition, inner wisdom, and knowing that hasn't surfaced yet. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the inner voice you hear when you watch quietly.
asks: Have you ever asked several people for advice and ended up more confused?
Does your heart seem to lean one way, but you're unsure whether to trust it?

now: The sense you have before you put it into words usually moves quietly and slowly. For example, if you answer "Yeah, I'm fine" when someone asks how you are, while replaying many scenes inside, your heart may still be choosing its words. Looking calm on the outside while weighing a lot inside means you're handling this worry with real care.

If you gave the feeling sitting under your heart right now a one-word name, what would it be? It doesn't have to be exact. Before sleep, with the lights off, you could name it once by comparing it to weather or a color, like "my heart feels like the sky before rain." Naming it however it comes lets that sense slowly take shape.
hold: Other people's opinions and "shoulds" are loud and clear, so they're easy to hear. Your inner voice, on the other hand, is often small and hesitant, so it's easy to miss on busy days. If you choose by following "this is the right way to do it," at work or at home, and then feel uneasy for no clear reason, that unease may be a trace your own voice left.

Set someone's expectations aside for a moment and ask, "If no one were judging, what would I choose?" It's good practice to ask this with small choices first, like what to have for lunch or weekend plans. It's okay not to answer right away. If you carry the question through the day, the way your heart leans quietly shows itself.
step: Putting off judgment for a while is different from avoiding a decision. For example, if a choice is weighing on you, you hold off for about three days and quietly notice which option makes your body relax when you think of it. A choice made after looking long enough wavers less, and you blame yourself less after making it.

Decide not to reach a conclusion today, and each time the worry comes up, jot down only the feeling it brings. It's enough to leave a word or two in your phone's notes, like "stuck" or "a little excited," and close it right away. If you collect these for a few days and read them back, you'll see the feelings that keep coming up, and they can be a clue to the direction you want.

now: When you're thinking a lot, your intuition feels like it's shrunk. For example, if you've weighed the pros and cons over and over with no conclusion, yet one option keeps tugging at you, that tug may be the voice of your quieted intuition. Your inner voice hasn't disappeared; it may be waiting quietly under the noise.
hold: Looking up other people's opinions starts from not wanting to get it wrong. But the more information piles up, the more easily your own feeling gets pushed back, so you may need a break from searching. For example, if you keep reading similar reviews and advice right up until bed, tonight you can turn off the screen and first ask yourself, "How do I feel?"
step: Ten minutes of listening only to your heart, with no information at all, may feel strange at first. For example, before turning on your phone in the morning, sit by the window for 10 minutes and quietly ask, "How am I feeling today?" If you write down what comes up in one line without judging it, after a few days you'll start to hear your own voice in it.

theories: Segal et al.'s Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT)

image.scene_prompt: The character standing still at the water's edge under a crescent moon, watching its calm reflection, quiet and wise.

key_rx.title: Note down small feelings
key_rx.how: For a choice you're facing, write the feeling that comes up in a word or two in your notebook, like "easy" or "heavy." You don't need to write reasons.
key_rx.why: When you focus on listening to the small feelings inside you, you start trusting your senses and waver less after you choose.

today.title: Write one feeling word
today.how: Picture each option you're weighing, one at a time, and write the feeling each brings as one word in your notes.
today.why: When you focus on listening to small feelings, your own sense shows up first, without having to rush to an answer.

week.title: One line of feeling every evening
week.how: Every evening this week, write one line about how you felt today about the choice you're weighing, and on the weekend look for the words that came up most.
week.why: Writing your feelings down every day builds up reasons to trust your senses, so you waver less after you choose.

direct.slow_short: the habit of following other people's standards

slow_rx.title: Write others' standards and your feelings separately
slow_rx.how: Split your reasons for a choice into two columns: on the left, the standards others have told you; on the right, what you feel.
slow_rx.why: If you only follow other people's standards, even a right choice won't feel settled, so write your feelings separately where you can see them.

three.title: Compare the two columns
three.how: Put your two columns side by side, and mark which one your heart leans toward more: others' standards or your feelings.
three.why: The habit of following others' standards becomes visible when you compare the two columns, and you can see which choice feels settled.

signs: At a menu, you look first at what draws you rather than what others are ordering.
Even while weighing things, you can feel which option makes your body relax and which makes it tense.
The day after making a choice, you second-guess "Was that right?" less often.
cards.tendency: You often look calm on the outside while feeling and weighing a lot inside. So you see situations deeply, but when you face a worry, you may keep what you feel to yourself without putting it into words.

cards.name: The Embrace
cards.core: Just as you hold others close, now it's your turn to hold yourself.

positions.now: Until now, you've likely looked out for the people close to you first and tried to be there for them. Because of that, people gathered around you, but your own rest always came last. When making plans, fitting in with the time and place that suited the other person may have felt natural.
positions.hold: Right now, a sense that you're not getting back as much as you give is starting to rise. If this keeps up, care that began with good intentions can easily turn into resentment. When someone asks you for a favor, instead of feeling glad like before, you find yourself counting: "Am I the only one doing this again?"
positions.step: From here, focus on taking care of your own needs the way you would someone else's. You need enough energy of your own to stay by others for the long run. Once you put your needs into words, the people close to you will learn how to look after you too.

reversed.core: While holding others close, you've been left empty.

positions.now: Until now, even when you needed help, you've likely laughed it off and said you're fine because you didn't want to be a bother. That thoughtfulness made things easy for the people around you, but your energy quietly wore down. Even on days you felt sick, you may have answered calls in a voice that sounded perfectly fine.
positions.hold: Right now, your energy is close to empty, so your body feels heavy even when resting and everything feels like too much. If this keeps up, small things can easily irritate you and you can drift into isolation. You put off replying even to messages and get-togethers you used to enjoy, and spend more time lying down alone.
positions.step: From here, focus on gratefully accepting the kindness someone offers you. Once you learn to receive, you get refilled too, and giving becomes much lighter. When a relationship becomes give-and-take, asking for help brings gratitude before guilt.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that as much as you hold others, you deserve to be held too, and that care becomes the strength to share again.
asks: When someone looks after you, do you feel sorry before you feel grateful?
Are there more and more days when you put off your own meals or sleep to look after others?

frag.now: time spent only giving
frag.hold: room to breathe that keeps shrinking
frag.step: practice receiving with ease

basic.desc: The Embrace reversed means you're running empty while caring for others. Receiving may feel so awkward that you're missing chances to get help. It's close to feeling sorry before grateful when someone looks after you, or to constantly pushing your own meals and sleep aside.
basic.overview: You've spent all your heart on looking after others and are running empty yourself. It speaks to a time when feeling awkward about accepting kindness leaves little room for you to be refilled.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you turned people down first, saying you're fine, even when they offered to help?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, even with no strength left to look after anyone, are you still pretending you're okay?
asks_pos.step: From here, which do you want to choose: doing everything on your own, or comfortably accepting the help offered?

key_rx.title: Record the kindness you received
key_rx.how: Write in your notebook a kindness or help someone gave you today. After writing it, add one line: "It's okay to just accept it."
key_rx.why: When you focus on seeing receiving as just as okay as giving, you can accept kindness with ease and refill your shrinking reserves.

today.title: Write down one kindness you received
today.how: Think of one small kindness you got today, write it in your notes, and add one line of thanks with no apology.
today.why: As a first step toward seeing receiving as okay, you comfortably acknowledge what you got today.

week.title: Three things you received each day
week.how: Every night this week before bed, write three kindnesses or bits of help you got that day. If there seem to be none, very small things count too.
week.why: Writing down what you received every day makes accepting kindness feel familiar, and your shrinking reserves start to refill.

direct.slow_short: brushing off tiredness that won't go away

slow_rx.title: Score your tiredness
slow_rx.how: Twice a day, at midday and in the evening, rate your tiredness from 1 to 5 in a notebook. If it's 4 or higher, stop what you're doing and rest for 10 minutes.
slow_rx.why: Brushing off tiredness that rest doesn't fix stretches out the time you push through alone, so writing it as a score makes it visible.

three.title: Rest according to your score
three.how: Find the times your tiredness score was high, add a 10-minute rest slot after them on your schedule, and actually rest.
three.why: Seeing tiredness that won't go away as a score makes it hard to brush off, so you spend less time pushing through exhausted.

signs: When someone offers to help, "Thank you" comes out before "I'm fine."
When you get a gift or a coffee, you no longer immediately figure out how to pay it back.
On a hard day, the words "Could you help me out today?" actually come out.
reversed.tendency: Giving comes easily to you, but receiving makes you feel sorry, so you often decline. Your thoughtfulness puts the people around you at ease, but when you face a worry, it's easy to hold out alone without asking for help.

basic.desc: The Embrace is a card of acceptance, care, and taking things as they are. It means you can hold yourself warmly, just as you hold others. Its message is to offer yourself the kindness you've given others, starting by refilling the basics of rest, food, and sleep.
basic.overview: Like a sea otter holding its pup on its belly, this card stands for care that accepts you as you are. It says your strength fills back up when the hands that look after others turn toward you too.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you put your own feelings aside while checking on other people's moods and needs first?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you used to looking after others but finding it awkward to look after yourself?
asks_pos.step: From here, which do you want to choose: always putting others first, or caring for yourself as well?
