practices.title: A kind pause for yourself
practices.how: In a hard moment, say three sentences to yourself: "This is hard right now. Everyone goes through times like this. Let me be kind to myself."
practices.why: Noticing a hard feeling without blaming yourself for it helps your tense body loosen little by little.

practices.title: Book 10 minutes for yourself
practices.how: Write 10 minutes just for you into today's schedule, and don't swap it for anything else.
practices.why: When rest is on your schedule instead of left to willpower, it's easier to practice resting without guilt.

practices.title: A warm hand
practices.how: Place a hand on your chest or belly, feel its warmth, and take three slow breaths.
practices.why: The warmth of your hand and slow breathing send your body a "you're okay now" signal that helps calm you down.

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that caring for yourself is just as precious a responsibility as caring for others.
cards.about: This card speaks to times when you're running empty from caring for someone else. It sits in the place of The Empress in traditional tarot, which means abundance, care, and the power to help things grow. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as self-care: holding yourself the way you hold others.
cards.about_when: This card speaks to times when you're running empty from caring for someone else.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of The Empress in traditional tarot, which means abundance, care, and the power to help things grow. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as self-care: holding yourself the way you hold others.
asks: Are you taking care of other people's things first while often putting off your own meals or sleep?
Has "I'm fine" become such a habit that it's hard to actually accept help?

now: Caring for someone takes a lot of heart. For example, if at the end of the day you remember everyone else's schedule and mood but can barely recall your own meals or feelings, your care may be flowing only one way. That warmth is a great strength, but if what you give isn't refilled, your own bowl can quietly run empty.

How much time a day have you spent on yourself lately? If you put a number on it, it may be less than you think. Tonight, even for just 15 minutes, put your phone down and spend the time drinking a tea you like or listening to one song. Stretching that time a little doesn't mean caring less; it refills you so you can keep caring for a long time.
hold: If looking after yourself feels selfish, it may be because putting others first has long been what you're used to. For example, even on days your body feels heavy, you may keep doing others' favors first and pushing your own rest to "later." That habit began with kindness, but when you're worn out, even kindness can feel heavy.

If someone you love were as worn out as you are now, what would you say to them? Try saying exactly that back to yourself. You could also write the words that come to mind, like "You worked so hard today, this is enough," on a sticky note and put it on your desk or mirror. You're simply allowing yourself, little by little, the same rest you'd see as obvious for others.
step: Holding yourself doesn't have to be grand. A warm drink, an evening when you go to bed early, a kind word to yourself: any moment when your body and mind feel "cared for" is enough. For example, after your day ends, just washing your hands slowly in warm water and saying to yourself "Good work today" can help your body register rest.

Decide ahead of time on one act of care you can give yourself today. If you set both a time and an action, like "at 10 p.m., put my phone down and listen to one song I love," you're less likely to put it off. And for that time, set aside thoughts of looking after others. Only arms that are refilled can hold someone again with room to spare.

now: Receiving may feel awkward because you've long been used to being the one who gives. For example, if "No, it's fine" pops out first when someone hands you a coffee or takes work off your plate, receiving may still feel unfamiliar. Simply saying "Thanks" and accepting someone's small kindness is also practice in caring for yourself.
hold: The feeling that you have to look after things began with kindness, but when you're worn out, that kindness can feel like a heavy load. Pick one thing today that you don't have to take care of. For example, even if you put down one cleanup or schedule check you've always taken on first, the day may go by just fine.
step: A glass of water you give yourself first may look small, but it signals "I'm allowed to be cared for too." For example, as you start your day, before looking after anything else, pour water into your own cup first and drink it slowly. As those signals add up, your strength to care for others refills too.

image.scene_prompt: The character floating on its back, hugging a small baby of its kind on its belly, wrapped in kelp, warm and nurturing.

key_rx.title: Kind words for yourself
key_rx.how: Say to yourself the words you'd say to others. Write one line in your notebook to your tired self, like "You worked hard."
key_rx.why: When you focus on sharing with yourself the kindness you've given others, you get refilled first and your caring heart lasts longer.

today.title: Write "good work" to yourself
today.how: Pick one thing you did today and write yourself one line like "That was hard work, well done."
today.why: As a first step toward sharing kindness with yourself, you offer a word about a thing you did today.

week.title: One kind line every evening
week.how: Every evening this week, write yourself one kind line you might say to someone else. On the weekend, read them all together.
week.why: Saying kind words to yourself every day refills you first, so your heart for caring for others lasts longer.

direct.slow_short: the habit of ignoring your strength running low

slow_rx.title: Check how much strength you have left
slow_rx.how: At the end of each day, write in a notebook how many of five bars of strength you have left, and if it's two or fewer, move one task of looking after others to tomorrow.
slow_rx.why: If you ignore your strength running low from looking after others, kindness turns into hurt feelings or exhaustion, so check what you have left first.

three.title: Record your strength and lighten the load
three.how: For three days, write down your remaining strength each day, and on low days move one task of looking after others to another day on your schedule.
three.why: Seeing your strength drop in numbers makes it hard to ignore, so you can stop before kindness turns into exhaustion.

signs: On a day off, what you want to eat comes to mind before what you have to do.
After listening to a friend's worries, you think, "I should rest for a bit too."
On a night after you've made a mistake, the words you blame yourself with get shorter than usual.
cards.tendency: You often look after and care for the people around you first. Your warmth draws people close, but when you face a worry, the room to check on your own heart easily gets pushed back.

cards.name: The Guardian's Post
cards.core: The shakier things get, the more one small bit of order can protect you.

positions.now: Until now, you've likely held on without leaning on anyone, believing you had to see your share through to the end. That steadiness earned you trust, but you never had the chance to learn how to ease off. When a schedule looked like it might fall apart, you may have stepped in first to fix it and kept things from wobbling for everyone.
positions.hold: Right now, your mind can't rest because you're worrying even about things that are out of your hands. If this keeps up, your days off won't feel refreshing and you'll easily run out of energy. Even on weekends, when a work message comes in, you open it right away and start thinking about how to reply.
positions.step: From here, focus on separating what you can move with your own strength from what you need to let go. Once you know where to spend your energy, the same load feels much less heavy. You'll be able to wait for results on things you've handed off, and your rest on days off will last longer.

reversed.core: Your strength to protect has grown so rigid that it's boxing you in.

positions.now: Until now, the more anxious you felt, the more you've likely steadied yourself by planning every schedule and method down to the last detail. Because of that, nothing big went wrong, but you always lived with tense shoulders. Even when traveling, you may only have felt at ease leaving once your itinerary was planned to the minute.
positions.hold: Right now, your heart lurches every time the unexpected comes up. If this keeps up, even small surprises can put you on edge, and neither you nor the people around you can relax. The moment things don't go to plan, your body tenses, and on many days your neck and shoulders are stiff.
positions.step: From here, focus on keeping just one thing you must protect instead of preparing perfectly. As you hold on to less, you get room to breathe, and people around you relax too. Even on days your plans fall apart, you'll quickly think of another way, and the unexpected will feel less scary.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that you don't need to hold on to everything; one small, easy-to-keep bit of order can support you.
asks: Are you unable to relax because you feel everything will fall apart if you let go?
Have you ever felt your whole day was thrown off just because a small plan went wrong?

frag.now: days spent holding on with tight plans
frag.hold: control you can't let go of
frag.step: the ease of protecting just one thing

basic.desc: The Guardian's Post reversed means your strength to protect has grown so rigid that it's boxing you in. Trying to control everything can wear you out quickly. It often comes up when your whole day feels ruined if a plan goes even slightly off, or when you end up redoing work you handed off.
basic.overview: Your wish to protect has grown so big that you're trying to control everything with your own hands. It speaks to a time when even a small change in plans can shake you badly.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you felt anxious whenever plans went even a little off, and tried to hold on even tighter?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you spending all day tense, feeling you can't let a single thing slip?
asks_pos.step: From here, which do you want to choose: keeping everything to plan, or protecting just the one thing that matters?

key_rx.title: Pick the one thing to protect
key_rx.how: Write down just one thing you really want to protect in your day, and note that it's okay if the rest changes order or gets dropped.
key_rx.why: When you focus on the one thing you really want to protect, there's less to guard, and you get room to let the rest loosen.

today.title: Write today's one thing to protect
today.how: Underline just one thing on today's schedule you'll protect, and write next to the rest that it's okay if they change.
today.why: When you focus on the one thing to protect, you mind less if the rest of today's schedule goes off.

week.title: One thing to protect each day
week.how: Every morning this week, write just one thing to protect, and in the evening only check whether you kept it. Don't count what went off with the rest.
week.why: As days of checking only your one thing add up, the ease of letting the rest stay loose gradually settles in.

direct.slow_short: the urge to bend even small changes to your will

slow_rx.title: Leave one slot open
slow_rx.how: Deliberately leave one slot in today's schedule unplanned, and watch how it goes.
slow_rx.why: The urge to bend even small changes to your will builds tension, so try letting an open slot go however it goes.

three.title: Watch the open time
three.how: During 15 minutes of unplanned time, do whatever you feel like with no plan, and afterward write one line about how it went.
three.why: The urge to bend things to your will loosens when you see open time go fine, so less tension builds up.

signs: While doing chores, you decide to finish just the dishes today and leave the rest.
Even on a day that didn't go to plan, if you did the one thing you meant to protect, you let it go.
You can look at a messy desk without feeling very uncomfortable.
reversed.tendency: The more anxious you get, the more you tend to make tight plans and handle things yourself. That keeps things from falling apart, but when you face a worry, tension builds easily with even small changes.

basic.desc: The Guardian's Post is a card of responsibility, order, and the strength to protect what matters steadily. It means small rules and structure hold you up when you feel shaky. Its message is to start with small bits of order, like getting up at a set time or a habit that closes out your day.
basic.overview: The Guardian's Post stands for the strength that holds you up through responsibility and order. The shakier you feel, the more one small habit you keep every day becomes a support to lean on.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you held on to work even on days off, afraid things would fall apart if you let go?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you holding on even to things you can't control, so that rest no longer feels refreshing?
asks_pos.step: From here, which do you want to choose: holding everything yourself, or spending your strength only on what you can change?

frag.now: time spent carrying it all alone
frag.hold: tension that rest doesn't ease
frag.step: the strength of sharing the load

practices.title: Draw two circles
practices.how: Draw a small circle inside a big one; in the inner circle write what you can change, and in the outer ring what you can't.
practices.why: Separating what you can change from what you can't gives you a reason to put down worries you don't need to hold.

practices.title: Set up one pillar for your day
practices.how: Choose one of these, waking up, a meal, or bedtime, and do it at the same time every day this week.
practices.why: When one small rule anchors your day, you have a place to come back to even on shaky days.

practices.title: Ask for one thing
practices.how: Pick one task you've been handling alone, and briefly ask someone to do it with you.
practices.why: Sharing the load lets your body learn the belief that you don't have to carry everything alone.

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that one small bit of order makes a steady place for a shaky heart.
cards.about: This card speaks to times when responsibility feels heavy or there's a lot to protect. It sits in the place of The Emperor in traditional tarot, which means order, responsibility, and solid structure. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the small bit of order that protects you when you feel shaky.
cards.about_when: This card speaks to times when responsibility feels heavy or there's a lot to protect.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of The Emperor in traditional tarot, which means order, responsibility, and solid structure. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the small bit of order that protects you when you feel shaky.
asks: Are you tense even on days off, feeling things will fall apart if you let go?
Do you often end up taking on work because doing it yourself feels easier than handing it off?

now: People with a strong sense of responsibility choose to hold their post even when things are shaky. For example, if everyone naturally looks to you first when work gets tangled or trouble comes up at home, it means you're holding a steady post. Your quiet steadiness can bring calm to those around you, but it also puts that much weight on your shoulders.

Think of the things you're protecting right now, one by one. Is "yourself" on that list? Write all of them down on paper, add "me" as one more line at the bottom, and next to it write one thing you'll protect for yourself today. Today, just for a moment, remember that the one who protects needs protecting too.
hold: The urge to hold on to everything often starts with the worry that "if I let go, it'll all fall apart." But if you hold on even to what you can't control, you have no strength left for what you can change. For example, if you lie awake late worrying about other people's decisions or things that haven't happened yet, you'll easily be drained the next day when facing what you actually need to do.

Sort the things on your mind lately into "what I can change" and "what's out of my hands." Draw a line down the middle of a sheet of paper, write them on each side, and just drawing one big circle around the right side with a pen can help settle your mind a little. Putting down what's out of your hands isn't giving up responsibility. If anything, it makes clear where you need to spend your strength.
step: Small bits of order become footholds on shaky days. When you have a predictable routine, like tidying up at a set time or a habit that marks the end of the day, your heart has a place to lean. For example, if every night at the same time you spend just three minutes straightening your desk or table and tell yourself "that's it for today," it can become a small ritual that closes the door on your day.

Is there any of the weight you've carried alone that you could share? Pick one favor to ask, one task to hand off, and one thing that can wait. You can start by marking one item on this week's to-do list as "fine to push to next week." Like a penguin colony taking turns in the huddle, the cold feels less harsh when you trade places.

now: The tension of not being able to let go of responsibility and the shakiness of having no order to lean on are both signs that your heart is looking for a place to rest. For example, if you keep worrying about phone notifications even on days off, or, the other way around, your daily routine is different every time so you don't know where to start, that sign may have grown loud. What you need now may not be a sturdier wall but a small pillar to lean on for a while.
hold: The urge to control grows as anxiety grows. For example, if changing just one appointment makes your whole day feel thrown off, it may be a sign you've been gripping a lot very tightly. The more you try to hold on to everything, the more easily small changes wear you out, so today, leave one thing that's out of your hands as it is.
step: One small rule a day becomes a foothold on shaky days. If you start with a rule that's easy to keep, like "a glass of water before bed," rather than a grand plan, order starts protecting you again. For example, keep one rule for a week, and on each day you keep it, mark a small dot on your calendar so you can see the order building up.

theories: Rothbaum et al.'s Primary and Secondary Control

image.scene_prompt: The character standing tall and steady on an ice ledge, sheltering a small chick behind it, protective and reliable.

key_rx.title: Sort what you can change
key_rx.how: Write what's worrying you in a notebook and split it into two columns: "things I can change" and "things I can't change."
key_rx.why: When you focus on separating what you can change from what you can't, it becomes clear where to use your strength, and the same responsibility feels lighter.

today.title: Split into two columns
today.how: Take three worries you're holding right now and write them in two columns: "can change" and "can't change."
today.why: When you focus on sorting things, where to spend your strength today gets settled first within those three.

week.title: Two columns every evening
week.how: Every evening this week, split that day's worries into two columns, and pick just one thing to do tomorrow from the "can change" column.
week.why: Repeating the two-column sort makes it clear each day where to use your strength, so responsibility feels lighter.

direct.slow_short: the habit of holding on even to what can't be helped

slow_rx.title: Put down what you can't change
slow_rx.how: Next to each item in the "can't change" column, write "this stays here during my breaks," and decide not to bring it up again while resting.
slow_rx.why: Holding on even to what can't be helped keeps you tense while resting, so draw a line: you don't think about it during your breaks.

three.title: Stop the thinking during breaks
three.how: Pick one thing you can't change and take a 15-minute walk or stretch. If it comes to mind, write just one line in your notebook and come back.
three.why: The habit of holding on to what can't be helped loosens when you write the thought down and move your body, so the tension eases while you rest.

signs: When a worry comes up, you first ask yourself whether you can do anything about it.
After a meeting, you less often come back carrying other people's share of the work.
When faced with what can't be helped, there are moments you put it down, thinking "this isn't mine to carry."
cards.tendency: You often take full responsibility for what's yours to the very end. That's why people call you reliable, but when you face a worry, you can hold on alone so long that you forget to rest.

cards.name: Old Wisdom
cards.core: You don't have to find the answer alone. There's wisdom from those who walked this way before you.

positions.now: Until now, when a hard situation came up, you've likely tried to work it out by mulling it over alone rather than opening up to someone. That carefulness deepened your thinking, but the same story kept looping in your head. There may have been days you searched late into the night, rewording your question in the search bar over and over.
positions.hold: Right now, while you've been holding it alone, the worry has grown bigger than it really is. If this keeps up, your thoughts will only get deeper and the feeling of being blocked will easily drag on. Even when a friend asks if anything's wrong, you say it's nothing and change the subject.
positions.step: From here, focus on listening to people who've already been down a similar road. Borrowing experience from those ahead of you eases that stuck feeling and helps you find your direction faster. Once you realize your worry isn't yours alone, your shoulders relax and asking gets easier.

reversed.core: You haven't yet knocked on the door to ask for help.

positions.now: Until now, believing you'd only be accepted if you did what everyone else does, you've likely put up with ways of doing things that didn't sit right with you. While getting by smoothly like that, your own tastes and pace slowly got pushed aside. You may have picked up the planner or study method everyone else uses and dropped it within a few weeks.
positions.hold: Right now, you can't bring yourself to ask a hard favor or question because you're afraid of looking weak. If this keeps up, you'll spend longer struggling alone and the stuck feeling can easily grow. Even when a question comes up in a meeting or class, you let it go and tell yourself you'll look it up later.
positions.step: From here, focus on finding someone you can share your situation with exactly as it is, rather than imitating the "right answer." Once you've spoken honestly, a way that fits you slowly comes into view. Once you've opened up honestly even once, you'll hesitate less before asking your next question.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that you don't need to strain to find the answer alone; it's okay to reach for wisdom you can lean on.
asks: Have you been stuck alone for days on a problem that asking would quickly solve?
Have you recently followed the way others do things, only to find it really didn't fit you?

frag.now: time spent fitting into other people's ways
frag.hold: worries piled up without asking
frag.step: a place where you can speak as you are

basic.desc: Old Wisdom reversed means you haven't yet knocked on the door to ask for help. While fitting yourself to other people's ways, you may be missing the answer that fits you. It's worth thinking of when you keep putting off asking, telling yourself "I should handle this much on my own," and end up circling the same spot for a long time.
basic.overview: Believing you have to manage on your own, you've kept putting off asking. It speaks to a time when trying to fit others' ways hides the method that suits you.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you put up with ways that didn't suit you because "that's how everyone does it"?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, do you know you need help but can't bring it up, so you're holding out alone?
asks_pos.step: From here, which do you want to choose: solving it alone, or opening up to one person you trust?

key_rx.title: Write what you want to say
key_rx.how: Imagine telling someone exactly how things are, and write your situation and true feelings in a notebook without dressing them up. You don't have to show anyone.
key_rx.why: To focus on relationships where you can speak honestly about your situation, you can first write down what you'd say if you opened up as you are.

today.title: Write five honest lines
today.how: Write five lines in your notes about your situation right now, without dressing it up. Don't try to write well; just write what comes.
today.why: As a first step toward relationships where you can speak honestly, you put your situation as it is into words.

week.title: Write one honest page a day
week.how: Every day this week, write one page about today's situation and your true feelings without dressing them up. On the weekend, read them and look for what keeps repeating.
week.why: Writing down every day what you'd say if you opened up shows you, one by one, paths you couldn't see on your own.

direct.slow_short: the belief that you have to solve it alone

slow_rx.title: Write the questions you want to ask
slow_rx.how: Take the parts that are hard to solve alone and write three of them in a notebook as questions: "If I asked someone, what would I ask?"
slow_rx.why: If you don't ask because you think you have to solve it alone, the worry stays yours alone and you feel stuck, so writing it as a question shows you a way forward.

three.title: Refine your three questions
three.how: Read your questions out loud and rewrite them more specifically. Refine them so it's clear what you're stuck on.
three.why: The habit of not asking eases when you make your questions specific, and the belief that you have to solve it alone gets lighter.

signs: When someone asks how you've been, you tell them honestly instead of saying "I'm fine."
After sharing how you really feel, the worry "What if they think I'm weird?" settles quickly.
A worry you'd been turning over alone in your head boils down to two or three lines once you say it out loud.
reversed.tendency: You often fit yourself to the way others do things and go along even when it doesn't suit you. You've held on diligently, but when you face a worry, asking is hard and you easily end up stuck on your own.

basic.desc: Old Wisdom is a card of learning, trustworthy advice, and a place to lean on. It means you don't have to find the answer alone, because there's wisdom from those who walked this way before you. Its message is to look for clues in the writing of people who've been through the same worry, or in methods tested over time.
basic.overview: Like a sea turtle, this card stands for wisdom built up over a long time and learning you can lean on. It carries the meaning that the experience of people who walked the road before you can guide you through your worry, too.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you tried to find answers on your own, unsure whether it was okay to ask?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, have you been stuck alone for a long time on a problem that asking someone would quickly solve?
asks_pos.step: From here, which do you want to choose: finding the answer on your own, or leaning on wisdom you can trust?

frag.now: a worry held alone for a long time
frag.hold: weight you've carried by yourself
frag.step: learning you can trust and lean on

practices.title: Send one question
practices.how: Send one line to someone who's had a similar experience: "What did you do when this happened to you?"
practices.why: The experience of someone who's been there opens a new path for thoughts that were going in circles, and asking itself eases loneliness.

practices.title: Carry a line of wisdom
practices.how: Pick one sentence that stays with you and keep it on your phone's lock screen or in your notes for a week.
practices.why: Seeing a sentence that speaks to you often makes it an anchor you can pull out in shaky moments.

practices.title: Write advice to a friend
practices.how: Imagine a friend with the same worry, and write five lines of what you'd tell them.
practices.why: The advice we give others is kinder than what we tell ourselves, so it lets you see your worry from a step back.

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that you don't have to find the answer alone; there's wisdom beside you to lean on.
cards.about: This card speaks to times when you've been circling for a long time trying to find the answer alone. It sits in the place of The Hierophant in traditional tarot, which means tradition, teaching, and trustworthy advice. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the strength to lean on wisdom instead of carrying it all alone.
cards.about_when: This card shows up when you've been circling for a long time, trying to find the answer on your own.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of ‘The Hierophant’ in traditional tarot, which stands for tradition, teaching and trustworthy advice. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the strength to lean on wisdom instead of carrying everything alone.
asks: Is there a worry you've held onto alone for a long time, thinking “Is this even okay to ask?”
Do you feel like you've been going over the same thought for days, stuck in the same spot?

now: Wanting to find the answer yourself is a real strength. But when you hold the same question alone for too long, your thinking tends to walk the familiar path again instead of finding a new one. If you've been turning the same worry over for days and keep stopping at a similar conclusion, your thoughts may be going around a familiar loop.

How much has your thinking changed between when this worry first started and now? If it hasn't changed much, it may be time to borrow an outside view. One way is to pick a book or article about this kind of worry, read it, and underline the parts that differ from what you think. A worry you've built up alone takes on new shape when you share it with someone.
hold: Asking for help is often hard because you don't want to be a burden, or because you think, “I should handle this much on my own.” If there's been a task you stayed up late with alone, at work or at home, its weight may have felt bigger than it really was. That consideration and sense of responsibility may actually be isolating you.

When someone told you their worries, did it often feel like a burden? You may have more memories of being grateful they trusted you enough to tell you. If you write your worry on paper while imagining that someone you care about confided it to you, you may feel how willingly you'd listen. Asking isn't weakness; it's also a way of trusting the relationship.
step: Time-tested wisdom can be a book, a few words from someone more experienced, or help from a professional. The stories of people who walked the path before you can hold a map you haven't seen yet. If you slowly read a memoir by someone who went through a similar worry, or an essay people have read for years, you may find one sentence that fits your situation exactly.

Think of one person or resource you'd like to hear from about this worry. There's no need to rush, just as a sea turtle moves slowly. This week, it can help to spend about 20 minutes a day reading a book or article about a similar experience and copying down one sentence that stays with you. Writing down one question you want to ask is enough to start.

now: Hesitating to ask often comes from not wanting to impose. If you have a question but spend hours wandering on your own, thinking “I should figure this out myself,” it may be because you wanted so much to save other people's time. It may be worth checking, just once, whether that consideration is leaving you alone.
hold: The way everyone does it looks safe, but it may not be the answer that fits you. If you planned your day the way others recommend and just kept getting worn out, a different pace may suit your life better. Next to other people's way, write one line about “how I'd want to do it.”
step: Saying things as they are isn't about getting the right answer; it's about putting down some of the weight you've been carrying alone. If it's hard to say out loud, it can help to sort out the situation in writing first. If you write five or six lines, in order, about “what's been weighing on me lately,” a vague situation may become a little clearer.

image.scene_prompt: The character resting on a sunlit seabed beside old stones and shells, small fish gathered around listening, wise and patient.

key_rx.title: Read a trustworthy firsthand story
key_rx.how: Find a book or article by someone who went through a situation like yours, read it, and copy the sentences that helped into a notebook.
key_rx.why: When you focus on leaning on trusted people's experience or time-tested learning, the worry feels lighter and the answer shows up sooner.

today.title: Read one helpful passage
today.how: Read one passage of a trustworthy article or book related to your worry, and write the sentence that stays with you in your notes app.
today.why: As a first step toward leaning on trusted experience, even five minutes of reading makes the worry feel lighter.

week.title: Read three times, collect sentences
week.how: This week, read a passage of an article or book that could help with your worry three times, and keep the sentences that stay with you in one place.
week.why: Repeating time spent leaning on proven learning gives you more to lean on, so the worry gets lighter and the answer shows up sooner.

direct.slow_short: the habit of holding a worry alone and chewing on it

slow_rx.title: Put your worry on paper
slow_rx.how: Write the worry that's circling in your head on one page of a notebook, and at the end, write “the one thing I need right now.”
slow_rx.why: Holding a worry alone and chewing on it only makes it look heavier; once it's on paper, you can see its real size and the answer is easier to find.

three.title: Write the worry, underline one line
three.how: Write about your worry for 15 minutes without stopping, then reread it and underline the one sentence that feels heaviest.
three.why: The habit of chewing on things alone stops when you write them out and reread them, and once one heavy sentence is picked, you can see where to look for an answer.

signs: When a worry comes up, you look for writing or a book by someone experienced before you feel stuck.
You hear a few words from someone more experienced and nod, thinking, “Oh, I can do it this way.”
You spend less time wandering through search results and check just one or two trustworthy sources.
cards.tendency: When a worry comes up, you often think it over alone for a long time, trying to find the answer. You dig deep with persistence, but in front of a worry, you can end up circling the same spot for a long time.

cards.name: Swimming Side by Side
cards.core: The connection your heart wants starts with a choice that's true to you.

positions.now: Until now, you've probably worried about how others would see you and quietly adjusted your opinions to the mood. It meant fewer clashes, but you missed chances to say what you actually wanted. When people asked what you'd like, you may often have said “anything's fine” and let it pass.
positions.hold: Right now, you're going back and forth, weighing the person you want to get closer to against what you want. If this goes on, people and chances can drift away while you can't decide. You keep hesitating over whether to send a message, and in the end you close the chat without sending it.
positions.step: From here, whether you're meeting people or choosing work, focus on figuring out which standards really fit you. Once your standards are clear, it's easier to spot people walking in the same direction. You'll be able to turn down offers that feel wrong with a smile, and the time left goes to what you want.

reversed.core: Your heart is caught between connection and choice.

positions.now: Until now, you've probably kept your real feelings folded away out of fear of rejection, managing distance by just matching the mood. It was safe, but chances to really know each other kept shrinking. You may have only thought of what you wanted to say after the get-together ended, and gone over it alone on the way home.
positions.hold: Right now, you're afraid that showing yourself first will make things awkward, so you're keeping the door half-locked. If this goes on, the other person can't read you either, and misunderstandings can pile up. Even a small change in their tone has you replaying its meaning all day, and you wear out easily.
positions.step: From here, focus on what you want to say rather than how the other person will take it. Once your words are clear, even a short line can carry warmth. When you speak first, the other person starts sharing their own story too, and the conversation begins to run longer.

reversed.closing: What these three cards say together is that when you recognize your own feelings before checking theirs, connection gets easier too.
asks: Can you think of a moment when you wanted to get closer but stepped back for fear of getting hurt?
Have you decided not to share your feelings until you're sure of theirs?

frag.now: time spent watching for reactions first
frag.hold: crossed signals built on guesses
frag.step: the strength to know what you really feel

basic.desc: Swimming Side by Side reversed means the wish to get closer and the wish not to get hurt are pulling against each other. You may be so busy checking the other person's reaction that your real feelings get pushed to the back. It often comes up when you're watching their replies or expressions so closely that you can't say what you actually want.
basic.overview: It's a state of hesitating between wanting to get closer and not wanting to get hurt. It points to a time when watching the other person's reaction first easily pushes what you want to the back.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you swallowed what you wanted to say for fear of rejection, and watched the other person's face first?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you holding back your real feelings, waiting until you're sure of theirs?
asks_pos.step: From here, which would you rather choose: moving after you check their reaction, or moving once you know what you want?

key_rx.title: Write down what you want
key_rx.how: Leave out their reaction and write three things you want from this relationship in a notebook. Start each with “I'd like it if…”
key_rx.why: When you focus on what you really want rather than on their reaction, your own feelings get clearer and one reaction doesn't shake you as much.

today.title: Write one sentence about what you want
today.how: In your notes app, write one sentence about what you really want from this relationship, leaving out their reaction.
today.why: As a first step toward focusing on what you want, you put your feelings into one sentence, whatever their reaction.

week.title: Reread your wish every day
week.how: This week, read the wish you wrote down every day and check whether it's still the same today. If it's changed, rewrite it.
week.why: Checking what you want every day makes your feelings clearer, so one reaction shakes you less and it's easier to stay true to what you feel.

direct.slow_short: the habit of only guessing at their feelings

slow_rx.title: Separate guesses from facts
slow_rx.how: In a notebook, write what you've guessed about the other person and what actually happened in two columns. In the guess column, write “not confirmed.”
slow_rx.why: When you only guess at their feelings and put off checking, time passes with crossed signals; separating guesses from facts shows you what's missing.

three.title: Shrink the guess column
three.how: Read each item in the guess column, ask “Is that really true?”, and cross out the ones with no evidence.
three.why: The habit of only guessing at their feelings fades as you cross out guesses with no evidence, and crossed signals happen less.

signs: You spend fewer days shaken all day by one look on someone's face.
There are nights when you ask yourself, “What do I really want from this relationship?”
You say what you want to say briefly and from your side, without talking around it.
reversed.tendency: To avoid getting hurt, you often share your feelings only after seeing the other person's reaction. You avoid big fights, but in front of a worry, your real feelings pile up and both of you are left guessing.

basic.desc: Swimming Side by Side stands for relationships where hearts connect and choices that are true to you. It means good relationships and decisions start from the values you hold dear. When you're torn about who to be with or what to choose, it tells you to think first about what really matters to you.
basic.overview: Like a pair of mandarin ducks swimming side by side, it stands for relationships where hearts connect and choices that are true to you. It says you feel at ease when your choice fits what you value, not what others expect.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you made choices based on how others would see them rather than on what you feel?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you putting off your choice until you're sure of the other person's feelings?
asks_pos.step: From here, which would you rather choose: the option that looks good to others, or the one that fits what you value?

frag.now: choices made to meet others' expectations
frag.hold: hesitation between two pulls
frag.step: a choice in step with your values

practices.title: Three value cards
practices.how: Write the three values you care about most in relationships, and pair each with one action that fits it.
practices.why: Once it's clear what you value, the other person's reaction shakes you less and it's easier to make choices that are true to you.

practices.title: One sentence starting with “I”
practices.how: Tell someone you're comfortable with one feeling, in the form “When ___, I feel ___.”
practices.why: When you explain your feelings instead of blaming the other person, there's room for understanding instead of defensiveness.

practices.title: A small step closer
practices.how: Send a short message to someone you're grateful to, with a specific reason.
practices.why: Small acts of specific thanks build up warm moments of connection in a relationship, one at a time.

cards.closing: What these three cards say together is that when you know what you value, both connection and choice get easier.
cards.about: This card shows up when your heart is going back and forth over a relationship or an important choice. It sits in the place of ‘The Lovers’ in traditional tarot, which stands for love, harmony and choosing by your values. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as connection that starts from values that are true to you.
cards.about_when: This card shows up when your heart is going back and forth over a relationship or an important choice.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of ‘The Lovers’ in traditional tarot, which stands for love, harmony and choosing by your values. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as connection that starts from values that are true to you.
asks: Do you keep putting your own feelings off because you want to be sure of theirs first?
Have you been torn for a long time between the choice others recommend and the one you're drawn to?

now: Wanting to get closer and hesitating before a choice both come from the fact that it matters to you. If you pick lunch in seconds but stall for a long time only on things you care about, like people or your career path, those things may take up that much space in your life. Going back and forth doesn't mean you're indecisive; it means you care enough to be careful.

What do you most want to protect in this relationship or choice? Write it in a word or two, like ease, respect, growth or time together. That word can become your guide when you make up your mind. For example, you could type “respect” in your phone's notes app and open it whenever you feel unsure.
hold: Wanting to be sure of the other person's feelings first often comes from not wanting to get hurt. Following the choice that looks good to others can also feel safe, since at least you'll be blamed less. It's the moment when you wait for others to pick even though there's a place you want to go, or when you lean toward the path everyone around you calls good while choosing your career.

If you set aside the other person's reaction and how others see it, and look only at your own heart, what do you want? You don't have to say the answer out loud right away. At the end of the day, before bed, write one sentence starting with “What I really want is” in a note only you can see. Just knowing it yourself first can keep you from losing yourself in the relationship.
step: Swimming side by side doesn't mean moving exactly alike at the same speed. If one person shows care in words and the other in actions, there's little strain in going together as long as you care about the same things. At work or at home, people clash less when their ways differ but they want the same thing. Even with different moves, when you're facing the same direction, connection feels easy without forcing it.

Write down three values you hold dear, and look at how close the relationship or choice you're weighing is to them. For example, on a weekend morning, write three words like “honesty, ease, learning,” and next to each, score from 1 to 5 how close your current worry is. When you use those values as your guide, it's easier to own your choice, whatever the result.

now: It's natural to want to get closer and not want to get hurt at the same time. At work or in relationships, if you want to take a step closer and then freeze, thinking “What if they turn me down?”, both feelings are moving together. Rather than trying to get rid of one, recognize that both are ways of looking after yourself.
hold: Wanting to check the other person's reaction first is a shield against disappointment. But meanwhile your real feelings keep getting pushed back, so you may need time to sort out your own feelings first. If you've ever rewritten what you wanted to say several times and then deleted it, you can start by keeping that sentence in a note only you can see instead of deleting it.
step: When you write down one thing you really want, the other person's reaction shakes you less and you have a standard for choosing as yourself. If you write a short line like “I need time to myself on my days off,” you can reread it when someone's reaction unsettles you and remember where you stand. With that standard in place, connection feels easy without forcing it.

key_rx.why: When you focus on checking what you value, your values get clearer and it's easier to face the same direction in relationships and choices alike.

signs: When making plans, you think first of the time you value before you answer.

When the path people around you recommend differs from what you want, you notice the gap.
cards.tendency: You often read the expectations of the other person and those around you and try to fit in. That keeps relationships smooth, but in front of a worry, what you want easily gets pushed to the back.

cards.name: Riding the Wave
cards.core: Instead of fighting the water with all your strength, ride the wave forward.

positions.now: Until now, whenever you had a goal, you've probably thrown yourself at it and cleared the way by pushing through nonstop. That passion got you this far, but wanting too many things at once also split your energy. When those around you felt slow, you may often have stepped up first and pushed the pace.
positions.hold: Right now, you're full of drive, but what you want to do and what you have to do point in different directions. If this goes on, you can feel let down by how little ground you've covered for all your effort. Every time a new idea comes up, you drop what you were doing and switch to it, so few things get finished.
positions.step: From here, focus on narrowing your goals to one and growing whatever is going most smoothly. On a path that suits you, you pick up speed with less effort. Once a small win comes, help and chances from those around you start gathering there too.

reversed.core: Your drive to move forward has lost its direction and is going in circles.

positions.now: Until now, you've probably kept filling your schedule and running because staying still made you uneasy. You built up results as you stayed busy, but bit by bit they drifted from who you wanted to be. When someone asked how you've been, you may not have been able to think of anything to say besides “busy.”
positions.hold: Right now, you feel like you're sweating hard and getting nowhere, so you're in a rush. If this goes on, you may run even harder until you wear out and collapse. Looking back on the day before bed, you did a lot, but nothing seems left in your hands, and it feels empty.
positions.step: From here, focus on deciding where you really want to get to, rather than how fast you're going. Once your destination is clear, unneeded effort falls away and your steps get lighter. When the items you don't really need drop off your to-do list, your rest time comes back too.

reversed.closing: What these three cards say together is that when you reset your direction instead of your speed, the same strength can take you further.
asks: Have you often felt rushed lately because you're working hard but seem to be standing still?
Are you pushing your tired body on because you feel you'll fall behind if you rest?

direct.slow_short: the impatience to speed up first

slow_rx.title: Check direction before speeding up

slow_rx.why: Pushing hard without checking direction just drains you and keeps you in place, so check your direction before you speed up.

three.why: The impatience to speed up first settles when you sort your efforts by direction, and you can see where your strength will count.

signs: Even while busy, you stop for a moment and ask, “Where am I actually going right now?”
Out of a schedule scattered in many directions, you put one thing at the center and move around it.
Even if you seem slower than others, you feel less rushed because you trust your direction.
reversed.tendency: You often keep pushing your speed without rest, afraid you'll fall behind if you stop. So you get a lot done, but in front of a worry, you have no time to check where you're going and easily feel rushed.

basic.desc: Riding the Wave stands for the drive to move forward and the wisdom to ride the current. basic.overview: This card shows the strength to move forward by riding the waves instead of fighting them. It points to the strength of riding what's already running smoothly, rather than forcing your way through.

cards.closing: What these three cards say together is that you go further by riding the current in one direction than by fighting it with all your strength.
cards.about: This card shows up when the urge to move forward is building. It sits in the place of ‘The Chariot’ in traditional tarot, which stands for will, drive and the strength to set a direction and go. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the strength to move forward by riding the current instead of fighting it.
cards.about_when: This card shows up when the urge to move forward is building.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of ‘The Chariot’ in traditional tarot, which stands for will, drive and the strength to set a direction and go. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the strength to move forward by riding the current instead of fighting it.
asks: With so many directions to go, do you feel your energy doesn't really land anywhere?
Are you so eager to get ahead fast that you've been running without remembering to rest?

now: When the urge to move forward builds, you can feel a little excited and a little impatient. You might think of a new thing you want to try and look things up late into the night, or feel your mind racing ahead before you've even started. Seeing a direction, even faintly, is a sign that things have already started to sort themselves out inside you.

If you said the direction you most want to go right now in one sentence, what would it be? The shorter and clearer the sentence, the easier it is to decide where to put your energy. For example, write “I want a little more time for myself” and put it on your phone's lock screen or above your desk, and you'll be reminded of your direction several times a day.
hold: Trying to meet many expectations at once scatters your energy fast. Wanting to satisfy everyone is a sign of conscientiousness, but in the middle of it, the direction you meant to go can blur. If you try to be the reliable one outside, the warm one at home and the one who always makes time for friends, there may be no slot left for you on your own calendar.

Of the expectations you're working to meet, how many really have to be met right now? Some may be fine to push to later. If you write the expectations that come to mind on paper and mark them “this week,” “this month” or “later,” you may see what you can put down for now. Don't forget that rest is also preparation for riding the next wave.
step: Using the current means adding your strength to what's already working. Instead of cutting a new path from scratch, growing what's already moving, even a little, takes you further with less effort. For example, if the morning walks you've kept up are looking after your mood, add 10 minutes to the walk instead of starting a new workout from zero.

Think of a task that went even a little well recently, or a try that got a good response. How about putting your energy into that once more this week? For example, if jotting a short to-do list last week made your day easier, do it again this week on the same day at the same time. Like a dolphin borrowing the wave's strength, your movements get much lighter.

now: When you're trying hard but don't feel any progress, it's easy to get impatient. If you're holding onto a bit of everything each day, like work, chores and things you want to learn, you may be tired every evening with nothing feeling finished. That may not be from lack of strength, but because your strength is split in many directions.
hold: When you're used to pushing on without rest, stopping can actually feel unsettling. You may be there if, even on a rare day off, you check your to-do list again, or you get up quickly after sitting down because it feels like you've missed a thing. But you can't ride a wave on empty, so rest is part of moving forward too.
step: Resetting to one direction lets the same strength take you further. Write the direction you most want to go right now in one sentence, and this week set aside one task unrelated to it. For example, if your direction is “recovering body and mind,” take one non-urgent clean-up or one prep job that can wait off this week's list.

slow_rx.why: When your direction is split many ways, your energy can't gather and you move forward less; keeping just one gathers your energy.

three.why: Straining with your direction split stops when you narrow the options to one, and your energy gathers in one place so you get further.

signs: You can say the direction you want to go this month in one sentence.
You put a little more energy into what's already running well and let the rest go.
You notice and remember things that went smoothly without straining.
cards.tendency: You often push hard toward what you want to do. Your drive is strong, but in front of a worry, chasing many expectations at once can split your energy and wear you out.

cards.name: Making the Pearl
cards.core: Time spent holding uncomfortable feelings makes you stronger.

positions.now: Until now, even when you felt hurt or upset, you've probably kept it inside without showing it. You looked calm, but the residue that settled stayed unresolved. When feelings came up, you may often have found a busy task so the moment would pass.
positions.hold: Right now, feelings you tried hard to ignore keep suddenly coming back and shaking you several times a day. If this goes on, you'll spend so much energy pushing them down that there's not enough left for what you need to do. On quiet nights, the feelings you held down rise up all at once and make it hard to fall asleep.
positions.step: From here, focus on calmly looking at why this feeling came. Once you know the reason, the discomfort that was bothering you turns into a signal telling you what you need. You'll be able to bring up what hurt you calmly with the other person, and the same thing will happen less often.

reversed.core: You've been holding discomfort alone for too long.

positions.now: Until now, saying it's hard felt like a weakness, so you've probably smiled and handled everything alone. People said you cope well, but few were beside you to help. Even on hard days, you may have kept your plans as if nothing was wrong and kept cutting your rest time.
positions.hold: Right now, you're brushing off the tiredness your body is signaling and keeping on running. If this goes on, a moment can come when all your motivation suddenly cuts out. More days are getting by on coffee and sweets, and some weekends end with you just lying down.
positions.step: From here, focus on sorting out which parts of the load you carry alone you can put down. Carried with someone, the same load is much lighter and lasts longer. Once you've had the experience of getting help, asking comes more easily the next time things get hard.

reversed.closing: What these three cards say together is that holding it in isn't the only kind of strength; letting uncomfortable feelings out is also a way to protect yourself.
asks: Did you brush off a task that was too much this week too, telling yourself “This much is fine”?
Is there a feeling you haven't voiced because saying it's hard might make you look weak?

basic.desc: Making the Pearl reversed means you've been holding discomfort alone for too long. The idea that only enduring is strong may be blocking the path to asking for help. It's worth thinking of when you keep brushing off overwhelming things with “This much is fine” until one day you're completely worn out.
basic.overview: It's a time when you've held hard things in alone and endured for too long. It points to a time when you've spent all your strength enduring, and your share of the weight has grown far too big.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you brushed off even overwhelming things as “fine” and endured them alone?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you putting off asking for help because saying it's hard might make you look weak?

key_rx.how: Write everything you've been carrying alone lately in a notebook, and circle the heaviest one.
key_rx.why: When you focus on sharing your load, you can let uncomfortable feelings out, and the same tasks feel much less heavy.

week.why: Letting your load out every day keeps uncomfortable feelings from piling up, so the same tasks feel less heavy.

direct.slow_short: the habit of just putting up with what's too much

slow_rx.title: Score how overwhelmed you are
slow_rx.how: Twice a day, rate how overwhelmed you are from 1 to 10 in your notebook, and if it's over 7, stop what you're doing and rest for 10 minutes.
slow_rx.why: Putting up with what's too much means you notice the exhaustion late and run out of strength; scoring it in writing helps you notice early.

three.title: Lighten the overload
three.how: List everything that feels overwhelming, check each one for “Can this wait until after this week?”, and take those off your schedule.
three.why: The habit of just putting up with what's too much loosens when you pick out what to drop, and you get room to rest before you run out of strength.

signs: After swallowing hard things alone, you hear yourself say, “It's been a lot lately.”
After talking through your load, you feel your shoulders drop a little.
When work piles up, you don't try to finish it all alone and can hand some of it off.
reversed.tendency: When things are hard, you often hold it in alone rather than ask for help. So you endure well, but in front of a worry, you can go on without noticing you're already worn out.

basic.desc: Making the Pearl stands for the gentle strength of holding uncomfortable feelings. It means that taking time to feel your emotions instead of avoiding them makes you steadier. It's a card that encourages you to practice noticing, “This is how I feel right now,” instead of forcing uncomfortable feelings away.
basic.overview: Making the Pearl means the gentle strength of holding uncomfortable feelings instead of avoiding them. It points to the strength that grows steadier when you acknowledge uncomfortable feelings instead of pushing them away.

practices.title: Name the feeling
practices.how: Give the feeling you have right now a one-word name and say, “I'm feeling ___ right now.”
practices.why: Naming a feeling is known to soften how strong it feels.

cards.closing: What these three cards say together is that time spent holding uncomfortable feelings can become the pearl that makes you stronger.
cards.about: This card shows up when you've been enduring uncomfortable feelings for a long time. It sits in the place of ‘Strength’ in traditional tarot, which stands for the inner strength that tames what's rough with gentleness. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the strength that grows steady by holding discomfort.
cards.about_when: This card shows up when you've been enduring uncomfortable feelings for a long time.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of ‘Strength’ in traditional tarot, which stands for the inner strength that tames what's rough with gentleness. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the strength that grows steady by holding discomfort.
asks: Are you pressing uncomfortable feelings down, telling yourself “It's no big deal”?
Are you so used to enduring that you let even overwhelming things slide?

now: Getting through the day while holding discomfort you don't show takes more strength than you'd think. There may be days when you smile through the day as usual despite what's bothering you, and only notice how stiff your shoulders are once you get home. Even if no one else knows, the effort your heart made to get through that time deserves recognition.

When did this discomfort first start? It's okay if you don't remember exactly. If a time comes to mind, just write one line about the situation back then, and that's enough for today. Simply recognizing “So I've been carrying this” can ease some of the tension.
hold: When you try to get rid of an uncomfortable feeling fast, your mind checks on it more often. The feeling seems as big as the effort you spend pushing it away. You may have noticed that on the days you vow “I'll stop thinking about it,” it comes back even more often and keeps circling in your head until bed.

When a feeling comes up, instead of “It has to go,” try naming it once: “So this is how I feel right now.” For example, when you feel a wave of emotion, at work or while doing chores, just note it to yourself in one sentence: “Ah, I'm feeling hurt right now.” A named feeling feels less strange, and a feeling that's less strange feels less scary.
step: When a clam can't spit out a grain of sand, it wraps it up and makes a pearl. Practicing being with discomfort is similar: the time when you can't fix a feeling right away can make your heart sturdier. For example, if you keep a hurt feeling to one side for a day or two and quietly watch it, what that feeling really wanted can become a little clearer.

When an uncomfortable feeling comes up, breathe slowly for about five minutes and notice where in your body it is. For example, if your chest feels tight, rest your palm gently on your chest, breathe in for a count of four and out for a count of six. As you practice keeping it beside you without trying to change it, the same feeling may sweep you away less.

now: When you get used to brushing off what's too much as “fine,” you lose track of how tired you really are. If someone asks if you're okay and “Yeah, I'm fine” comes out before you even think, but when you're alone you don't feel like doing anything, it may be a small signal from your heart. You're allowed to say it's okay not to be okay.
hold: Holding it in isn't the only kind of strength. Saying it's hard and accepting help is also a solid way to protect yourself, and it actually helps you last longer. For example, if today was especially overwhelming, moving one task to tomorrow or turning off the lights earlier than usual is also a way of helping yourself.
step: Letting uncomfortable feelings out in words or writing isn't becoming weak; it gives your heart room to breathe. Even one short note is fine. Before bed, you can write a few words under the heading “What bothered me today” and close the notebook. The more you let out, the lighter the weight on your heart gets, bit by bit.

theories: Linehan: Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), distress tolerance

key_rx.why: When you focus on acknowledging uncomfortable feelings as they are rather than getting rid of them, you can keep them beside you and grow steadier.

today.why: As a first step toward acknowledging uncomfortable feelings, you accept one in a single line without trying to get rid of it.

week.title: Acknowledge a feeling once a day

week.why: Repeating the act of acknowledging uncomfortable feelings builds your ability to keep them beside you, and you grow steadier.

direct.slow_short: the habit of pushing uncomfortable feelings away

slow_rx.how: When an uncomfortable feeling comes up, don't try to erase it; set a five-minute timer and just notice where in your body it is.
slow_rx.why: The more you push an uncomfortable feeling away, the more often it returns and the more energy you spend; watching without pushing means less energy spent fighting.

three.title: Watch a feeling for 10 minutes
