three.why: The habit of pushing uncomfortable feelings away loosens as you watch them, and the energy you spent fighting them each day is left over.

signs: When irritation comes up, you name it: “I'm irritated right now.”
Even with uncomfortable feelings, your days go on: you eat and you get your work done.
Even on days when tears come, you don't treat yourself as strange and just let them be for a while.
cards.tendency: You often don't show uncomfortable feelings easily and quietly carry them. Your patience helps you get through the day, but in front of a worry, discomfort you've held for a long time can stay just as it is.

cards.name: My Own Lantern
cards.core: Time alone can be a lantern that lights up who you are.

positions.now: Until now, whenever things got complicated, you've probably stepped away from crowded places and cleared your head in a space of your own. It kept you centered, but some days you went over things alone and got stuck in the same thoughts. You may have found a few ways of sorting out your thoughts that only you know, like walks or music.
positions.hold: Right now, you want to be quiet, yet a sense of emptiness keeps washing over you, and you're unsure what you want. If this goes on, time can slip by while you don't know whether to rest or to see people. Even during time you set aside to rest, you keep checking your phone, curious about what others are up to.
positions.step: From here, focus on protecting your time alone while staying in touch with one person you can open up to. When solitude and human warmth go together, your direction gets much clearer. Having one name that comes to mind when a worry comes up makes your rest time less lonely.

reversed.core: Your time alone is turning from rest into isolation.

positions.now: Until now, whenever things felt noisy inside, you've probably cut back on contact and quietly disappeared. It was easier for a while, but before you knew it, fewer people were reaching out. You may have muted the group chat and let unread messages pile up.
positions.hold: Right now, seeing people feels like a hassle, and you're sunk in the feeling that talking won't help anyway. If this goes on, the loneliness gets deeper while your strength to reach out keeps fading. You're not comfortable alone, and you feel out of place among people too, so the days go by heavily.
positions.step: From here, focus on thinking of just one person you feel safe opening up to. Sharing even a small story loosens the stuck feeling. Once a conversation with one person keeps going, the energy to show up to other gatherings slowly comes back too.

reversed.closing: What these three cards say together is that when time alone gets heavy, one small bit of warmth can light the way again.
asks: Are there times when being alone weighs on you more than it rests you?
Have you swallowed what you wanted to say, thinking “No one would understand anyway”?

frag.now: time spent hiding away inside
frag.hold: distance that keeps growing
frag.step: one person you reconnect with

basic.desc: My Own Lantern reversed means your time alone is turning from rest into isolation. The thought that no one would understand may be widening the distance between you and others. It often comes up when the longer you're alone, the heavier you feel instead of lighter.
basic.overview: It's a state where time alone weighs on you more and more instead of resting you. It points to a time when the thought that no one would understand easily feels bigger than it really is.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you chosen to swallow it alone, thinking “They wouldn't get it if I told them”?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you closing off even from people you're comfortable with, thinking no one would understand?
asks_pos.step: From here, which would you rather choose: enduring alone inside, or sharing how you feel with one person you're comfortable with?

key_rx.title: Words for someone you can open up to
key_rx.how: Think of one person you can open up to, write their name, and write in your notebook what you'd like to tell them. You don't have to send it.
key_rx.why: When you choose one person you can open up to instead of enduring alone, heavy thoughts lighten and time alone becomes rest again.

today.title: Write five lines you want to say
today.how: Think of one person you can open up to, and write five lines in your notes app of what you'd like to tell them.
today.why: As a first step toward choosing someone you can open up to, you put what you want to say into writing and lighten heavy thoughts.

week.title: Add one line each day
week.how: This week, every day, add one line of what you'd like to tell that person. On the weekend, read it over and pick what you most wanted to say.
week.why: Writing out what you want to say every day lightens heavy thoughts, and your time alone becomes rest again.

direct.slow_short: the thought that no one understands

slow_rx.title: Find experiences that prove it wrong
slow_rx.how: Write “No one would understand,” then find three experiences that don't fit that thought and write them in your notebook.
slow_rx.why: Believing that thought as it is widens the distance from others; finding experiences that don't fit lets you check whether it's really true.

three.title: Find more experiences that prove it wrong
three.how: Add two more to the three experiences you wrote, and for each, write one line about who understood you and how.
three.why: The thought that no one understands weakens as experiences that don't fit it pile up, so the distance from others stops growing.

signs: After saying what you'd been struggling with alone to one person, you notice you feel lighter.
Over a meal, you find yourself opening up: “Actually, this has been going on lately.”
After the conversation, time alone feels like comfortable rest again.
reversed.tendency: The harder things get, the more you tend to tell no one and go inward. That's how you protect yourself, but in front of a worry, you can drift away from people and the loneliness grows.

basic.desc: My Own Lantern stands for time alone and deep reflection. It means quiet time looking at yourself lights the way. It's a card that goes well with stepping away from people for a while to take a walk or write in a journal and sort out your thoughts.
basic.overview: This card stands for time spent quietly sorting out your thoughts alone and finding your own way. If you're worn out from being around people, stepping away to be alone for a while is good rest too.

asks_pos.now: Until now, when things got hard, haven't you tried to find the answer alone rather than telling anyone?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you going along not quite sure whether your time alone is rest or loneliness?
asks_pos.step: From here, which would you rather choose: finding answers only on your own, or keeping one person you trust within your quiet time?

frag.now: time spent sorting out thoughts alone
frag.hold: unsure if it's rest or loneliness
frag.step: stillness with one lantern lit

practices.title: A walk without your phone
practices.how: Leave your phone behind and walk for 20 minutes, letting whatever thoughts come up just pass.
practices.why: Walking without input gives your thoughts room to sort themselves out.

practices.title: One-question journal
practices.how: Write an answer to just one question: “What matters most to me these days?”
practices.why: When you answer just one question, scattered thoughts gather around what matters to you.

practices.title: One lantern person
practices.how: Send a short message to one person you'd like to check in on.
practices.why: Keeping one connection going, even in your time alone, protects your solitude from turning into isolation.

cards.closing: What these three cards say together is that even in time alone, one lantern and one connection keep you from losing your way.
cards.about: This card shows up when you need to step back from people for a while to think. It sits in the place of ‘The Hermit’ in traditional tarot, which stands for reflection in solitude and a lantern that lights the inner self. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the strength to turn time alone into time that lights up who you are.
cards.about_when: This card shows up when you need to step back from people for a while to think.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of ‘The Hermit’ in traditional tarot, which stands for reflection in solitude and a lantern that lights the inner self. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the strength to turn time alone into time that lights up who you are.
asks: These days, does time alone feel more comfortable than being with people?
Are there days when your thinking goes deeper and deeper alone and you keep landing on the same conclusion?

now: Wanting to be alone is often less about disliking relationships and more about needing space to sort things out inside. It's like when you want to mute the group chat for a while, or walk home quietly with just your earbuds in. A stretch when you talk less may be time when your heart is quietly digesting what's happened.

What do you mostly think about when you're alone these days? If a question keeps repeating among those thoughts, it may be the topic your heart is trying to sort out right now. It can help to write that question on a page of your notebook. For example, write a question like “What do I want to change right now?” at the top, and add one line a day for a week as answers come to you.
hold: Wanting to be alone and feeling lonely look alike on the outside, so they mix easily. When they mix, you get worn out seeing people and feel empty being alone. If you've put off all your plans and stayed home but still can't rest and keep staring at your phone, rest and loneliness may be mixed together.

When you're alone, do you feel more at ease, or do you sink lower? If you feel at ease, you need rest right now; if you sink, it may be a sign you need someone's warmth. For example, after about 30 minutes alone in the evening, write how you feel as a number from 0 to 10, and over a few days the pattern starts to show. Just noticing that difference shows you what you need.
step: Time alone that you choose on purpose is different from isolation. You need time to look back at yourself to find the strength to return to people. For example, you can spend two hours on a weekend morning walking alone or journaling, and just looking at a photo with someone you care about in the evening keeps the thread connected. A lantern is a small connection that keeps you from losing your way, even alone.

Set aside one quiet time just for you this week, and separately, think of one person you'd like to check in with. For example, spending an hour on Sunday evening walking or journaling with your phone put away, and writing down the name that came to mind in a corner of your planner, is enough. When time going deep and a thread that keeps you connected go together, time alone feels warmer.

now: When time alone goes on for long, your thoughts tend to deepen in only one direction. If you're feeling heavier and heavier, it may be a sign that right now you need a little warmth more than rest. There are small things that can warm you up even alone, like sitting in a sunny spot or putting on a song you love.
hold: The thought that no one would understand comes from wanting not to get hurt. If you've ever been about to share a worry and swallowed it, thinking “They wouldn't get it even if I explained,” that thought protects you and leaves you alone at the same time. Even if you can't be understood completely, there can be people around you who understand a small part.
step: Taking just one step outside doesn't have to mean a big get-together. Start with low-pressure warmth, like a hello on a walk or a short chat at a shop you like. For example, just walking a loop around your neighborhood for about 15 minutes a day, taking in the sounds and sunlight, counts as one step out of your room.

theories: Winnicott: the capacity to be alone

image.scene_prompt: The character holding a small warm lantern in a quiet boat on a dark calm sea at night, solitary but peaceful.

cards.caution: If loneliness is strong and there are crisis-watch signs, lead the reading with ‘one lantern person (connection)’ rather than ‘staying alone’.
cards.art_note: Final art should use the relationship test's hidden character ‘Old Man of the Sea’ illustration as is (do not use the turtle-like sage from the draft). No Hemingway name, likeness, or quotes from the original.

key_rx.title: Write down alone time and one trusted person
key_rx.how: Set one time a day to reflect alone, and write the name of one person you trust in your notebook.
key_rx.why: When you focus on protecting time to reflect alone while keeping a thread with one person you trust, your path gets clearer.

today.title: Block out alone time
today.how: Put one slot in today's schedule to reflect alone, and write the name of one person you trust in your notes app.
today.why: As a first step toward focusing on time to reflect alone and one trusted person, you put both on today's schedule.

week.title: 15 minutes of reflecting alone each day
week.how: This week, protect your alone time at the same time each day, and write down what came up afterward. Keep the trusted person's name at the top of the notebook.
week.why: As days with both quiet time and a trusted person add up, your path becomes clearer.

direct.slow_short: not knowing whether you need rest or company

slow_rx.title: Score rest and loneliness
slow_rx.how: In your notebook, score “I want to rest” and “I feel lonely” from 1 to 10 for how you feel right now, and treat the higher one as what you need today.
slow_rx.why: If you can't tell whether you want rest or company, you just keep thinking; scoring them shows you what you need.

three.title: Compare the two scores
three.how: Recall and write your scores for wanting rest and feeling lonely over the last three days, and compare which was higher.
three.why: Not knowing whether you need rest or company clears up when you compare the two scores, so you can act knowing what you need.

signs: Evenings alone feel like time to reflect rather than lonely.
A short talk with someone you trust comes back to you at the end of the day and steadies you.
When you want to sort out complicated thoughts, you have a place of your own, like a walk or a journal.
cards.tendency: When things get complicated, you often step away from people and sort out your thoughts alone. You keep to your own standards well, but in front of a worry, your thinking can deepen in only one direction.

cards.name: The Turning Current
cards.core: This current will pass too. The tide keeps turning.

positions.now: Until now, whenever the unexpected hit, you've probably accepted it first and worked out how to hold on within it. Your adaptability grew, but you couldn't show anyone how uneasy you felt inside. Even after big changes like moving or changing jobs, you may have jumped straight into the next thing without a break.
positions.hold: Right now, things around you are changing so fast that you can't tell where to set your footing. If this goes on, you can be weighed down by the fear that everything will keep shaking without end. Even when you make plans, you worry they'll change soon, so you put off anything far ahead and barely hold onto what's in front of you.
positions.step: From here, focus on the small things you can choose today rather than blaming your circumstances. Once you see the share that's in your hands, you stay centered even as things change. As small things you've done add up, you start to trust that you can hold steady through the next change too.

reversed.core: You're tensed up from fighting the current of change.

positions.now: Until now, when unfamiliar change came, you've probably clung to familiar ways first and looked away from the new reality. That stubbornness kept you centered, but you didn't notice new chances passing by. You may even have lost out by holding off on a new app or system after it changed.
positions.hold: Right now, you keep looking back on times you miss, and your strength to adjust to the present is draining away. If this goes on, frustration piles up and a fresh start keeps slipping further away. Your face only lights up when you talk with people from before, and you go quiet where you are now.
positions.step: From here, focus on looking at what you miss and what you've newly gained separately. Once you see what you can use in your new surroundings, your steps get much lighter. When you hit a moment where skills you learned before still work in the new place, unfamiliar days start to feel comfortable.

reversed.closing: What these three cards say together is that your heart gets lighter when you look for small moves you can choose within the current, instead of fighting it.
asks: Are you still holding onto the old ways because the new situation feels unfamiliar?
Does the thought “It was better before” come up several times a day?

frag.now: holding on to familiar ground
frag.hold: a heart that clings to the past
frag.step: steps into a new current

basic.desc: The Turning Current reversed means you're tensed up from fighting a changing current. Wanting to go back to how things were may be keeping you from riding the new current. It's close to finding it hard to accept a changed situation and often thinking, “It used to be like this.”
basic.overview: It's the picture of finding it hard to accept a changed current and holding onto how things were. It points to a time when you're using a lot of strength fighting a current that has already changed.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you held on, hoping to go back to how things were, instead of accepting the change?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you spending so much energy getting the old days back that you're missing what you can do now?
asks_pos.step: From here, which would you rather choose: holding on to get the old days back, or finding what you can do within the changed current?

key_rx.title: Write down what you can choose now
key_rx.how: Write three things you can choose in your notebook, given how things have changed, then pick one and add it to this week's to-dos.
key_rx.why: When you focus on what you can choose in the changed situation rather than the way back, you can see where to stand even somewhere unfamiliar.

today.title: One thing you can choose now
today.how: In your notes app, write one thing you can choose today in the changed situation, and choose it right away.
today.why: When you focus on what you can choose in the changed situation, you get one place to stand today, even somewhere unfamiliar.

week.title: Choose one new thing a day
week.how: This week, every day, choose one thing you can choose in the changed situation and try it, then write one line in the evening about how it went.
week.why: As you keep choosing within the changed situation, the strength you used to hold on goes into the new current, and you find more places to stand.

direct.slow_short: the thought that you have to go back to how things were

slow_rx.title: Split before and now
slow_rx.how: In two columns of your notebook, write what you miss about how things were and what has changed now, then look for anything you've gained from each change.
slow_rx.why: The thought that you have to go back makes it hard to accept the changed situation; splitting before and now saves the strength you'd spend fighting it.

three.title: Write to let go of what you miss
three.how: Write about what you miss from before for 15 minutes in your notebook, like a letter, and at the end, write one thing to try in the current situation.
three.why: The thought that you have to go back loosens when you put what you miss into writing, and you save the strength you spent fighting.

signs: You think about the old ways less and look for what you can do now.
Even somewhere unfamiliar, you're getting to know a place to sit and a tool to use, one at a time.
Your shoulders, stiff from holding on, loosen a little when you try a new thing.
reversed.tendency: Even when things change, you often hold on by keeping to familiar ways. That persistence is reassuring, but in front of a worry, it's hard to accept a changed current and you easily run out of strength.

basic.desc: The Turning Current stands for the turning cycles of life and change. It means the current situation will pass too, and even within it, there are choices you can make. It often comes up in times when things change regardless of what you want, like a job change, a move or a shift in a relationship.
basic.overview: This card tells you that good times and hard times don't stay in one place; they keep turning. Even when things aren't going your way, there's still one thing you can choose within it.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you worked hard to adjust on your own every time an unexpected change came?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you going along as if this hard stretch will last a long time?
asks_pos.step: From here, which would you rather choose: waiting for the current to change, or finding what you can choose within it?

frag.now: adapting in a shifting current
frag.hold: a heart shaken by change
frag.step: a direction chosen within the current

practices.title: Remember a wave that passed
practices.how: Write down one hard time that has passed and what helped you through it.
practices.why: Memories of getting through hard times are the closest proof that this current can pass too.

practices.title: Three things you can choose today
practices.how: Write three things in your day today that you can choose, then pick one and do it.
practices.why: When you find what you can choose even in a current you can't change, your sense of direction comes back instead of feeling swept along.

practices.title: A week of mood weather
practices.how: For a week, once a day, record your mood weather as sunny, cloudy or rainy.
practices.why: Recording your mood weather lets you see for yourself that moods change and pass, like weather.

cards.closing: What these three cards say together is that this current will pass too, and even within it, there are moves you can choose.
cards.about: This card shows up when things are changing regardless of what you want. It sits in the place of ‘Wheel of Fortune’ in traditional tarot, which stands for the turning cycles of life and times of change. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the moves you can choose within a changing current.
cards.about_when: This card shows up when things are changing regardless of what you want.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of ‘Wheel of Fortune’ in traditional tarot, which stands for the turning cycles of life and times of change. In Ssol Tarot, we read it as the moves you can choose within a changing current.
asks: Facing an unexpected change, have you ever thought, “Why now, of all times?”
Does it weigh on you that this hard stretch feels like it will go on and on?

now: When things change regardless of what you want, your mind looks for footing first. It's like when your role changes, a close relationship shifts, or your daily rhythm is suddenly shaken, and for a while you freeze, not knowing what to do first. Looking around and checking things right now isn't only anxiety; it's a natural move to find your place in a new current.

What has stayed the same through this change? Thinking of what hasn't changed, like the people beside you, habits you keep and things you love, gives you a place to hold onto in a shaky current. For example, keep one small habit going today, like your morning cup of tea or the music you listen to before bed.
hold: In hard times, it can feel like this will go on forever. That's because time seems to stop as much as your heart is worn out. For example, when the same worry drags on for weeks, it's easy to think “It'll always be like this,” but that may be a feeling created by how tired you are right now.

Looking back over the last few years, was there a time that “felt like it would never end, but passed”? Bring that memory out for a moment. If you write that time in one line and add next to it “what got me through then,” you may also see the strength you can use now. It reminds you that currents keep changing, and this one can pass that way too.
step: Accepting the current is different from giving up. It means pulling back the energy you spent on what you can't change and moving it to small moves you can choose. For example, you can't undo a changed schedule, but within it, you can choose to set aside 10 minutes a day as your own rest.

Write down three things you can choose in your current situation. Even very small ones are fine. When the choices in your hands add up, like how you start your day, when you check the news and who you lean on, you can keep your direction. It's even better to pick one tonight and jot it down so you can do it first thing tomorrow morning.

now: It's hard to accept a changing situation because the place you had before meant so much to you. If you keep looking at old photos or records after a familiar place changes, like with a move, a job change or a shift in a relationship, that place held that much meaning. Instead of blaming yourself for holding on, first recognize what you wanted to protect.
hold: Wanting to go back is missing the stability that familiarity gives. If you find one part of that stability you can still bring with you, the new current may feel less strange. For example, there may be habits you can carry into your life now even though your place has changed, like a morning routine you used to enjoy or a walk you loved.
step: The one thing you can choose in a changed situation can be very small. For example, decide just one thing for tomorrow morning, like opening the window and drinking a glass of water instead of checking your phone as soon as you wake up. Deciding even just how you start your day eases the feeling of being dragged along by the current.

image.scene_prompt: The character gliding in a wide circle along a spiral sea current, golden spiral pattern in the water, cycles and time.

key_rx.title: Find the part you decide
key_rx.how: In your notebook, split what won't change in your situation these days from what you can decide, and circle the part you can decide.
key_rx.why: When you focus on the part you can decide yourself, even within a current you can't change, change becomes less frightening.

today.title: Three things you can decide today
today.how: In your notes app, write three things within today that you can decide yourself. Small things like what to have for lunch are fine.
today.why: As a first step toward focusing on the part you can decide, you make the choices in your hands today visible.

week.title: Decide one thing a day
week.how: This week, every day, pick one of the things you can decide and decide it your way, then write one line in the evening about what you decided.
week.why: As experiences of deciding for yourself add up, change becomes less frightening, even within a current you can't change.

direct.slow_short: the certainty that things will stay this way

slow_rx.title: Rewrite the certain sentence
slow_rx.how: Write “It's going to stay like this,” then rewrite it as “It's like this now, but it could change,” and write two things that could change.
slow_rx.why: When you're certain things will stay this way, worry gets heavy; rewriting the sentence lightens the worry.

three.title: Rewrite three worry sentences
three.how: Write three sentences in your notebook that state a worry as certain, and rewrite each in the form “Right now ___, but it could change.”
three.why: The certainty that things will stay this way weakens when you rewrite the sentences, and your heart keeps pace with how fast things change.

signs: Even as things change, you work out what you can choose.
Even when your work schedule suddenly changes, you make the small choices that are yours.
When you hear news of a change, instead of your heart sinking, you think, “So what will I do?”
cards.tendency: Even when things change, you often find a foothold one way or another. Your ability to adapt is strong, but in front of a worry, carrying your shaken feelings alone can weigh you down.

cards.name: Still Balance
cards.core: Hold out a fair scale to yourself, too.

positions.now: Until now, you've probably eased conflicts quietly by thinking of other people's side first. Because of that, putting your own hurt feelings on the back burner has become a habit. There may have been nights when you got home from a get-together and kept going over whether anyone had felt left out.
positions.hold: Right now, you're working out how much of this is yours to carry. If things stay as they are, it's easy to lose track of what you really feel while you worry about how others see you. With a decision in front of you, you keep checking whether it's the fair choice, and the days feel long.
positions.step: From here, focus on giving their side and your side the same weight. Then you can choose an answer calmly without taking anyone's side. Once you see that saying what you think doesn't break the relationship, the next round of working things out gets easier.

reversed.core: The scale is tipped to one side.

positions.now: Until now, whenever things went wrong, you've probably come down on yourself before anyone else. You've stayed responsible and kept going, but kindness toward yourself kept getting pushed to the back. Even on days you were praised, you may have thought first of the one thing you fell short on and refused to grade yourself generously.
positions.hold: Right now, you're spending your day's energy measuring how much of this is your fault. If things stay as they are, it's easy to wear yourself out without touching the things that actually need doing. Even an offhand comment sounds like blame, and you end up chewing on it for a long time.
positions.step: From here, focus on what you'd say to a close friend who went through the same thing. Then the words you give yourself get much gentler. Once you start counting what you did well as carefully as what you did wrong, the tipped scale levels out little by little.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that balance comes back when you give yourself a fair look, instead of blaming the tipped scale.
asks: Do you understand other people's mistakes but come down especially hard on your own?
Have there been nights your mind couldn't rest because you kept arguing over who was right?

frag.now: the time spent blaming yourself first
frag.hold: a scale that's strict only with you
frag.step: a standard that's kind to you, too

basic.desc: Still Balance reversed means the scale is tipped to one side. You may be strict only with yourself, or your mind can't rest because you keep weighing right and wrong. Letting other people's mistakes go while chewing on your own for days, or lying awake over who was right, is close to what this card means.
basic.overview: This is a time when you're especially strict with yourself, or your mind can't rest because you keep weighing who was right. It points to a time when going over past mistakes makes even your current judgment feel heavy.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you kept grilling yourself over mistakes you'd easily let a friend off for?
asks_pos.hold: Are you going back over what happened right now, still trying to work out whose fault it was?
asks_pos.step: From here, would you rather keep grilling yourself over mistakes, or understand yourself the way a friend would?

key_rx.title: Talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a friend
key_rx.how: When self-blaming thoughts come up, write down in a notebook what you'd say to a friend who went through the same thing, then read those words back to yourself.
key_rx.why: When you focus on using the same standard for yourself that you use for a friend, the scale tips less and your judgment calms down.

today.title: One line you'd say to a friend
today.how: Think of one thing you blamed yourself for today, and write one line you'd say to a friend in the same spot.
today.why: Using your friend standard on yourself brings a scale tipped by self-blame back a little.

week.title: Turn self-blame into a friend's words
week.how: This week, each time a self-blaming sentence comes up, write it in a notebook, and underneath, rewrite it as what you'd say to a friend.
week.why: Rewriting self-blame as a friend's words again and again builds the habit of treating yourself by the same standard.

direct.slow_short: the habit of weighing right and wrong

slow_rx.title: Measure how big the thing you blamed yourself for really was
slow_rx.how: When you catch yourself blaming yourself over a small thing, write it in a notebook and rate how big it really was on a scale of 1 to 5.
slow_rx.why: When your measuring stick points at yourself, small things feel huge, so rating the size of the problem cuts down the self-blame.

three.title: Score the small stuff
three.how: Write down three recent things you blamed yourself for, rate how big each one really was from 1 to 5, then cross out the low scores.
three.why: Seeing the real size of what you blame yourself for saves the energy you were spending on weighing it.

signs: When you make a mistake, you think of what a friend would say and say it to yourself, too.
You grade your own work a little more generously.
Even while looking back on what went wrong, the tone you use with yourself gets softer.
reversed.tendency: When things go wrong, you often look for your own fault first and blame yourself. You have a strong sense of responsibility, but in the face of a worry, it's easy to shrink back while going over past mistakes.

basic.desc: Still Balance is a card of fairness and balanced judgment. It means you can be as fair to yourself as you are to others. Its message: when you feel wronged or sorry, separate feelings from facts, and apply the same standard to yourself.
basic.overview: Like a swan, calm and still, this card stands for fair judgment that doesn't lean to one side. It asks whether you can use the same generous standard on yourself that you use on other people.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you been kind to others while holding yourself to a stricter standard?
asks_pos.hold: Are you replaying only one side of the story right now and rushing to a conclusion?
asks_pos.step: From here, would you rather settle who was right, or calmly look at the facts?

frag.now: the time spent weighing right and wrong
frag.hold: weighing that never rests
frag.step: an eye that separates facts from interpretation

practices.title: Separate facts from interpretation
practices.how: Divide a sheet of paper in half: on the left, write what actually happened; on the right, write your interpretation.
practices.why: Pulling facts and interpretation apart makes it easier to see how much of what's weighing on you actually happened and how much is your reading of it.

practices.title: A friend's scale
practices.how: Write down how a close friend would judge it if they went through the same thing.
practices.why: Looking at yourself the way you'd look at a friend makes the standard you've kept only for yourself a little fairer.

practices.title: One “and” sentence
practices.how: Rewrite one “It's true that…, but…” sentence as “It's…, and it's also….”
practices.why: Joining with “and” instead of “but” lets two facts exist together, and black-and-white judgment softens.

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that it's okay to hold out a fair scale to yourself, just as you do for others.
cards.about: This card shows up when you're weighing right and wrong or fairness is bothering you. It sits in the place of Justice in traditional tarot, which stands for balance, fairness, and cause and effect. In Ssol Tarot, it's read as holding out a fair scale to yourself, too.
cards.about_when: This card shows up when you're weighing right and wrong or fairness is bothering you.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of Justice in traditional tarot, which stands for balance, fairness, and cause and effect. In Ssol Tarot, it's read as holding out a fair scale to yourself, too.
asks: Do you keep going over in your head who was more in the wrong?
Are you kind to others but especially hard on yourself?

now: The urge to figure out what's right comes from feelings tied to fairness, like feeling wronged or feeling sorry. For example, if you replay that day's conversations over and over before bed, weighing who was right, it may mean you don't want to brush this off lightly. A busy mind means you want to settle this the right way.

What's sitting on the two sides of your scale right now? It could be one person and another, or your feelings and your responsibilities. For example, if you give each side a short name, like “I feel hurt” and “a promise I want to keep,” and write them on paper, you can see at a glance what you're weighing. Knowing what you're measuring makes the weighing less confusing.
hold: It's easy to assume others had their reasons while telling yourself, “I shouldn't have done that.” For example, you might shrug off someone who was late with “they must've been busy,” then scold yourself all day on a day you were late. When you replay only one side of the story, the scale keeps tipping and you rush to a conclusion.

How would you judge it if a dear friend went through the same thing? Try applying that same standard to yourself. For example, for five minutes before bed tonight, pick one thing that's bothering you, imagine it's a friend's story, and write a line or two you'd say to that friend. A fair scale isn't only for others; you can hold it out to yourself, too.
step: Separating facts from interpretation turns the emotional heat down a little. When you look separately at what actually happened and the meaning you attached to it, it gets a bit clearer where the facts end and your interpretation begins. For example, “my idea wasn't taken this time” may be the fact, and “I always get ignored” may be the interpretation stacked on top.

Make two columns on a sheet of paper and write “what happened” on the left and “what I felt and how I read it” on the right. One event a day, about 10 minutes, is enough. For example, on the left, “the plan suddenly changed,” and on the right, “I felt like I didn't matter.” If you reread it once you've calmed down, you can put both sides on the scale a little more calmly.

now: When the scale tips to one side, your heart gets heavy on that side, too. If you spend the whole day blaming only yourself over one small mistake, at work or in a relationship, the scale may already be tipped far toward you. If you're strict only with yourself, think of what you'd say to a friend who went through the same thing.
hold: If you stay stuck on weighing right and wrong, your mind gets no break. For example, if you keep replaying “should I have said it differently?” even in the shower or on a walk, your mind is still judging during your downtime. You don't have to rush to a conclusion; setting judgment aside for today is one way to go.
step: When you write facts and interpretation separately, it gets clearer what actually happened and what meaning your mind attached to it. For example, if the line “things didn't go as planned” has the thought “it's all my fault” stuck to it, write the two on separate lines. That separation can bring the scale back to the center.

image.scene_prompt: The character floating perfectly still on a mirror-like lake, its reflection symmetrical below, soft morning light, balance.

key_rx.title: Write facts and interpretation separately
key_rx.how: Write down an issue that's been bothering you lately in a notebook, then split it into one line for what actually happened and one line for the interpretation you put on it.
key_rx.why: When you focus on separating facts from interpretation, a fair answer shows up once your feelings settle.

today.title: One line of fact, one line of interpretation
today.how: Pick one thing that bothered you today and split it into one line of fact and one line of your interpretation.
today.why: Starting small with separating facts from interpretation builds a fair eye little by little.

week.title: Split it out each time an issue bothers you
week.how: This week, each time an issue bothers you, write the facts and your interpretation separately. After about three times, you'll start to see your habits of interpretation.
week.why: Separating facts from interpretation again and again helps you notice sooner when feelings get ahead of you.

direct.slow_short: the habit of replaying who was right

slow_rx.title: Set replay time to 5 minutes
slow_rx.how: When you feel the urge to replay who was right, set a timer for 5 minutes, think about it only for that time, then write down just one line of fact and close the notebook.
slow_rx.why: Replaying who was right keeps tipping your thinking to one side, so setting a time limit helps you notice facts you missed in the rush.

three.title: Set a 10-minute replay timer
three.how: Set a timer for 10 minutes and write down every thought that comes up about who was right. When the alarm goes off, close the notebook and get up.
three.why: Pouring out your replaying thoughts within a time limit gives your rushed, one-sided judgment a break.

signs: When a situation makes you angry, you think about “what actually happened” and “what I think” separately.
You're less in the habit of reading a friend's short reply in the worst way.
When you reread the situation the next morning after your feelings settle, it feels less sharp.
cards.tendency: You often try to judge fairly by working out what's right. That earns you people's trust, but in the face of a worry, you can get especially hard on yourself and your mind can't rest.

cards.name: Rest on the Rock
cards.core: Pausing isn't falling behind; it's time to see things differently.

positions.now: Until now, you've probably packed every day full and refused to slow down. You've gotten a lot done, but time to look after yourself kept getting pushed back. There were probably many days you skipped lunch or grabbed a quick bite at your desk.
positions.hold: Right now, frustration is growing because the results aren't matching the effort. If things stay as they are, it's easy to push your tired body harder until even your motivation runs dry. Even after sleeping in on the weekend, you don't wake up refreshed, and little things get on your nerves.
positions.step: From here, focus on putting time to step away and catch your breath into your daily plan. Then you can face the same work in a much lighter mood. Sometimes the answer to a problem you were stuck on comes to you right after a short break.

reversed.core: Time standing still feels less like rest and more like being stuck.

positions.now: Until now, you've probably kept checking notifications and catching up on work even on days off, never really unwinding. Your body was lying down, but your mind was always on the clock. You may have even packed your laptop on vacation and checked email whenever you had a moment.
positions.hold: Right now, the wish to rest and the pressure to keep going are clashing, and you can't focus on either. If things stay as they are, even long stretches of time off just pile up more fatigue. Thoughts of your to-do list cut into your downtime, and you can't even finish a show you used to love.
positions.step: From here, focus on drawing a clear line between work time and rest time. Then you can rest fully when you rest and focus better when you work. Once your workday has a set end time, you'll have room in the evening for exercise or a hobby.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that a short, guilt-free rest lets the time that felt stuck breathe again.
asks: Have you ever blamed yourself because even a day off didn't leave you refreshed?
Even though you know you need rest, does part of you keep feeling uneasy?

frag.now: the time spent blaming yourself even while resting
frag.hold: being unable to either rest or move
frag.step: full, guilt-free rest

basic.desc: Rest on the Rock reversed means time standing still feels less like rest and more like being stuck. You may blame yourself even while resting, so you don't really recover. It often comes up when you're holding on to work in your head even on days off, so you don't feel refreshed afterward.
basic.overview: Your body is resting, but your head is still gripping work, so you don't feel refreshed. It points to a time when you can't really rest because you're blaming yourself for resting.

asks_pos.now: Until now, even when you had time off, haven't you felt oddly guilty and been unable to enjoy it?
asks_pos.hold: Is your body resting right now while your mind holds on to your to-do list and feels guilty?
asks_pos.step: From here, would you rather keep blaming yourself while resting, or count rest as one of your tasks?

key_rx.title: Put rest on your to-do list
key_rx.how: Write “rest 15 minutes” at the top of today's to-do list, and once you've done it, check it off like any other task.
key_rx.why: When you focus on rest as one of today's tasks, even a short, guilt-free break leaves your body and mind refreshed.

today.title: One rest check mark
today.how: Write “rest” on your to-do list, close your eyes and sit still for 3 minutes, then check it off.
today.why: Checking off rest makes your rest time count as a task you got done, and your mind feels much easier.

week.title: Check off rest once a day
week.how: This week, put “rest” on your to-do list every day, and after resting, check it off and write one line about how your body feels.
week.why: When rest piles up as a task you get done each day, the idea that it's okay to rest becomes more familiar.

direct.slow_short: the guilt that says you shouldn't rest

slow_rx.title: Rewrite the guilt sentence
slow_rx.how: When the thought “I shouldn't rest” comes up, write it down in a notebook exactly as it is, and underneath add one line about why it's okay to rest.
slow_rx.why: The guilt that says you shouldn't rest keeps your rest from feeling refreshing. Writing down why it's okay to rest eases the guilt.

three.title: Rewrite “I shouldn't rest”
three.how: Write the sentence “I shouldn't rest” three times, and each time add one line about why it's okay to rest, rewriting the sentence.
three.why: Rewriting the guilt sentence yourself turns time when you could neither rest nor move forward into real rest.

signs: During downtime, the thought “Is this okay?” doesn't follow you around.
After lying on the couch for a while, you notice your body feels much lighter when you get up.
You put a line that says “rest” on today's to-do list and check it off without apology.
reversed.tendency: You often keep working in your head even during downtime, blaming yourself for resting. You're diligent, but in the face of a worry, rest doesn't refresh you and you just run out of energy.

basic.desc: Rest on the Rock is a card of pausing, resting, and seeing with fresh eyes. It means time spent stopping isn't falling behind; it's time to gain a new view. When you've worked hard and still feel like you're in the same spot, it tells you some paths only show up once you stop for a while.
basic.overview: Like a harbor seal resting on a rock, this card stands for time to pause and look at things differently. It says pausing isn't time lost; it's time when new things come into view.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you kept holding on to your to-do list in your head even on days off?
asks_pos.hold: Frustrated that you're stuck in the same spot, are you pushing even harder right now?
asks_pos.step: From here, would you rather keep pushing through without a break, or pause and look at things differently?

frag.now: the time spent running without stopping
frag.hold: a body and mind that want to pause
frag.step: a wider view that comes with rest

practices.title: 15 minutes of doing nothing
practices.how: Set aside 15 minutes with nothing productive in it, and only rest during that time.
practices.why: Rest with no purpose is practice in pulling your mind away from work, and even a short break helps you recover.

practices.title: See it from a year out
practices.how: Answer in three lines: “What will this mean to me a year from now?”
practices.why: Looking from further down the road brings the weight of what feels huge right now back to its proper size.

practices.title: Go to bed 30 minutes early
practices.how: Tonight, turn off the lights and lie down 30 minutes earlier than usual.
practices.why: Enough sleep is the base for managing feelings and recovering, so a small change in sleep gives you more breathing room the next day.

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that pausing for a while isn't falling behind; it's time to see things differently.
cards.about: This card shows up when you feel you're not getting anywhere no matter how hard you try, and you want to rest. It sits in the place of The Hanged Man in traditional tarot, which stands for pausing, waiting, and a new point of view. In Ssol Tarot, it's read as rest that helps you see differently.
cards.about_when: This card shows up when you feel you're not getting anywhere no matter how hard you try, and you want to rest.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of The Hanged Man in traditional tarot, which stands for pausing, waiting, and a new point of view. In Ssol Tarot, it's read as rest that helps you see differently.
asks: Even on days off, are you still working in your head?
Are you worn out lately because you're working hard but feel stuck in the same spot?

now: When you've been working hard and still feel you're not moving forward, your body and mind are usually already pretty tired. For example, if you rested all weekend and Monday morning still feels heavy, it may mean you've been pushing through longer than you realized. Wanting to rest right now isn't laziness; it's an honest signal for the you who's been holding on so long.

When was the last time you felt you really rested? If nothing comes to mind, now may be the time to make room for it. For example, pick one evening this week, close your to-do list for an hour or two, and keep that time for a cup of hot tea or an early night. Rest isn't a prize you earn; it's what you need to keep going.
hold: The feeling that resting will make you fall behind often shows up in people who want to do a lot of things well. With that feeling, your body may stop but your head keeps gripping work, so you don't feel refreshed afterward. For example, if you finally get a day off and go for a walk, but the thought “I should be getting things done with this time” tags along, that feeling is holding your rest hostage.

What comes to mind most often when you're resting? Write it down and hand it off for now: “Tomorrow's me will deal with this.” For example, for three minutes before bed, write each thing circling in your head on its own line, and end the day by closing the notepad. When you set your thoughts down outside yourself, your mind gets room to rest along with your body.
step: A real pause isn't time spent doing nothing; it's time spent looking away from your to-do list for a while. While you pause, your mind slowly sorts through things you haven't had time to see. For example, if you keep your phone in your pocket on a walk and just listen to the wind and the leaves, a problem you were stuck on may suddenly look different.

Set aside at least 15 minutes a day that has nothing to do with work. Things that don't need a result are best, like looking out the window, taking a walk, or listening to music you love. If you pick about the same time each day, like after lunch or before bed, and turn off notifications, it's much easier to protect that time. Like a seal with its head tipped upside down, some paths only show up after you rest.

now: If rest doesn't refresh you, it may be because your body stopped but your mind is still gripping work. For example, if you're lying on the couch scrolling your phone while still tallying up overdue tasks in your head, only your body has stopped. Blaming yourself for stopping can also become noise that gets in the way of rest.
hold: Getting caught between “I shouldn't rest” and “I have no energy to move” wears you out even more. For example, if your body won't move in front of a task but your mind keeps pushing you, it's easy to drain your energy without resting or getting anything done. Right now, instead of choosing one or the other, start by allowing yourself a very short rest. Five minutes standing by the window, slowly drinking a glass of water, is enough.
step: Fifteen guilt-free minutes of rest takes practice. For example, around 3 or 4 in the afternoon, set a timer for 15 minutes and spend that time looking out the window or closing your eyes and just breathing. If a task comes to mind during that time, jot it on paper, tell yourself “I'll look at it later,” and set it down.

image.scene_prompt: The character lying lazily on a smooth rock, head tilted upside down to look at the sky, restful pause and a new perspective.

key_rx.title: Schedule time to pause
key_rx.how: Write “pause 20 minutes” into one slot of today's schedule, and keep it like any other appointment.
key_rx.why: When you focus on pausing as part of moving forward, paths you couldn't see come into view while you rest.

today.title: Pause 5 minutes between tasks
today.how: When you finish one task, don't jump straight to the next; stop and look out the window for 5 minutes.
today.why: Practicing short pauses between tasks lets you feel firsthand that breaks open up the road ahead.

week.title: Keep one pause slot every day
week.how: This week, put one 15-minute pause slot into your schedule every day, and when it ends, write one line about what came to mind.
week.why: Protecting your pause time every day lets you see for yourself, within the week, how rest widens your view.

direct.slow_short: the habit of pushing harder when you should rest

slow_rx.title: Take one thing off your to-do list
slow_rx.how: Look over today's to-do list and cross off one thing that can wait until tomorrow.
slow_rx.why: Pushing harder when you should rest drains your energy, so taking one task off makes room for a body and mind that want to pause.

three.title: Postpone the task that drains you more the harder you try
three.how: From this week's to-do list, pick one task that drains you more the harder you push, and move it to next week.
three.why: Taking one thing off your plate lets you follow your body and mind's signal to rest when it's time to rest.

signs: Stopping work to look out the window doesn't feel like wasted time.
After a short break, a new approach to a problem you couldn't solve comes to mind.
Even if others seem to be getting ahead, you accept that resting now is part of the process.
cards.tendency: You often keep running even when you're exhausted, afraid that resting will leave you behind. Your effort gets a lot done, but in the face of a worry, you can forget how to really stop and end up even more drained.

cards.name: Moving to a New Shell
cards.core: When you set down a shell that no longer fits, you can move into a new home.

positions.now: Until now, you've probably built stability by choosing to protect what you have rather than change it. Meanwhile you've grown, but your surroundings stayed the same, and the sense that things don't fit has slowly grown. Every time you opened a closet or drawer, you may have noticed things you never reach for anymore.
positions.hold: Right now, regret for the time that's passed is coming up alongside a sense of relief. If you ignore those feelings, the energy to move forward can scatter halfway. There are moments when you flip through old photos or notes and end up jotting down what you want to do next.
positions.step: From here, focus on sorting out what you gained from the past and what you'll leave behind. Then leaving feels less like losing and more like carrying on. When you send off what you can let go of with gratitude, you make room for new things.

reversed.core: You haven't yet let go of what you need to set down.

positions.now: Until now, even when things felt uncomfortable, you've probably soothed yourself by saying you're fine as you are. That way you avoided big clashes, but a tight, stuffy feeling kept building inside. You may have kept to familiar streets and familiar shops and answered new offers with “Maybe next time.”
positions.hold: Right now, you're gripping what you have so hard, afraid of losing it, that your hands are tense. If things stay as they are, it's easy to see new options and still not reach for them. You keep pulling things out to throw away, then putting them right back.
positions.step: From here, focus on figuring out the one thing you most want to let go of first. When you start by setting down small things, even big changes feel much less strange. Once you can tell whether you're holding on out of regret or out of fear, you'll see what you can let go.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that change starts when you name what you need to set down, even if you don't leave right away.
asks: Is there a part of your life you feel you should leave but are holding on to because it's familiar?
Does admitting an ending feel like failure, so you keep putting off wrapping it up?

frag.now: the time spent putting off change
frag.hold: a familiarity you can't let go of
frag.step: the courage to let go slowly

basic.desc: Moving to a New Shell reversed means you haven't yet let go of what you need to set down. You may be putting off change because you're afraid to leave a familiar shell. It's worth thinking of when you feel you should end a chapter but hesitate to wrap it up because the familiar feels too precious to lose.
basic.overview: Because the familiar feels too precious to give up, you haven't yet let go of a shell you've already outgrown. It points to a time when, rather than being ready to leave, you haven't yet put a name to what you want to clear out.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you known it was time to leave but kept putting off wrapping things up, afraid it would all fall apart?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you holding on to a part of your life you already know doesn't fit, just because it's familiar?
asks_pos.step: From here, would you rather keep holding on to the familiar, or clear things out slowly, one at a time?

key_rx.title: Write down three things you want to clear out
key_rx.how: Write down three things you want to clear out of where you are now, whatever comes to mind. Big or small is fine.
key_rx.why: When you focus on noticing what you want to clear out, what to let go of gets clearer, and change feels like a size you can handle.

today.title: One line: what you want to clear out
today.how: Write one line in a notebook about the thing you most want to clear out right now.
today.why: Putting what you want to clear out into one line shrinks a vague change down to a size you can handle.

week.title: Write one thing to clear out each day
week.how: This week, add one thing you want to clear out to your notebook each day. After a week, you'll see what keeps coming up.
week.why: Writing down what you want to clear out every day makes it clearer what you really want to let go of.

direct.slow_short: the part of you that's clinging to an ending

slow_rx.title: Write five lines on what remains after the ending
slow_rx.how: Picture the ending and write five lines in your notebook about “what's still here anyway.”
slow_rx.why: You cling because admitting an ending feels like everything will collapse, so writing down what remains afterward eases the fear of collapse.

three.title: Fill ten lines with what remains after the ending
three.how: Next to the feeling that admitting the ending will make everything collapse, write ten lines about what's still here anyway.
three.why: Seeing for yourself what remains after the ending gives room to move to a heart that found both staying and leaving too much.

signs: Instead of trying to clear out everything at once, you're emptying just one drawer today.
You can say, one line at a time, what you want to let go of as it comes to mind.
A change that felt vague and huge starts to break down into smaller pieces.
reversed.tendency: You often know change is needed but put off deciding because the familiar feels too precious to give up. You avoid big upheavals, but in the face of a worry, the stuck feeling stays, and both staying and leaving feel like too much.

basic.desc: Moving to a New Shell is a card of one chapter ending and a new one beginning. It means that when you set down what no longer fits, you can move on to the next place. It fits times when you're clearing out what you've outgrown, like a job, a relationship, or an old habit, and moving on.
basic.overview: It stands for a time to close one chapter and, like a hermit crab, move into a new home that fits better. It points to a change where you set down, with gratitude, what no longer fits who you are now.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you stayed in the same place because it's familiar, even though you knew you'd outgrown it?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, does admitting an ending feel like failure, so you keep putting off wrapping it up?
asks_pos.step: From here, would you rather stay in the familiar shell, or move into a new home that fits you?

frag.now: the time spent guarding a familiar shell
frag.hold: the mess between an ending and a beginning
frag.step: an ending you send off with thanks

practices.title: A thank-you and goodbye letter
practices.how: Write a short letter to what's ending, with “what I'm grateful for” and “what I'll set down now.” You don't have to send it.
practices.why: Saying both thank you and goodbye to what's ending lets you wrap it up without pushing down the regret.

practices.title: Two lists
practices.how: Write two lists side by side: “what I'll take with me” and “what I'll leave behind.”
practices.why: Sorting what you'll take from what you'll leave shows you an ending isn't losing everything.

practices.title: A day six months from now
practices.how: Describe an ordinary day in your life six months from now in five sentences.
practices.why: A future you've pictured in detail becomes a scene you can walk into instead of a vague fear.

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that when you set down a shell that no longer fits, you can move into a new home.
cards.about: This card shows up when a part of your life is ending or needs to change. It sits in the place of the thirteenth card in traditional tarot, which stands for one chapter ending and a new one beginning. In Ssol Tarot, it's read as a transition: setting down a shell that no longer fits and moving into a new home.
cards.about_when: This card shows up when a part of your life is ending or needs to change.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of the thirteenth card in traditional tarot, which stands for one chapter ending and a new one beginning. In Ssol Tarot, it's read as a transition: setting down a shell that no longer fits and moving into a new home.
asks: Are you holding on to a part of your life your heart has already left, just because it's familiar?
Is there a chapter you keep putting off closing because admitting the ending would feel like failure?

now: When a chapter ends, your heart usually catches up a step behind what's happening. For example, even after wrapping up long-running work or leaving a familiar place, you may catch yourself stopping short as you go through your old daily routine. Feeling regret and relief at the same time isn't strange; it's proof that time mattered to you.

In what's ending, what do you miss most, and what feels lightest to let go of? For example, tonight, fold a notebook page in half and write three things you'll miss on the left and three things that feel lighter on the right. Seeing the two side by side helps you feel that letting go isn't only about losing.
hold: Familiar things feel safe because they're predictable, even when they're uncomfortable. That's why it's hard to set down a shell you've already outgrown, and admitting an ending can feel like failure. For example, you may know a habit or role no longer fits you but keep hanging on because quitting would make all that time feel wasted.

Is what you're holding on to still protecting you, or is it boxing you in? You don't have to settle on an answer. For example, for a week, at the end of each day, write one word for whether today with it felt comfortable or confining. Just quietly carrying that question gets your heart thinking about its next home.
step: A small ritual for sending off an ending helps your heart accept that it's okay to move on now. Once you've sorted out what you're grateful for, setting things down feels less like throwing them away and more like moving to the next place. For example, silently saying “thanks for everything” as you clear out a long-used item, or slowly walking a familiar route one last time, can be a small ritual.

Write down three things you're grateful for and three things you'll set down now. This weekend, set aside about 20 minutes and write slowly in a quiet spot. Clearing out one photo or writing a short letter works too. Like a hermit crab picking a new shell, you can find a place that's the right size for who you are now.

now: You know you need a change but are afraid to leave because the familiar shell has protected you all this time. For example, your current place or role may feel confining, but when you picture the unfamiliar days after it, you hesitate again. Fear also means you've valued the place you've been.
hold: Sometimes admitting an ending feels like falling apart. For example, you may feel that changing a long-held way of doing things would erase all your past effort, so you keep pushing the decision off even though you know. But recognizing an ending isn't failure; it may be the start of finding the right size for who you are now.
step: Just naming what you need to set down gets your heart starting to prepare, little by little. You don't have to leave right away. Slowly write down what the thing you named means to you right now. For example, giving it a short name like “the worry I've held on to every night” and writing a line or two about how you feel next to it is enough.

key_rx.title: Write what you're grateful for and what to set down, separately
key_rx.how: Think about what's ending, and in a notebook write what you were grateful for on the left and what you'll set down now on the right.
key_rx.why: When you focus on separating what you were grateful for from what you'll set down, a new home that fits who you are now moves into the space you cleared well.

today.title: Two columns, three lines each
today.how: Draw two columns in a notebook, and write three things you were grateful for and three things you'll set down from what's ending.
today.why: Writing gratitude and what to set down separately lets you see regret and relief apart instead of tangled together.

week.title: One line in each column a day
week.how: This week, each day, write one line about what you were grateful for and one line about what you'll set down from what's ending, and build up the list.
week.why: Writing a little each day keeps the send-off going without feeling heavy.

direct.slow_short: the habit of putting off wrapping up

slow_rx.title: Set a date for one wrap-up
slow_rx.how: Pick one thing to wrap up from what's ending and write a date for it on your calendar.
slow_rx.why: Putting off wrapping up leaves regret and relief tangled together, so setting a date keeps your energy for starting over from scattering.

three.title: Do the smallest part of the wrap-up
three.how: From the wrap-up you dated, pick the smallest part and finish it in 15 minutes.
three.why: Finishing a small part of a wrap-up you've been putting off helps you save up energy for a new start.

signs: As you clear out a long-used item or a past chapter, you say “thanks for everything.”
You feel both regret and relief about what you've set down.
One new habit that fits who you are now moves into the empty space.
cards.tendency: You often treasure familiar places and ways of doing things and steadily stay in one spot. That steadiness is reassuring, but in the face of a worry, it can be hard to let go of what no longer fits, so you move on late.

cards.name: Between Water and Land
cards.core: Both sides are your life. You just need the right mix.

positions.now: Until now, you've probably held on without giving up either your responsibilities or your time for yourself. Because you protected both, you've had little room to look at where you actually stand. You may have been answering messages and juggling plans even on your commute, never stopping.
positions.hold: Right now, you're stuck thinking it has to be one or the other, and you keep putting off the choice. If things stay as they are, time can slip by without you putting real energy into either side. You find yourself asking the people around you the same question again and again, hoping someone will decide for you.
positions.step: From here, focus on the idea that you can mix other people's expectations and your own standards in different amounts depending on the situation. Then the pressure to pick the one right answer every time eases. Once you set how much goes to each side, you get a feel for not dropping either one.

reversed.core: Leaning too far to one side, your balance is wobbling.

positions.now: Until now, you've probably been running on the belief that you've only done it right if you pour all your energy into one thing. That brought you achievements, but resentment built up on the side you couldn't look after. When a stretch of total focus ended, you may have been so drained that you didn't want to do anything for a while.
positions.hold: Right now, you're holding on to only one side, either your responsibilities or your time for yourself, and your body is sending signals first. If things stay as they are, even the side you've been holding can start to wobble. Your daily rhythm is already slipping, with less sleep and irregular meals.
positions.step: From here, focus on sorting out, one by one, what you want to protect and what you can set down. Then you can split up the energy you've been pouring into one side. When you give a little time back to the side you've neglected, balance slowly starts to return.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that even a heart tipped to one side can find the right spot again by moving one step at a time.
asks: Do you feel you're putting too much energy into just one side, whether it's work or relationships?
Wanting to keep both, are you wearing yourself out without choosing either one?

frag.now: the time poured into one side
frag.hold: a day tipped to one side
frag.step: a middle you're working your way back to

basic.desc: Between Water and Land reversed means you're leaning so far to one side that your balance is wobbling. With an all-or-nothing mindset, it can be hard to find a middle that works. It often comes up when you're worn out from putting too much energy into only work, or only taking care of other people.
basic.overview: You've poured so much of yourself into one side, whether work or people, that your balance has tipped. It points to a time when it's easy to swing to one extreme: doing everything or nothing at all.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you moved in only two modes, doing everything or nothing at all?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you spending all your energy on just work or just people, while you come last?
asks_pos.step: From here, would you rather pour everything into one side, or spread the weight out little by little?

key_rx.title: Give more time to the other side
key_rx.how: Take 20 minutes from the time you spend on one side today, and move it in your schedule to the other side.
key_rx.why: When you focus on shifting a little weight from the heavy side to the other, you see a middle that works instead of extremes, and you get some breathing room.

today.title: Spend 5 minutes on the other side
today.how: Right now, spend just 5 minutes on the side you usually neglect.
today.why: Even 5 minutes on the other side lets you feel the weight start to shift.

week.title: Shift 20 minutes of weight each day
week.how: This week, each day, spend 20 minutes from your heavy side on the other side, and afterward write one line about how your body feels.
week.why: Shifting a little each day lets you see breathing room come back even to a worn-out heart.

direct.slow_short: the pattern of pouring all your energy into one side

slow_rx.title: Break down where your energy went today
slow_rx.how: Split today into morning, afternoon, and evening, and write in a notebook which side you put your energy into.
slow_rx.why: A day spent pouring energy into one side wears out even the side you've been holding up, so writing down where your energy went shows you where it's piling up.

three.title: Mark where your energy went
three.how: Split each of the last three days into morning, afternoon, and evening, write which side you put your energy into, and circle the slots that went all to one side.
three.why: Marking the lopsided slots yourself helps you catch the pattern before your balance wobbles.

signs: You're taking a little time from work and spending it on an evening walk.
Your habit of doing everything in one big push is turning into doing a little each day.
Even on a weekend when you're worn out, at least one thing you'd like to do comes to mind.
reversed.tendency: You often pour a lot of yourself into one side, whether work or people. You get results by going all in, but in the face of a worry, the other side sits empty and your body and mind wear out easily.

basic.desc: Between Water and Land is a card of adjusting, of mixing different things in the right amounts. It means finding the ratio that fits you rather than choosing one of two. Between work and rest, or between yourself and others, it's okay to adjust little by little, like 70/30 today and 50/50 tomorrow.
basic.overview: This is a card of adjusting: instead of choosing just one of two, you mix different things in a ratio that fits you. It carries the flexibility of letting the balance between work and rest change from day to day.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you held on to both because choosing one felt like losing the other?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you treating only one of the two as the right answer and putting off the choice?
asks_pos.step: From here, would you rather choose just one, or mix the two in the right amounts?

frag.now: the time spent looking after both sides
frag.hold: a heart stalled between two

practices.title: Set this week's ratio
practices.how: Set a number for this week's ratio of work to rest (or you to others), and check at the end of each day whether you stuck to it.
practices.why: Setting a ratio instead of all-or-nothing gives you a realistic balance that takes care of both sides.

practices.title: Join with “and”
practices.how: Take two clashing feelings, join them with “and,” and write them as one sentence.
practices.why: Acknowledging two clashing feelings together eases the tension of wearing yourself out trying to pick one.
