practices.how: Write down three middle options that fit between the two extremes.
practices.why: Adding options between the two extremes gives breathing room to a worry that felt like a dead end.

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that instead of choosing one of two, you can mix them in the right amounts to find your life's balance.
cards.about: This card shows up when you're worn out trying to find balance between two things. It sits in the place of Temperance in traditional tarot, which stands for harmony, moderation, and the wisdom of mixing different things. In Ssol Tarot, it's read as the strength to find the right ratio rather than picking one of two.
cards.about_when: This card shows up when you're worn out trying to find balance between two things.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of Temperance in traditional tarot, which stands for harmony, moderation, and the wisdom of mixing different things. In Ssol Tarot, it's read as the strength to find the right ratio rather than picking one of two.
asks: Between work and rest, or you and others, do you feel you're leaning hard to one side?
Thinking you have to pick one of two, are you ending up picking nothing at all?

now: You're trying to find balance between two things because both matter to you. For example, while you're working you want to rest, and once you rest your to-do list pops into your head, so neither side feels comfortable. Not wanting to give up either one makes the weighing drag on, but it's also an effort to make room for a full life.

What's sitting on each side of your scale right now? Write one word for how each one feels when you think about it. For example, put “what I have to do” on one side and “time for me” on the other, and write words like “heavy” and “exciting.” When you see which side your mind lingers on longer, you also see the ratio you need right now.
hold: All-or-nothing thinking seems to make choices simpler, but in practice it keeps you from choosing either side. That's because choosing one feels like losing the other completely. For example, deciding that if you can't work out for an hour every day you might as well not work out at all, or putting off starting until you're perfectly ready.

Instead of choosing one of two, what if you thought in terms of “a little more” and “a little less”? Even without fully choosing, you can adjust the ratio. For example, this week you could cut your workload by just 30 minutes a day and spend that time on yourself. Once you see that wiggle room, the tension in your heart eases a lot.
step: The right ratio isn't a one-time setting; it can change every day. Like a frog going back and forth between water and land, you can stay a little longer on the side you need today and adjust again tomorrow. For example, on a day when tasks pile up, you stay a little longer on that side, and on a day you're especially tired, you shift the weight toward resting early.

Set a number for this week's ratio. For example, work to rest at 70/30, or yourself to your relationships at 60/40. If you write that number on your calendar or a corner of your notepad, you'll see it often during the week and remember it more easily. If you look back on the weekend and reset the ratio for next week, balance becomes not one right answer but a feel you adjust yourself.

now: A life tipped to one side eventually sends signals to your body and mind. For example, if you say yes to every favor while your own tasks keep getting pushed back, or you hold on to your to-do list even on days off, the scale may be tipped to one side. The exhaustion you feel now isn't blame for losing your balance; it may be a reminder that it's time to readjust.
hold: If you think choosing one means losing the other, it's hard to choose anything. For example, cutting back on work may feel like you'll miss everything, and deciding to rest may feel like you have to drop it all, so in the end nothing changes. Remember there are lots of options between “all” and “nothing at all.”
step: Moving just one step may look small, but it's a solid first step toward getting your balance back. For example, finishing work that usually runs late 30 minutes earlier for just one day, or putting the me-time you've been postponing on your calendar just once, is enough. If you look back a week later at the difference that one step made, the next adjustment gets much easier.

theories: Linehan's Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT): Wise Mind

key_rx.title: Set today's ratio

key_rx.why: When you focus on finding the ratio that's right for you, you accept that it can change every day, and choosing gets much lighter.

today.title: One line: today's ratio

today.why: Setting just today's ratio lets you feel, lightly, that you don't have to pick only one.

week.title: Write a new ratio each day

week.why: Writing it down yourself, seeing that it's okay for the ratio to change each day, shows you the ratio that's right for you.

direct.slow_short: all-or-nothing thinking

slow_rx.title: Write the steps between all and nothing
slow_rx.how: Write down the thing that's hard to choose, then write three middle steps that fit between “all” and “nothing at all.”
slow_rx.why: All-or-nothing thinking keeps you from choosing either side, so writing down the steps in between gives you a path to choose.

three.title: Write five middle steps

three.why: Seeing the middle steps narrows a worry you couldn't fully commit to either way down to what you can do right now.

signs: You gauge how to split your day, like “today about seven parts work, three parts rest.”
Even when what you need today differs from yesterday, you don't call yourself fickle.
A worry about picking one of two turns into “this much of each this week.”
cards.tendency: You often try not to drop either side, between work and rest or yourself and others. You handle many roles well, but in the face of a worry, the weighing drags on and your mind gets busy.

cards.name: The Puffed-Up Heart
cards.core: Check whether the spines you raised to protect yourself are now holding you back.

positions.now: Until now, whenever things got uncomfortable, you've probably gotten through by quickly dodging the way you always do. That helped in the moment, but it's also part of why the same things keep happening. When an awkward conversation started, you may have laughed it off or been the first to leave.
positions.hold: Right now, afraid of getting hurt, you're on guard and bristling at even small comments. If things stay as they are, it's easy to push away even the kindness coming your way. You're spending so much energy on defense that you have less room to relax, laugh, and talk.
positions.step: From here, focus on quietly watching how you react the moment you start to feel guarded. Then you slowly learn that you're safe even without bristling. If you know the first signal your body gives when you get defensive, you'll have more options.

reversed.core: The defenses that held you back are starting to loosen.

positions.now: Until now, even while your old ways of protecting yourself felt confining, you've probably been trying to change them one at a time. Those attempts have added up, and now there are days you react differently than before. There may have been a day you stayed in a conversation you'd usually avoid, all the way to the end.
positions.hold: Right now, the tension is easing, and your body and mind still feel a little awkward about it. If things stay as they are, it's easy to treat slipping back into familiar behavior in an anxious moment as failure. Change feels slow, and you wonder if this is enough, but then you steady yourself and decide to try again.
positions.step: From here, focus on not scolding yourself on days you slip back into old ways. Then it's much easier to step toward the new way again. After the back-and-forth days pass, reactions that felt strange start to come naturally.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that now that the spines holding you back are starting to loosen, one small new habit keeps that change going.
asks: Lately, has there been a moment when you were a little less shaken by what would once have set you off?
As you try to put down a familiar habit, are you worried you'll slide right back?

basic.desc: The Puffed-Up Heart reversed means the defenses that held you back are starting to loosen, little by little. Even if it feels strange, you're getting ready to move on to new habits. If you were a little less shaken by what would once have set you off, that change is exactly what this card looks like.
basic.overview: The spines you raised so firmly are coming down, and a heart that was tied up is starting to loosen. It means the moments when you're less shaken than before are growing, even if only a little.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you been getting a little less shaken by things that would once have rattled you?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, even as you feel better, are you on edge, afraid you'll slip back?
asks_pos.step: From here, would you rather worry about falling apart again, or trust the person you're becoming?

key_rx.title: Write down moments you were less shaken

key_rx.why: When you focus on noticing the small change of being less shaken than before, you start to trust how you've changed, and the new habit gets stronger.

today.title: One line: a less-shaken moment

today.why: Writing down a less-shaken moment gives you one more reason to trust how you've changed.

week.why: Seeing small changes add up lets you trust and wait out the time it takes a new habit to settle in.

slow_rx.why: Worrying about slipping back makes you watch your progress anxiously, so writing it down and checking shows you whether the worry is true.

three.title: Reread your worry box
three.how: Reread your worry box from the beginning, and mark only the ones where what you worried about actually happened.
three.why: Seeing worries and reality side by side lets you watch yourself settle with less anxiety.

Even if you skip your new habit for a day, you let it go: “I'm still keeping it up.”
Before bed, a few words acknowledging what's changed come to mind on their own.
reversed.tendency: You're often in the middle of looking back at the habits that protected you and putting them down bit by bit. Change is starting, but in the face of a worry, even a small wobble can make you worry about slipping back into old habits.

basic.desc: The Puffed-Up Heart is a card of self-protective defenses and repeating habits. It means noticing the spines you raised to protect yourself is the first step out of a habit. It's a card that has you look back at habits you repeat without realizing it, like checking your phone or putting things off whenever you're anxious.
basic.overview: Like a pufferfish puffing up when startled, this card stands for defenses meant to protect you and the habits that have hardened around them. It shows that the things you repeat without thinking when you're anxious were really your way of protecting yourself.

asks_pos.now: Until now, when you got anxious, haven't you gotten through by repeating the same behavior without realizing it?

practices.title: Three-column habit check

practices.why: Recording the moment a habit shows up and how you felt right before turns what happened on autopilot into a pattern you can see.

practices.title: 10-second pause
practices.how: When a habit is about to start, stop, take a step back and breathe, check what's happening right now, choose, and then act.
practices.why: Putting a 10-second gap between the urge and the action gives you room to choose instead of reacting the way you always do.

practices.how: Decide ahead of time on one small action you can do instead of the habit.

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that the moment you notice the spines you raised to protect yourself, your heart starts to loosen, little by little.
cards.about: This card shows up when habits or defenses you repeat when anxious are holding your heart back. It sits in the place of the fifteenth card in traditional tarot, which stands for attachments and habits that tie you down. In Ssol Tarot, it's read as noticing the spines you raised to protect yourself.
cards.about_when: This card shows up when habits or defenses you repeat when anxious are holding your heart back.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of the fifteenth card in traditional tarot, which stands for attachments and habits that tie you down. In Ssol Tarot, it's read as noticing the spines you raised to protect yourself.
asks: Is there a habit you fall into without realizing it whenever you're anxious, one that's hard to stop?
Are there moments you put your guard up first so you won't get hurt?

now: When you're on edge, it's easy to blame yourself for being too sensitive. For example, there are times a single comment you'd usually let slide bothers you all day, or you snap at even a small request. But a puffed-up heart means there's a part of you worth protecting, and it's also a sign of how hard you've been trying.

Think about when you've been especially touchy lately. There may be particular words, situations, or times of day. For example, for a week, each time you get touchy, jot down the time, the place, and what was said in one line in your phone's notes. Once you know those moments, you'll also start to see what you puffed up to protect.
hold: Habits you repeat when you're anxious can bring brief relief in the moment. That's why you keep doing them, but over time the thing that soothed your anxiety can turn into a tie that holds you back. For example, if you check the same thing over and over out of anxiety, or scroll your screen for ages before bed, you may feel fine at the time but more drained the next day.

What's the thing you do most often when you're anxious? Notice whether you really feel calmer after doing it, or calmer for a moment and then anxious again. For example, for three days, rate how you feel right after doing it and 30 minutes later on a scale of 0 to 10. This isn't about blaming yourself; it's about finding better ways to help yourself.
step: Noticing is a gentler starting point than forcing a habit to stop. When you put a name to it, like “I'm puffing up right now,” a small gap opens in a reaction that used to run on autopilot. For example, when a comment or situation makes your chest flare up, silently saying those words to yourself can give you room to take a breath before you react.

When you feel yourself puffing up, take three slow breaths and jot a quick note about the moment. Just three things are enough: when, where, and what set it off. Even a week of notes draws you a map of when your spines go up. Just as a pufferfish shrinks back down once the danger passes, your heart can return to its usual size, too.

now: Noticing a puffed-up heart and letting it settle isn't easy. For example, if today you let go a little sooner of a comment you once would have chewed on all day, that's a small sign your heart is settling. Take a moment to feel that loosening, and give yourself credit for getting this far.
hold: When putting down your defenses feels unfamiliar, old habits can wave you back. For example, if the checking or late-night screen time you'd cut back on returns on a tiring day, that may not be failure but a tired heart reaching for a familiar fix. Worrying about slipping back also means you're already changing, so you don't need to rush.
step: If you decide ahead of time on a small action to do instead of the habit, you have one more path to choose when anxiety rises. The easier it is, the better, like taking three breaths or drinking a glass of water. For example, when the urge to check again comes up, you could decide to put your phone down and look out the window for a minute.

theories: Linehan's Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT): STOP Skill

cards.name: Rebuilding the Dam
cards.core: Where things fell apart is also where you can build again.

positions.now: Until now, you've probably prepared for the future by building step by step according to plan. That's why the shock hit harder when sudden change came. When unexpected things piled up all at once, the thought that all your effort had been for nothing may have crossed your mind.
positions.hold: Right now, you're busy counting what you've lost, and you can't bring yourself to start. If things stay as they are, time can slip by without you seeing what you can still use. You open the planner with your old plans in it, then close it again right away.
positions.step: From here, instead of trying to start over from scratch, focus on the experience and people you can still draw on. Then a daunting task turns into picking up where you left off. Sometimes catching up with someone you used to work with gives you a lead on what's next.

reversed.core: You're even more worn out from trying so hard not to fall apart.

positions.now: Until now, you've probably been pushing your feelings down so you wouldn't look weak. That kept daily life going, but the weight you carry alone kept growing. When worrying things came up, you may have laughed them off as no big deal while running through backup plans over and over inside.
positions.hold: Right now, afraid things will go wrong again, you keep freezing up in front of anything new. If things stay as they are, it's easy to spend all your strength holding the line and have none left to move forward. Even rest doesn't loosen your body, small news makes you jump, and your energy for the day runs out fast.
positions.step: From here, instead of doing it perfectly, focus on doing only what you can today. Then the built-up tension eases and you find the strength to start again. As you keep finishing small tasks all the way through, you hesitate less when taking on new ones.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that even if you're afraid it'll fall apart again, the one branch you stack today is the start of a new dam.

basic.overview: Worried it'll fall apart again, you're pretending to be fine, and it's draining a lot of your energy. It points to a time when you're so drained you can't bring yourself to rebuild what fell apart.

key_rx.title: Choose one small piece to stack today

today.title: A 5-minute piece

three.title: Write three worry-and-backup pairs

three.why: Pairing each worry with a backup plan lets you spend the strength you used on holding on on starting again.

basic.desc: Rebuilding the Dam is a card of unexpected upheaval and the rebuilding that comes after. It means even a place that fell apart can be rebuilt one piece at a time. It fits times when plans have fallen through or what you counted on has been shaken, and you're rebuilding piece by piece, starting with what's left.
basic.overview: Rebuilding the Dam stands for the strength to rebuild where things were shaken and fell apart. Even if your plans fell through, it's not too late to build step by step, starting with one thing still in your hands.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you pushed ahead believing one plan had to work out exactly as laid out?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you so focused on what fell apart that you're missing what's still standing?

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that even where things fell apart, one branch to stack today is enough.
cards.about: This card shows up when a plan you counted on is shaken or suddenly falls apart. It sits in the place of The Tower in traditional tarot, which stands for unexpected change and the new understanding that comes after. In Ssol Tarot, it's read as the strength to recover by rebuilding where things fell apart.
cards.about_when: This card shows up when a plan you counted on is shaken or suddenly falls apart.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of The Tower in traditional tarot, which stands for unexpected change and the new understanding that comes after. In Ssol Tarot, it's read as the strength to recover by rebuilding where things fell apart.
asks: Has a plan you counted on been shaken, leaving you lost about where to start again?
Are you so focused on what fell apart that you're missing what's still there?

now: When what you counted on gets shaken, your mind can go blank for a while, and emptiness and confusion can take turns. For example, on the day a long-prepared project falls through, your tasks are still there but you may feel like you can't get a grip on anything. That's not weakness; it means you put that much of yourself into the plan or the hope.

What got shaken the most right now, and what's still standing anyway? Right now you may only see what fell apart, but writing even one line about what's left shows you where to start again. Tonight, take just five minutes before bed and write what got shaken on the left side of a page and what's still standing on the right. It's enough if the right side has small things, like “the energy to get up in the morning” or “my favorite walking path.”
hold: When you think “start over from scratch,” everything you have to do piles up in front of you at once. It's like looking at a messy room and thinking “I have to clean all of it” — suddenly even picking up one sock feels like too much. Then your mind tends to choose stopping over starting.

Among what fell down, which posts can you still use? Your earlier time left you things: experience, relationships, what you learned. Whether it's work, study or daily life, recalling just one habit you noticed last time or one stretch you got through shows you you're not starting on empty ground. Thinking “picking up again” instead of “starting from zero” makes it much lighter.
step: Rebuilding doesn't get done in one go. Sorting just one page of the paperwork you put off, or turning off the lights at a set time tonight to steady your routine, is one branch too. Like a beaver carrying branches one at a time, steadily adding one piece a day is what builds the new dam.

Pick the smallest piece you can do today. One check, one tidy-up, or one line of a plan is enough. For example, while brushing your teeth in the morning, choose one thing that takes under 10 minutes, like “clear one shelf of my desk,” and when it's done, put a small mark on your calendar. If you keep a record of the pieces you add each day, you can see with your own eyes that new growth is coming up where things fell down.

now: Holding yourself together so you don't fall apart takes a lot of strength too. If you get through the day at work or at home with a calm face and then go limp the moment you're alone, it may mean you've been trying that hard. Admitting you're shaken isn't falling apart; it can be getting ready to use that strength for rebuilding.
hold: You worry it'll fall down again because you've already been hurt once. Instead of blaming yourself for that worry, think about what you'd like to build a little differently this time. A one-line promise is enough, like “This time I won't try to do it all at once” or “I'll set rest days ahead of time for when I'm worn out.”
step: If you focus only on the one branch you'll add today, the pressure of rebuilding the whole thing gets smaller. Whether it's work or tidying the house, narrow the scope way down today — “fill in just the first box” instead of “make the whole plan.” When a day's small pieces add up, the dam takes shape faster than you'd expect.

image.scene_prompt: The character calmly rebuilding a small dam of branches after a soft flood, a few fallen sticks around, determined and reassuring.

key_rx.title: List what's still left
key_rx.how: In a notebook, write down five things that are still left from what fell apart. Small things count.
key_rx.why: When you focus on what's still in your hands rather than what you lost, you can start again from the posts that remain, and feeling stuck eases.

today.title: Write down one thing that's left

today.why: Writing down even one thing that's left lets you feel you're not starting from scratch.

week.why: When you look for what's left every day, eyes that only saw what fell down start to see differently.

direct.slow_short: only seeing what fell apart

slow_rx.title: Break “start over” into one piece
slow_rx.how: When you think “I have to start over from scratch,” break that task into its smallest first piece, write it down, and pick just one piece to do tomorrow.
slow_rx.why: When you only see what fell apart, it feels like starting from scratch and you put off beginning; breaking it into a small first piece shows you where to start.

three.title: Choose one first piece and do it
three.how: Break the thing you're restarting into small pieces and write them down, then pick the easiest one and work on it for 15 minutes.
three.why: When you break a big task into pieces and do just one, the part of you that kept putting off the start begins to move.

signs: You spend less time counting what you lost and recall, one by one, what's still left.
You've broken the overwhelming task into a tiny first step and started on it.
You feel that the people, habits and experience you still have are ground to start again from.
cards.tendency: You often build step by step, using the plans and hopes you've trusted as your posts. You put your heart into it as much as you put in effort, but when a worry hits, you may see only what fell apart and find it hard to start again.

cards.name: The Star Shines Again
cards.core: Slowly, but bit by bit, recovery can happen.

positions.now: Until now, you've kept hold of daily life, getting through what needed doing one thing at a time even on hard days. That steadiness laid the ground for how things have changed now. Small routines like getting up each morning, washing your face and eating your meals may have given you a lot of strength.
positions.hold: Right now, you're better than before, but because you keep measuring against how things used to be, you treat the change as small. If this keeps up, it's easy to push yourself without ever crediting the progress you've already made. Even when people say you look better, you laugh it off and say you've got a long way to go.
positions.step: From here, focus on comparing last week's you with today's you to find what's changed. Then you'll come to trust the pace that fits you, and things get much easier. Once you can spot small improvements, you'll know the way back even when a hard day comes.

reversed.core: The light of recovery still feels faint.

positions.now: Until now, you've carried the pressure of getting back to your old self as fast as possible. So the days you got a little better, you brushed off as nothing. You may have set a deadline for recovering and been disappointed in yourself when you weren't better by then.
positions.hold: Right now, waiting for a big, visible change is hiding the day-to-day progress. If this keeps up, it's easy to feel you're standing still even while you're actually moving forward. When you hear about other people's quick recoveries, you feel left behind and get impatient.
positions.step: From here, focus on small changes, like whether you slept better or how your food tasted. As those changes add up, you'll grow sure that you're getting better. Once you can read the small signals your body sends, you'll know when to rest before you push too hard.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that even a light that seems faint gets a little brighter as you notice it, bit by bit.

today.title: One line: today's score
today.how: Rate how you feel right now between 1 and 10 and write it as one line in your notebook.
today.why: Writing today's score gives you a starting point for checking the direction later.

week.title: Score once a day and collect them

week.why: When you collect a score every day, you can see for yourself whether the direction is improving, even if the pace is slow.

direct.slow_short: rushing to be disappointed that nothing's changed

slow_rx.title: Put off disappointment for two days
slow_rx.how: When you're disappointed that nothing's changed, write that feeling in your notebook and read it again two days later.
slow_rx.why: Rushing to be disappointed when you can't feel change wears you out first; looking again two days later may show you what's changed.

three.title: Reread and compare your disappointment note
three.how: Write down what disappoints you, then two days later spend 10 minutes rereading it and write down three things that changed in between.
three.why: When you don't believe your disappointment right away and look again after some time, you see change that's slow but real.

You measure your speed of recovery less and just check that you're heading the right way.
The impatience you felt has calmed down a lot by evening.
reversed.tendency: You often push yourself, telling yourself you need to be okay soon. Your will to recover is strong, but when a worry hits, you can easily miss the moments you're getting a little better and feel disappointed.

basic.desc: The Star Shines Again is a card of recovery and hope. It means you're finding your light again, slowly but bit by bit. If, after a hard stretch, your mornings feel a little less heavy and you have one more moment of laughing, that's the recovery this card shows.
basic.overview: A card of recovery and hope, finding your light again bit by bit after a hard stretch. If this morning feels a little less heavy than yesterday's, that's a real sign you're getting better.

asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you comparing yourself with your old self and walking right past the parts that have gotten better?

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that recovery comes slowly, but it grows bit by bit when you notice the small lights.
cards.about: This card shows the time when, after a hard stretch, you slowly start to breathe again. It sits in the place of The Star in traditional tarot, meaning hope, healing and light that returns. At Ssol Tarot House, we read it as recovery that grows slowly.
cards.about_when: This card shows the time when, after a hard stretch, you slowly start to breathe again.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of The Star in traditional tarot, meaning hope, healing and light that returns. At Ssol Tarot House, we read it as recovery that grows slowly.
asks: You're getting better, but are you pushing yourself because you're “not like before”?
Are you passing over small recoveries as if they're nothing?

now: Recovery after a hard stretch usually starts very quietly. Your mornings are a little less heavy, or you have one more moment of laughing. If you suddenly feel like playing music you hadn't touched in a while, that's a sign your mind is catching its breath too. The small light that's on right now may be that kind of signal.

Have you had a moment lately when you felt “a little better”? It can be tiny. A day when food tasted good for the first time in a while, or your worrying before sleep got a little shorter, counts. When you notice those moments, recovery gets clearer and you can believe in it yourself.
hold: Compared with your old self, your recovery now can always look like it's not enough. If you're putting down today by thinking “I used to get this much done in a day,” that standard may not fit who you are now. But having been through that time, you're already a different person, so going back to the same place isn't the only kind of recovery.

What if you used “better than last week” as your measure instead of “like before”? If you overslept three times last week and twice this week, that alone is a change worth writing down. Keeping your comparison close makes small changes visible and softens the urge to push yourself.
step: When you record small recoveries, hope stops being a vague wish and becomes a fact you can see. As short notes pile up — “I didn't skip a meal today,” “I stepped outside and looked at the sky” — you can see how far you've come even on overwhelming days. Just as a starfish slowly regrows a lost arm, everyone's recovery has its own pace.

At the end of the day, write down one thing that was okay today. One line in your phone's notes before bed, like “I had a warm cup of tea,” is enough, and on days when writing is hard, a single word is fine. When you reread the list a week later, you may find more light gathered there than you thought.

now: Recovery usually happens bit by bit, where you barely notice it. Not seeing change doesn't mean recovery has stopped, so tune your eyes to small differences. If pushing back the covers was a little less hard than yesterday, or you spent a little less of the day staring blankly, that's a small difference too.
hold: Expecting to get better fast pushes a tired heart even harder. Just as you don't get your old stamina back in a day after being sick, your mind regains its strength little by little. Remembering that recovery has its own pace for each person, you start to see even today's small light as precious.
step: The habit of recording one thing that got even a little better is a way of collecting faint light. For example, pick the same time each day, like after you finish the dinner dishes, and write “one thing that got better today” in a single word. Collect them for just a week and you may find more light piled up than you'd think.

slow_rx.title: Finish the “not like before” sentence

three.title: Finish three “not like before” sentences

three.why: Finishing your comparing sentences lets you notice for yourself the change that looked small.

You find that what used to take you all day now gets done in half a day.
You compare yourself with others less and measure against last month's you instead.
cards.tendency: You often get through each day quietly, even in hard times. That time is bringing your strength back, but when a worry hits, the thought that you're not as good as before can make you miss what's gotten better.

cards.name: Drifting in Moonlight
cards.core: Even when you can't see it all, you can go one step at a time.

positions.now: Until now, you've held still and watched the situation until an answer was settled. That caution cut down on mistakes, but the scenarios in your head kept multiplying. When people pushed you to decide, you may have bought time by saying “let's wait a little longer.”
positions.hold: Right now, you're filling in the parts you can't see with imagination, so the worry is growing bigger than the reality. If this keeps up, it's easy to wear yourself out over things that haven't happened yet. Even one small message makes your heart drop as you wonder whether anything's wrong.
positions.step: From here, focus on doing whatever you can get your hands on today, one thing at a time. Then you'll feel you're moving forward even before everything is known. Once you separate what's confirmed as fact from what's a guess, the size of the worry changes.

reversed.core: The fog is starting to lift, little by little.

positions.now: Until now, even while anxious, you've worked to separate facts from guesses. That effort added up, and the things that were cluttering your mind found their names one by one. The person you used to share your worries with may have told you that you look more relaxed lately.
positions.hold: Right now, you're much better, but one or two things that aren't settled yet keep bothering you. If this keeps up, it's easy to stay tense without enjoying the parts that have already improved. Even as things get better, you hesitate to share good news with others.
positions.step: From here, focus on using the facts you've already learned as footholds and moving forward one step at a time. Then the anxiety quiets down a lot even with unknowns left. The more you know, the more clearly you can tell what to ask about and what to wait for.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that even if the fog hasn't fully lifted, the one step you can see now opens the next stretch of road.

asks: Are there nights when your thoughts keep spiraling over things that haven't happened yet?
Are you not starting anything because you're waiting for things to become certain?

now: When you can't see well ahead, your mind tries to fill the blanks with worry. When you're waiting on an answer, for example, you may already be picturing the worst outcome in your head even though no news has come yet. A vague anxiety feels big because your mind may be rushing to fill the spots where information is missing.

Write down separately what you know for sure right now and what you don't know yet. Fold a sheet of paper in half and spend about 10 minutes writing “what I know” on the left and “what I don't know yet” on the right. You may know more than you thought, and just seeing that the unknowns are only “unknown for now” settles your mind a little.
hold: Wanting to wait until things are certain comes from caution, from not wanting to make a mistake. But while you wait, the scenarios in your head keep growing, and they easily become much bigger and darker than reality. Whether it's work or a relationship, during the days you wait for a result, what started as a small worry may get added to a little each night until it's a big story.

If there's a worry scene that comes up most often right now, rate how likely it is to actually happen from 0 to 10. Turning it into a number starts to show you the distance between the worry and the facts. If it feels like an 8 but comes out around a 3 when you think it through calmly, it's okay to give yourself that much more room.
step: Even if you can't see everything, you can move forward as long as you can light up the next step. Just as a jellyfish glows softly without fighting the current, there are small things you can do even in uncertainty. Even if a few months from now feels overwhelming, you can decide what to eat tonight and set tomorrow's alarm right now.

What's the next one thing you can check right now? Looking up one piece of information, jotting down a question, or finishing one task for today. For example, spend 10 minutes this evening on just that one thing, and when it's done, write “checked.” As you light up one step at a time, the road shows itself bit by bit as you walk.

now: When a vague anxiety slowly takes shape, it starts turning into a worry you can actually handle. Give a name, one by one, to the things that are coming into view now. If you turn “I'm just anxious” into a specific sentence like “I'm worried next week's plans will clash,” you start to see what to look at first.
hold: When you want certainty badly, even small shakes make you sensitive. If a schedule changing by a day or an answer coming a little later than expected stays on your mind all day, it may be a sign that the part of you looking for certainty is working very hard. Remember that even if not everything becomes certain, there are things you can do with what you know now.
step: When the fog starts to lift, walking only as far as you can see is enough. If a task isn't fully sorted, it's fine to plan only the first line today and look at the next line tomorrow. After you take one step and look around again, the next step starts to show a little too.

theories: Hayes's Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT): defusion

cards.name: Sunny Rock
cards.core: It's okay to fully enjoy the warmth of the here and now.

positions.now: Until now, when good news came, you've braced for the bad thing you expected to follow. While being that careful, your chances to laugh and enjoy quietly shrank. When you were praised, you may have waved it off as just luck and quickly put your joy away.

positions.step: From here, when a good thing happens, focus on setting your worry aside for a moment and staying in that moment. Then the more joy builds up, the more the anxiety loses its grip. As experiences of simply enjoying joy add up, you'll take the next compliment with a “thank you.”

cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of The Sun in traditional tarot, meaning joy, vitality and things coming brightly into view. At Ssol Tarot House, we read it as the strength to enjoy the warmth of the here and now.
asks: When good things happen, do you hold back your happiness, thinking “It'll go bad again soon”?
Do you quickly forget the moments you laughed and remember only the hard things for a long time?

now: Having joy and hope alive even with a worry means your heart still has plenty of strength to recover. Being able to laugh doesn't mean you take the worry lightly. Those moments are what give you the strength to get through it. If you laughed for a moment over your favorite snack during a week full of worry, that moment is a sign your heart is taking care of itself.

What makes you laugh or warms your heart these days? People, places, small habits — anything counts. Write just three that come to mind in your phone's notes, like a favorite song, a walking route or a warm bowl of soup. Knowing them gives you sunlight you can draw on during hard days.
hold: Reining in your heart ahead of time in happy moments is often about wanting it to hurt less if you're disappointed. If, even on a day things went well, you rush to put your smile away thinking “I shouldn't get carried away,” your heart may be bracing in advance. But then you only feel half the joy, too.

Think of a recent good moment and slowly feel again how you felt then. Recall a meal you enjoyed or a day you wrapped up well, and stay with the look on your face and the mood for about 30 seconds. Fully enjoying joy doesn't bring bad things. If anything, the joy you enjoyed stays with you as strength for getting through hard days.
step: Savoring good moments charges your heart's battery. Even the same experience, held a little longer, leaves a warmth that lasts past the day. Just putting your phone down for a moment when you drink a warm tea and feeling the warmth of the first sip makes that same time stay with you a little differently.

Pick one good moment from today and stay with it for just one more minute. Recall the sounds, smells and faces from then, and say “that was good” to yourself. Setting a time when the day winds down, like after you've washed up and lain down, makes it easy to remember. Just as a fur seal warms itself in the sun, joy gets warmer the longer you stay in it.

now: When joy is hidden, even good things pass by in a blur. Laughing less can be a sign that your heart is worn out, so be a little gentler with yourself. If nothing that went okay today comes to mind, resting your body first — like a warm shower or going to bed a little earlier — is a way to start.
hold: Feeling you shouldn't be happy may be a shield to hurt less if you're disappointed. Enjoying a small joy doesn't make you lose anything. If your mood lifted when you opened the window on a clear day, starting by saying “this is nice” to yourself once is enough.
step: Staying one more minute in a good moment is practice in finding sunlight between the clouds. If the food you had for lunch was good, recall its taste and the sunlight at the time and slowly stay with it for just one minute. As those minutes add up, a warm spot forms in your heart again.

cards.name: Answering the Call
cards.core: It's time to answer the song you've long heard deep in your heart.

positions.now: Until now, even when you thought of what you wanted, you've pushed it back to deal with what was urgent first. But that wish didn't fade; it kept surfacing now and then. When you heard about someone else's fresh start, a flash of envy may have passed through you.
positions.hold: Right now, you're noticing the gap between what you want to do and what you have to do. If this keeps up, it's easy to write this discomfort off as tiredness and miss your heart's signals. Even after resting on the weekend, as Monday nears you find yourself asking whether things are okay as they are.
positions.step: From here, focus on thinking, one by one, about what you hold dear. Then your everyday choices naturally gather toward where you want to go. As you choose less by other people's standards, you'll have fewer regrets at the end of the day.

reversed.core: You're still hesitating to answer your heart's call.

positions.now: Until now, you've kept checking yourself, saying that to start fresh you have to be properly prepared. That thoroughness prevented mistakes, but the moment to move kept slipping by. You may have bought supplies or a course and left them unopened.
positions.hold: Right now, looking back over whether your past choices were right is scattering your view of what's ahead. If this keeps up, it's easy for the worry to deepen and your courage to shrink. The thought of wanting to change and the thought of leaving things as they are take turns, and the day gets used up.
positions.step: From here, focus on whatever draws you even a little right now, rather than perfect preparation. Then a blurry wish takes the shape of a plan worth trying. When a thing you started turns out more fun than you expected, you naturally get curious about the next step.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that even a blurry call gets clearer bit by bit when you write it down in one line.

cards.about_when: This card shows the times when a question that's been on your mind for a long time comes up again.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of Judgement in traditional tarot, meaning awakening, a calling, and looking back to make a fresh start. At Ssol Tarot House, we read it as answering the call deep in your heart.
asks: Does the question “What do I really want?” keep coming up lately?
Are you hesitating to try new things because of regret over past choices?

now: When the question “What do I really want?” comes up again, it's a sign your heart wants to check whether your current life fits you. Whether it's work, study or relationships, you may go through your days as usual and more and more often catch yourself thinking, “Is this really what I hoped for?” It may feel confusing, but that often happens at the threshold of growth.

Do you remember when that question first came up? Sort out what's changed between then and now and what's stayed the same. Write it briefly, like “Back then I vaguely wanted change; now I can see a bit of what I want to change.” The longer a feeling stays with you, the more likely it's pointing to what matters to you.
hold: When regret lingers as you look back on past choices, you hesitate before new ones for fear of getting it wrong again. The stricter the score you've given yourself, the scarier answering the call can feel. If, when you think of what you want to do, a voice saying “Last time you tried this, it fizzled out” comes first, your past judgment may be holding back your steps now.

Back then, you may have done your best with what you knew at the time. Write down one thing you learned from a past choice. One line is enough, like “When I rush, I lose track of my own heart” or “There's a pace that fits me.” When regret turns into learning, that experience becomes strength for your next choice.
step: Answering the call doesn't have to be a big resolution that changes your life all at once. Turning ever so slightly toward where your heart is drawn is enough for the answer to begin. Finding and reading one article in a field you've been curious about, or setting aside just 30 minutes a week to try what draws you, is also an answer.

Write the direction your heart is calling you toward in one sentence, and pick one action you can take in that direction this week. If you wrote “I want to live making things with my hands,” spending about an hour this weekend making a small thing yourself is enough. Just as a humpback whale rises from the deep, a small action brings a long-held wish up to the surface.

now: If the feeling that you need to change is blurry, it may be because the answer is still ripening. If part of your mind keeps glancing elsewhere even as you walk the same road every day, a wish that hasn't been named yet may be growing. Staying with that feeling without rushing is one way of answering the call too.
hold: High standards come from wanting to do well, but they can also keep you putting off the start. Today, lower your bar by just one notch and give yourself points for “trying.” For example, “a 10-minute walk today” instead of “an hour of exercise every day,” or “read one page” instead of “finish a whole book.”
step: When you write the direction your heart is drawn to in one line, a blurry call gets clearer bit by bit. A short sentence like “I want to live a little more slowly” is fine; write it in your phone's notes or on the first page of a notebook. Reread that line a few days later and check whether it still draws you.

cards.name: The Whole Sea
cards.core: The whole journey you've walked to get here is one sea.

positions.now: Until now, you've kept working toward your goal one step at a time without rest, doing your part. Looking back, even the hard moments all went into making who you are now. Even as important work wrapped up, you may have stayed busy with cleanup and getting ready for what's next rather than resting.
positions.hold: Right now, the end is near, but your mind is already on the next task. If this keeps up, it's easy to not fully credit what you worked hard to finish and be left with only emptiness. Even when someone close says “good work,” you change the subject and say it was nothing.
positions.step: From here, focus on thanking the people who've been with you this far, and yourself. Then you'll have the strength to close this chapter well and open a new one. An experience wrapped up this way stays with you as solid ground when you start the next thing.

reversed.core: You've almost gone the whole way around, but the wrap-up is still left.

positions.now: Until now, every time you saw a part you weren't happy with, you've gone back to fix it, so you couldn't let the work go. That care raised the quality, but the number of things you actually finished barely grew. You may have felt bad when the day you handed results to the people you work with kept getting pushed back.
positions.hold: Right now, it's oddly hard to take your hands off work that's almost done. If this keeps up, it's easy for that task staying open in your head to scatter your focus on other things too. As you keep fixing small parts and saving again, a lot of time slips by.
positions.step: From here, focus on setting in advance the standard at which you'll say “this is good enough.” Then you can wrap up and lightly move on even if a few regrets remain. As your finished work grows, you can use the responses you get to shape your next piece faster.

reversed.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that a good-enough finish, more than a perfect ending, lightly opens your next journey.

asks_pos.now: Until now, haven't you held on to nearly finished work without ending it, telling yourself it just needs a little more polishing?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you carrying nearly finished work around in a corner of your mind like a burden?
asks_pos.step: From here, which would you rather choose: finishing perfectly with no regrets, or tying it off at about where it is now?

key_rx.title: Set a one-line finish line
key_rx.how: For your last task, write one line saying “it's done when it reaches here,” and meet only that standard.
key_rx.why: When you focus on done over perfect, you can tie it off even with a few regrets and have room to move on.

today.title: One line: “it's done when…”
today.how: For your last task, write in your notebook one line on the standard at which you'll call it done.
today.why: Writing down your finish line ahead of time makes the last step feel less heavy.

week.title: Stop at the standard you set
week.how: This week, work on your last task only up to the finish line you wrote, then stop and write the date you finished in your notebook.
week.why: Once you've had the experience of stopping at your standard, you can move on even with a few regrets.

direct.slow_short: the pressure to make the ending perfect

slow_rx.title: Move regrets to a “next time” list
slow_rx.how: When a part you want to perfect comes to mind, move it to a “things I can do next time” list, and let it go as it is this time.
slow_rx.why: The pressure to make the ending perfect keeps unfinished work on your mind; moving the regrets to a list lightens your heart.

three.title: Gather your regrets in one place
three.how: Write down every regret about your last task, move them to a “things I can do next time” list, and mark this task as done.
three.why: Gathering your regrets in one place keeps unfinished work from taking up a corner of your mind, so rest feels refreshing.

signs: Even with a few regrets, you wrap up the work with “this is good enough.”
You fix and refix less, and you hit the submit button sooner.
On the evening you finish, the fact that you finished comes to mind before what you didn't get to.
reversed.tendency: Wanting to do better, you often keep polishing the finish and putting it off. You're thorough and your work is high quality, but when a worry hits, unfinished work stays on your mind and rest easily doesn't feel refreshing.

basic.desc: The Whole Sea is a card of a journey's completion and integration. It means all the time you've walked so far comes together into one meaning. When you wrap up a project or a chapter of life, it tells you to celebrate how far you've come before moving straight on to the next thing.
basic.overview: Like the sea friends all gathering to finish a full circle, this is a card of completion, of wrapping up one journey. It says that recognizing the road that brought you here, before moving on, is part of wrapping up.

asks_pos.now: Until now, even with hard moments, haven't you walked one chapter all the way to the end without stopping?
asks_pos.hold: Right now, are you moving on to the next goal as soon as you finish one, without giving yourself credit for the work you put in?
asks_pos.step: From here, which would you rather choose: heading straight to the next goal, or looking back on the road that brought you here before going on?

frag.now: a full circle filled in step by step
frag.hold: a wrap-up with no time to look back
frag.step: looking back on the journey you've made

practices.title: Journey map
practices.how: Write down five important moments from the past year in the order they happened.
practices.why: Seeing the road you've traveled at a glance shows you the growth you missed while chasing the next goal.

practices.title: Thank-you list
practices.how: Write down the people you were grateful for on this journey and why.
practices.why: Thinking of the people who were with you leaves a warm sense that the journey wasn't a fight you faced alone.

practices.title: A small celebration
practices.how: Give yourself, for coming full circle, a small gift or time doing what you love.
practices.why: Celebrating yourself for finishing a full circle fills up your strength to start the next journey.

cards.closing: The one thing these three cards say together is that the whole journey you've walked so far is already meaningful enough.
cards.about: This card shows the times when a chapter of life comes to a close. It sits in the place of The World in traditional tarot, meaning completion, integration and a journey that's come full circle. At Ssol Tarot House, we read it as recognizing the whole journey you've made.
cards.about_when: This card shows the times when a chapter of life comes to a close.
cards.about_origin: It sits in the place of The World in traditional tarot, meaning completion, integration and a journey that's come full circle. At Ssol Tarot House, we read it as recognizing the whole journey you've made.
asks: As you finish up a chapter, is chasing the next goal keeping you from giving yourself credit?
Are you making light of the time you worked so hard through, calling it “no big deal”?

now: When a chapter closes, an odd emptiness can come along with the pride. After finishing work you'd done for a long time or wrapping up a stretch of life, there may be evenings when you feel relieved yet suddenly notice an empty space. That means you poured that much of your heart into that time, and it's proof the journey meant a lot to you.

What have you gained, and what has changed, as you went through this chapter? It doesn't have to be grand. Even a small change, like “I notice my own feelings a little faster than before,” is well worth writing down. If you sum up the road you've traveled in one sentence, you can see more clearly the you who made it this far.
hold: Moving straight on to the next goal is a familiar habit for hardworking people. But if you move on without recognizing the journey you've made, it's easy to always feel it's not enough, no matter how much you get done. If you're writing the next task on your to-do list the moment you finish a big one, you may need a moment to stop and cross off what you just finished.

Among the things you've accomplished, is there one you never fully celebrated? Think of it and tell yourself “you worked hard.” It's also nice to have a small celebration of your own for about 10 minutes, with your favorite drink in front of you. A journey that's been recognized becomes solid ground for starting the next one.
step: The time of closing a full circle is both an ending and the start of the next round. Recalling the people and experiences you're grateful for ties the road behind you together firmly and lightly opens the road ahead. Looking through photos you took or notes you wrote during this chapter and recalling what gave you strength each time is a good way to wrap up too.

Write down three people and moments you were grateful for on this journey. Spend 10 minutes before bed writing a name or a scene on each line of a notebook, adding a short note on why you were grateful. If a face you're thankful for comes to mind, it's nice to say thank you to them in your heart too. Just as the sea friends gather in a circle, what you shared can light up the next sea.

now: The last step feels especially heavy because you poured so much of your heart into this journey. If only the final wrap-up is left but you keep reaching for other tasks first, it may mean finishing takes up that much space in your heart. Now that the end is in sight, first give credit to the you who made it this far.
hold: Wanting to finish perfectly is a way of treasuring the journey. But waiting for perfect easily keeps pushing the finish back, so let yourself accept that a “good enough ending” is an ending too. Whether it's an assignment or tidying your room, set a “this is good enough” line in advance, and when you reach it, mark it done.
step: Tying off one remaining task closes one circle and opens the next. For example, pick one thing you can finish within 30 minutes, like tidying up you've long put off or a final check, and get it done today. After you finish, take a moment to pause and look back on the journey so far.

image.scene_prompt: All Ssol sea characters together forming a gentle circle around a calm sea with a wreath of kelp and coral, wholeness and completion.

cards.caution: Hard to draw in one pass with AI. Make only the background and circular frame with AI; place the character PNGs by hand in a design tool.

key_rx.title: Look back on your journey on one page
key_rx.how: On one notebook page, write in time order what you accomplished on this round and where you got help.
key_rx.why: When you focus on looking back at your journey and the people who helped you, you tie off this round well and meet the next start lightly.

today.title: Write three things you accomplished
today.how: Write in your notebook three things you accomplished on this round.
today.why: Seeing what you accomplished makes a fading sense of achievement clear again.

week.title: Fill in the journey one box a day
week.how: Every day this week, recall one part of the journey you've made and fill in one box in your notebook. Write down the help you got too.
week.why: Filling in the journey a little each day leaves you feeling you wrapped up the round well.

direct.slow_short: the habit of looking at the next goal first

slow_rx.title: Write the next goal down separately
slow_rx.how: When your next goal comes to mind, write it in a “next” box on one side of your notebook, and for that day, look back only on what you accomplished.
slow_rx.why: Looking at the next goal before looking back on what you accomplished blurs your sense of achievement; writing the goal down separately gives you room to look back.

three.title: Make a “next” box and move your goals there
three.how: Move every next goal in your head into the “next” box, then spend 15 minutes looking back only on what you accomplished this round.
three.why: Moving your next goals aside gives you time to look back on what you accomplished, and leaves you with the feeling of having wrapped up.

signs: As you look back on the year, the names of people who helped you come to mind one by one.
Looking over what you've finished, you think, “I've come a long way.”
A new start doesn't feel like a burden; you look forward to it lightly.
cards.tendency: You often see a chapter through to the end, steadily doing your part. You keep getting things done, but when a worry hits, the next goal comes into view first and you may have no room to look back on what you accomplished.

today_practices.note: v4.2 (2026-10-23 CSO): the ‘Today’ practice on page 9 (formerly page 10) isn't written by AI; it's picked from this DB by The Key Ahead card (number_up/rev). ‘{conclusion}’ is the name of the chosen option for decision-type worries; otherwise the code replaces it with ‘resolving this worry’.

0_up.title: Set a 5-minute timer and start
0_up.how: Set a timer for 5 minutes and start one thing you can do related to what you're worried about. When the alarm goes off, you can stop.
0_up.why: Because you'll see for yourself that you can start even when you don't feel ready.

0_rev.title: Shrink the first step to 2 minutes
0_rev.how: Write down the first step toward ‘{conclusion}’, shrunk small enough to finish in 2 minutes, and do just that one thing now.
0_rev.why: Because when the bar for starting is lower, the energy that's been hesitating moves more easily.

1_up.title: List three resources you can use
1_up.how: Pick one each of the time, people, and experience you can use for this worry, and write them in your notes.
1_up.why: Because when you can see what you already have, the feeling of not having enough gets smaller.

1_rev.title: Keep just one task for today
1_rev.how: Of today's tasks related to this worry, keep only the most important one, and write down that the rest move to tomorrow.
1_rev.why: Because your energy narrows to one place, and what was scattered comes together.

2_up.title: Write a feeling word for each option
2_up.how: Think of each option or direction in this worry one at a time, and write the feeling each one gives you in one word. You don't have to pick an answer.
2_up.why: Because you can check your own sense of things before rushing to an answer.

2_rev.title: Turn off notifications and stay still for 5 minutes
2_rev.how: Turn off all phone notifications and sit still for 5 minutes without looking at the screen.
2_rev.why: Because with less outside noise, you can hear your own thoughts and feelings more clearly.

3_up.title: Tell yourself “good job” for what you did today
3_up.how: Pick one thing you got done today and say ‘good job’ to yourself out loud.
3_up.why: Because when you give yourself the credit you'd give others, the way you treat yourself softens.

3_rev.title: Recall help you received and feel thankful
3_rev.how: Think of one small bit of help someone gave you recently, and write only your thanks in your notes, leaving out any guilt.
3_rev.why: Because when receiving feels okay, you find the strength to refill what's been running empty.

4_up.title: Split things into what you can change
4_up.how: Write down three things that worry you in this situation, sorted into two columns: ‘can change’ and ‘can't change.’
4_up.why: Because once you know where to put your energy, you have a standard to hold on to even while you're shaken.

4_rev.title: Circle what you can give up
4_rev.how: Write down the things you're determined to protect right now, and circle one you could give up just this once.
4_rev.why: Because once you separate what to keep from what you can let go of, the pressure that's been boxing you in loosens.

5_up.title: Find and read a helpful passage
5_up.how: Find and read a passage from a trustworthy article or book related to this worry, and underline a sentence that speaks to you.
5_up.why: Because borrowing the experience of someone who's been there takes away some of the burden of finding the answer alone.

5_rev.title: Name someone to ask for help
5_rev.how: Choose one person you could open up to about this worry, write down their name, and set a time to contact them today.
5_rev.why: Because once you know exactly who to ask for help, your hesitation shrinks by a step.

6_up.title: Pick one standard you want to keep
6_up.how: Pick one standard you don't want to give up in this worry and write it as a sentence: ‘What matters to me is ~.’
6_up.why: Because once your standard is clear in one sentence, it's easier to compare which choice feels like you.

6_rev.title: Write down only what you want
6_rev.how: Leaving out the other person's reaction and what people around you think, write only what you want in this worry in one sentence.
6_rev.why: Because once your wish is separate from other people's reactions, your mixed feelings get sorted out.

7_up.title: Keep one thing that's going well going
7_up.how: Find and write down one thing connected to this worry that's going smoothly lately, and decide on one way to keep it going.
7_up.why: Because when you notice what's going well, you can see a way forward that takes less effort.

7_rev.title: Pause and write where you want to be
7_rev.how: Pause what you're doing and write in one sentence where you want to be once this worry is resolved.
7_rev.why: Because when where you want to go is clear again, the energy that's been going in circles gathers in one direction.

8_up.title: Name the uncomfortable feeling
8_up.how: Decide whether the uncomfortable feeling you have right now is closest to anxiety, sadness, or anger, and write down its name.
8_up.why: Because naming a feeling lets you step back from it without struggling to make it go away.

8_rev.title: Score how heavy it feels
8_rev.how: Rate how heavy this worry feels from 0 to 10, and write down one thing you'd need for the score to drop by 2 points.
8_rev.why: Because when the weight you're stuck under becomes a number, it's easier to find the part you can lighten.

9_up.title: Set an alarm for time to think alone
9_up.how: Choose 20 minutes today or tomorrow to look back on this worry by yourself, and set it as a phone alarm or calendar event.
9_up.why: Because when you have set time to think, the worry doesn't circle in your head all day.

9_rev.title: Send one check-in message
9_rev.how: Send a short check-in, like ‘How are you doing?’, to one person you haven't talked to lately. You don't have to bring up your worry.
9_rev.why: Because when a connection that was closing off opens up even a little, you feel less alone.

10_up.title: Find what you can decide today
10_up.how: Find and write down three things you can decide yourself within today. Small things, like what to have for dinner, count too.
10_up.why: Because when you can see the choices in your hands, you feel less swept along.

10_rev.title: Drop your shoulders and breathe out slowly
10_rev.how: Notice the tension in your shoulders and jaw, then breathe in through your nose and out slowly through your mouth, ten times.
10_rev.why: Because when your body's tension eases, the strength you've been using to fight the changed situation lets go too.

11_up.title: Write facts and interpretations separately
11_up.how: Write what actually happened in this worry on one line, and your interpretation of it on another.
11_up.why: Because when facts and interpretations are separate, it's easier to judge yourself more fairly.

11_rev.title: Rewrite it as what you'd tell a friend
11_rev.how: Think of one thing you blame yourself for in this worry, and rewrite it as what you'd say to a friend who went through the same thing.
11_rev.why: Because applying the standard you use for others to yourself brings a judgment tilted toward self-blame back into balance.

12_up.title: Drink a glass of water and walk for 5 minutes
12_up.how: Put down what you're doing, drink a glass of water, and walk slowly for 5 minutes. Set this worry aside for a while.
12_up.why: Because stepping away for a moment lets you see the same worry from a different angle.

12_rev.title: Set an end to your break
12_rev.how: Make the next 10 minutes a break, set a timer, and write down one thing to do when it ends.
12_rev.why: Because when rest has an end, the pause feels like recharging rather than being stuck.

13_up.title: Sort out what no longer fits
13_up.how: Write down, separately, one thing in this worry that no longer fits you and one thing you want to keep.
13_up.why: Because once what to let go of and what to keep are separate, you can see the regret and the relief apart.

13_rev.title: Move one thing you look at often to an archive
13_rev.how: Take one photo, note, or notification related to this worry that you keep opening, and move it to an archive instead of deleting it.
13_rev.why: Because just putting some distance there, without throwing it away completely, lets you start practicing letting go without pressure.

14_up.title: Decide how to split your time today
14_up.how: Decide how to split your time today between the two things pulling at you in this worry, like ‘60/40,’ and write it down.
14_up.why: Because you can confirm there's a way to share your time without giving one up.

14_rev.title: Schedule 15 minutes for the side you've neglected
14_rev.how: Decide which side of this worry you usually neglect, and put 15 minutes for one task on that side into today's or tomorrow's schedule.
14_rev.why: Because when the neglected side gets its time, the tilted balance finds its place again.

15_up.title: Find what you were protecting when you got defensive
15_up.how: Think of one moment today when you got defensive, and write down what you were trying to protect then.
15_up.why: Because when you know the real concern behind the defensiveness, you can see ways to protect yourself without putting up your spikes.

15_rev.title: Notice what shakes you less than before
15_rev.how: Think about whether there's anything that used to shake you badly but shakes you less these days, and write one down.
15_rev.why: Because seeing how you've changed gives you a reason to let your guard down further.

16_up.title: Find two things still standing
16_up.how: Among the things this worry has shaken, find and write down two that are still standing.
16_up.why: Because you'll see that you can start from what's left instead of from scratch.

16_rev.title: Cross off one thing you can skip today
16_rev.how: Of the things you're holding on to just to get through today, choose one that can wait a day and cross it off your list.
16_rev.why: Because with one less load to carry, the strength you've been using to keep from falling apart can go toward recovery.

17_up.title: Say one way you're better than yesterday
17_up.how: Find one way your body or mind is even a little better than yesterday, and say it out loud.
17_up.why: Because noticing small changes lets you see that recovery is underway.

17_rev.title: Log your condition score
17_rev.how: Rate how your body and mind feel right now, each from 1 to 10, and write it in your notes with the date.
17_rev.why: Because as the scores add up, you can see which way things are going even when recovery is slow.

18_up.title: Take one step you can take now
18_up.how: Pick one of the first steps toward ‘{conclusion}’ that you can do right now, and do it for just 5 minutes.
18_up.why: Because you'll see that you can take a step even when you can't see the whole picture.

18_rev.title: Write three things that are already clear
18_rev.how: Pick three things in this worry that have already become clear or that you've newly learned, and write them in your notes.
18_rev.why: Because once what's certain and what's unknown are separate, you can focus only on the questions that remain.

19_up.title: Relive a good moment for 1 minute
19_up.how: Think of one good moment from today and spend 1 minute slowly reliving the scene and how you felt.
19_up.why: Because when you fully take in a good moment, the joy stays in your body and the day feels lighter.

19_rev.title: Do one small pleasure right now
19_rev.how: Do one pleasure you can fit into a few minutes right now, like listening to a favorite song or having a cup of warm tea.
19_rev.why: Because even when joy feels hidden, actually doing a small pleasure shifts your mood.

20_up.title: Set a date for what's long drawn you
20_up.how: Think of one thing you've been drawn to for a long time, and set a day and time this week to try it for 30 minutes.
20_up.why: Because once there's a date, a wish that only lived in your head becomes a real plan.

20_rev.title: Sort out what's in the way of what draws you
20_rev.how: Think of one thing you're drawn to these days, write two reasons that keep you from going for it, then mark the ones that are facts.
20_rev.why: Because sorting the reasons into facts and worries lets you see exactly how big your hesitation is.

21_up.title: List three things you've done and pick one
21_up.how: Write down three things you've accomplished to get this far, and circle the one you're proudest of.
21_up.why: Because seeing what you've done brings your fading sense of accomplishment back into focus.

21_rev.title: Set one finish line
21_rev.how: Set and write down one standard for ‘if I get this far, it's done’ in this worry, and check what's left to do.
21_rev.why: Because once you know where it ends, the last step feels less heavy.
